issues.title: Fit xml_etree_parse's legacy gen 0 collections while each value serialises
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Under the legacy collector, the presets page draws xml_etree_parse's gen 0 examined 4% apart from its workers' after #284, with single collections out by 9%. The gap sits in the gen 0 collections while each value serialises its last two parsed trees. The workers' 39th collection examines 10,343 real objects there, the run's 64.

bench_parse keeps its last two parsed trees alive until it returns, through the 1,920 kB of tostring that ends each value. The run's parsed trees each go two slots after they build (ADR 0027), so its collections in that stretch find neither.

Done when

  • The run's legacy gen 0 collections while a value serialises examine within 20% of the workers'.
  • The incremental columns keep their fit from #284: gen 0 examined within 1%, budget within 1%.
  • The other presets' digests stay the same.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Fit async_tree_io_tg's collections over its worker
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
just plot (#256) draws async_tree_io_tg's run apart from its workers under both collectors. The figures are in real objects.

Legacy, gen 0. Each worker's gen 0 collections climb to between 25,600 and 39,388 as each run of the tree ends, at collections 63 to 67, 127 to 131, 191 to 196 and 256 to 260. All 20 workers peak at 39,388. The run's collections hold at 16,000 and never pass 16,080.

Incremental, old collections' work. 86 of the run's 130 old collections do 32,000. The workers' spread from 4,000 to 31,000. Those that do any work average 29,000 in the run and 22,600 in the workers.

The incremental figures come from main after #265, which starts the incremental collector with a young collection (#259).

Done when

  • The run's gen 0 legacy collections climb as each run of the tree ends, and its old collections' work spreads as the workers' does.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Fit connected_components' collections over its worker
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
just plot (#256) draws connected_components' run apart from its workers under both collectors. The figures below are the workers' medians at each collection number, in real objects.

Legacy, gen 0. The run examines 32,000 at each collection from 4 to 46, then 16 from 49 on. The workers examine about 4,500 from 2 to 7, then 27,600 falling to 24,700 from 9 to 62, then 1 to 3.

Legacy, gen 1. The run examines 328,000 to 384,000 at collections 12 to 48, and 16 at 60. The workers examine 163,000 at 12, 300,000 to 323,000 at 24 to 60, and 62,500 at 72.

Incremental, old collections' work. The run does 104,000 at 18, 64,000 and 168,000 at 22 and 24, 64,000 at 30 to 34 and 296,000 at 36, then about 64,000 at each from 46 to 58, then nothing. The workers do 11,000 to 232,000 at 22 to 30, nothing at 32 to 46, and about 50,000 at each from 48 to 74. The run's work budget falls to −232,000.

Incremental, young collections. The run examines 64,000 at each from 15 to 55. The workers examine about 9,000 at 11 to 17, 40,000 to 55,000 at 19 to 29, about 10,000 at 31 to 39, and 50,000 at 41 to 73.

In both, the workers' collections keep busy up to about collection 62 under legacy or 73 under incremental, and the run's stop near 47 and 58. The preset's comment says the load leaves out read_adjlist's churn and ends about 29 MB early.

The incremental figures come from main after #265, which starts the incremental collector with a young collection (#259).

Done when

  • The run's collections keep busy as long as the workers' under both collectors, and its old collections' work follows theirs.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Let a reader edit a collector's class on the playground and run it beside the original
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
A PEP reviewer asks what a change of rule would do to the collector: drop the
early return when the work budget runs out, cap the budget, credit it once
per old collection as the reference branch does, or have a young collection
take two aging spaces. No collector constant expresses any of these. Today
you clone the repo and edit incremental.py, and you cannot send what you
saw.

The playground gets a third view beside the legend and the workload source:
the class of the incremental or the legacy collector, as text the reader
edits.

  • What the reader edits. The whole IncrementalCollector or
    LegacyCollector class. The base Collector, Space, the heap and the
    trigger stay ours, so no edit reaches the trigger.
  • What the widget compares. The edit against the class it started from,
    on the same workload: incremental* beside incremental, or
    legacy* beside legacy. The legend shows which mode is on. The edit
    takes no glossary term.
  • The box. A textarea, as the shape's box has, that opens on the shipped
    class's text. Run or Ctrl+Enter runs it.
  • Faults. An exception or code that never returns behaves as an own
    shape's does (ADR 0014). After each collection the simulator also checks
    that every object alive in the heap sits in exactly one space that
    space_sizes() reports, comparing counts, and stops the run with the
    collection's kind and clock when one does not. Determinism is the reader's
    to keep (ADR 0007), as with an own shape.
  • The link. It carries the whole class text and waits for Run (ADR 0016).
    A diff would stop applying once the shipped class changed. With deflate-raw
    and base64url, incremental.py takes about 3,000 characters and
    legacy.py about 1,700.

The base class becomes something readers' code depends on, so a change to
Collector, Space or the heap can break saved links. An ADR records the
decision when the work starts, and CONTEXT.md's Playground entry gains
the third view.

Done when

  • A reader edits either class on the playground, runs it, and sees it beside
    the original.
  • An edit that leaves an object in no space stops with a message naming the
    collection.
  • A link carries the edit and opens it waiting for Run.
  • The ADR and the glossary entry land with it.
  • just check passes.

issues.title: Fit async_tree_io_tg's gen 1 and gen 2 collections where a tree ends
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Under the legacy collector, the presets page draws async_tree_io_tg's gen 1 and gen 2 collections apart from its workers' where a run of the tree ends. Real objects examined, workers' medians against the run:

Collection kB Workers Run
Gen 1, 132 264,000 37,693 178,368
Gen 2, 133 266,000 30,468 23,776
Gen 1, 193 386,000 199,934 89,024

The run frees each tree at once, 6 MB after it has built, and keeps what the finishing tasks allocate to the run's end (#276). The workers free a tree task by task over about 10 MB, so a gen 1 collection in that stretch finds part of it. At the 132nd the workers' tree has gone and the run still holds the finishing tasks' objects; at the 193rd the workers' tree is still there and the run's has gone. Elsewhere the run's gen 1 collections examine 177,000 against the workers' 183,000 to 187,000.

The gen 2 collection comes between two trees in both. The workers' heap then holds about 6,700 more real objects than the run's.

Done when

  • The run's gen 1 collections where a tree ends examine within 20% of the workers'.
  • Its gen 2 collection examines within 10% of theirs.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Fit xml_etree_parse's work budget over its workers'
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Under the incremental collector, the presets page draws xml_etree_parse's work budget apart from its workers'. Budget before each collection, real objects, workers' medians against the run:

Collections Workers Run
1 to 11 -100,000 -100,000
13 -91,410 -92,130
15 to 23 -76,720 -80,750
45 to 51 -66,400 -78,380 to -77,200

The young collections add less to the budget in the run than in the workers', and the gap grows over the run. The gen 0 running yield agrees until the 25th, 0.0101 against 0.0101, then the run's stays higher: 0.0090 against 0.0064 at the 51st. So the run's young collections find more garbage and fewer survivors than the workers'.

Done when

  • The run's budget stays within 3% of the workers' at each collection.
  • Its gen 0 running yield stays within 10% of theirs.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Fit each preset's start-up collections to its workers'
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Under the legacy collector, the presets page draws each preset's 2nd to 4th collections apart from its workers'. The five presets share one start-up (ADR 0011), so their runs examine 8,016 at the 2nd collection, while the workers' differ by benchmark. Real objects examined, workers' medians against the run:

Collection create_gc_cycles json_loads xml_etree_parse async_tree_io_tg connected_components
1 8,413 / 8,032 8,696 / 8,032 8,747 / 8,032 8,141 / 8,048 8,845 / 8,032
2 6,348 / 8,016 6,095 / 8,016 5,855 / 8,016 6,352 / 8,032 5,658 / 8,016
3 4,706 / 2,512 9,199 / 3,472 5,294 / 8,064 4,743 / 5,664
4 1,029 / 2,688 6,901 / 3,552 4,544 / 4,592

Every worker examines about 2,000 fewer than the run at the 2nd collection. From the 3rd on, each benchmark's own imports and set-up take over, which start-up leaves to each preset's set-up structure.

Done when

  • Each preset's 2nd collection examines within 5% of its workers'.
  • The 3rd and 4th collections follow the workers' where a preset's set-up covers them.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Tell apart the presets page's gaps below one simulated object
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The presets page draws two charts whose run differs from the workers' by a handful of real objects. Their scales are tiny, so they look as far off as the real gaps.

  • async_tree_io_tg, legacy, gen 1 freed and running yield. The workers' first gen 1 collection, the 12th, frees 34 real objects, so their running yield starts at 0.00023 and falls to 0.00001. The run's frees none, and its yield stays 0.
  • json_loads, legacy, gen 0 examined. From the 4th collection on, the run examines 16 real objects each, and the workers 2 to 6. A simulated object stands for 16 real ones (ADR 0002), so the run can't examine fewer than 16 without examining none. At the 3rd the workers free 3 and the run none.

Either the page shows that these gaps fall below what one simulated object can draw, or the presets close them.

Done when

  • A reader of the presets page can tell these two gaps from the ones that matter, or the run matches the workers within one simulated object.
  • just check passes.

issues.title: Fit xml_etree_parse's gen 0 legacy collections over its worker
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Under the legacy collector, just plot (#256) draws xml_etree_parse's gen 0 collections apart from its workers'. The figures are the workers' medians at each collection number, in real objects.

  • The workers examine 15,480 at nearly every gen 0 collection. They dip to 1,000 to 5,200 at the gen 0 collections after each gen 1 one, at 4, 15 and 16, 27 and 28, and 39 and 40.
  • The run examines 12,700 at collection 4 and falls by 240 a collection to 10,320, where it stays. It jumps to about 15,000 at 20, 28, 40 and 47, and falls again.

The averages agree, so just compare hides the drift.

Done when

  • The run's gen 0 collections hold level where the workers' do and dip where theirs dip.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Start xml_etree_parse's automatic collections as late as its workers'
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The allocation clock (#267) shows xml_etree_parse's automatic collections starting 2,162 kB apart in its workers, under both collectors, where every other benchmark's start 2,000 kB apart, threshold0. The preset starts its 51 collections 2,000 kB apart, so its last starts at 102,000 kB and its workers' at 108,086.

A guess at the cause: the branch schedules a collection when the budget runs out and runs it at the interpreter's next eval breaker check, which a parse in C reaches only once it returns. The simulator runs a collection on the kB the budget runs out.

Matching the workers' count and their length at once takes collections that come late. A preset that keeps them 2,000 kB apart matches one and misses the other by 6%.

#262 covers what the gen 0 collections examine under the legacy collector.

Done when

  • The preset's first and last automatic collections start within 2% of the workers' kB, and it makes their 51.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Fit create_gc_cycles' start and loops on the allocation clock
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The allocation clock (#267) shows create_gc_cycles' preset running apart from its workers. The workers' medians, in kB allocated:

Workers Preset
The first gc.collect() 5,484 incremental, 5,473 legacy 4,625
A loop's build, between its two calls 180.5 132
The last collection before shutdown 97,838 incremental, 51,576 legacy 72,208

_LOOP counts a loop's 2,100 Node objects as 131 simulated ones and the list as one, at 64 B a real object (ADR 0002). The workers' loops allocate about 88 B a node.

The 860 kB before the first call come after the shared start-up's 4,624 kB. The other presets make no call there, so their records cannot show where start-up ends.

The legacy workers ran 256 loops to the incremental ones' 512, as pyperf calibrated them. The preset follows the incremental workers (ADR 0011).

Done when

  • The preset's first and last gc.collect() start within 1% of the incremental workers' kB.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Put the workers' collections on the allocation clock
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
gcmon now carries allocated on each record (sergey-miryanov/gcmon#245). The reference branch counts it from b8d8db86a4c on: the bytes _PyObject_GC_Link has added up since the interpreter started, read as each collection starts. Those are the allocations whose budget triggers a collection, so bytes / 1,024 puts a worker's collections on the simulator's clock, in threshold0's kB. The figure is a running total, so a record gcmon loses moves no later one.

ADR 0011 measures a worker's length by its automatic collections, threshold0 kB each, and takes the code's counts where gc.collect() leaves none to count. These numbers rest on that:

  • Start-up's 4,624 kB, _START_UP.length.
  • create_gc_cycles' loop of 132 kB, _LOOP. Its gc.collect() calls reset the budget, so no automatic collection marks it.
  • connected_components' load, which its comment says ends about 29 MB early because it leaves out read_adjlist's churn.

The presets page (#256, #264) draws a run and its workers against the collection's number, so a collection that comes early or late on the clock lines up with the wrong one. #261 and #263 compare work budgets that way.

The CSVs in data/ come from traces without the field. A pyperformance run on the new build is under way.

Done when

  • data/pp-inc.csv and data/pp-legacy.csv come from the new traces, with their allocated column.
  • tools/benchmarks.py reads each collection's allocated in kB, and a CSV without the column still loads.
  • The presets page draws the workers and the run against kB allocated.
  • Start-up's length, create_gc_cycles' loop and each preset's run length follow the workers' allocated, or an issue of its own fits each one that does not. ADR 0011 says where the lengths come from.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Spread start-up's garbage over a worker's first two legacy collections
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Under the legacy collector, each preset's first collection frees 208 real objects, all of start-up's garbage, and the second frees none. The workers spread theirs over the first two. Their medians at each collection, from just plot (#256):

Benchmark 1st 2nd 3rd
create_gc_cycles, json_loads 129 84 3
xml_etree_parse 129 84 36
async_tree_io_tg 129 48 36
connected_components 91 44 11

The totals agree: _START_UP.garbage takes the 216 that 129, 84 and 3 make. So just compare's averages hide the split, and a worker's first collection frees 60% more in the run than in its benchmark.

Done when

  • Each preset's first two legacy collections free about what its workers' do.
  • just check passes, the yield test included.

issues.title: Decide which collection the incremental collector runs first
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Under the incremental collector, every preset's run makes an old collection first and alternates from there. Every worker in data/pp-inc.csv makes a young one first. just plot (#256) draws the two out of step in all five presets: the run's old collections fall on odd numbers, the workers' on even ones.

IncrementalCollector.__init__ sets young_next = False. ADR 0003 has the simulator follow the PEP's pseudocode where it and the branch differ, so the pseudocode's first collection settles this. If the pseudocode starts with an old collection, an ADR says why the simulator keeps it against the branch.

Changing the order moves every pinned digest (ADR 0007) and every incremental preset's yields.

Done when

  • The simulator starts with the collection the pseudocode starts with, or an ADR records why it differs from the branch.
  • just check passes.

issues.title: Plot a preset's collections over its benchmark's workers
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
just compare prints each preset's collections beside its benchmark's as
averages, so a preset can match its benchmark's mean and still drift from it
over the run, with a start-up too large or a loop that frees too late. A plot
of both over the worker shows that at a glance.

A dev-only page draws them. It ships nowhere: nothing goes into site/ or
sim.zip.

  • Series, per collection. Examined and freed, a panel per generation, and
    the running yield. On old collections, work too: increment_size on the
    branch, which sums what the collection marked and examined, and marked + survived + freed in the simulator. For the incremental collector, the work
    budget at each collection's start: old_work on the branch, read before the
    collection, and the record before's budget in the simulator. The two
    budgets differ by design (ADR 0003), and the panel says so. Everything in
    real objects, through the run's Constants.
  • x-axis. The collection's number in its worker. The trace has no
    allocation clock, and counting automatic collections stacks
    create_gc_cycles' gc.collect() calls on a few points.
  • Workers. All 20 of a benchmark's workers as thin, faint lines, and the
    preset's run as one bold line.
  • Page. It lives under tools/, since assemble_site.py deploys every
    page in site/, and draws with Observable Plot and theme.css. just plot
    writes one git-ignored JSON file, the real rows through
    tools/benchmarks.py and the presets' records through run() under both
    collectors, as compare_presets.py reads them, then serves the page. The
    page runs no Pyodide.

sergey-miryanov/gcmon#242 asks for the trigger's remaining budget with each
record. Once a fresh trace carries it, the page can take the allocation clock
as a second x-axis, and ADR 0011 can read create_gc_cycles' loop length from
the records.

Done when

  • just plot draws each of the five presets under each collector against its
    benchmark's workers, with the series above.
  • just check passes.

issues.title: Publish the presets' plot on the site
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
#256 kept the presets' plot off the site. The plot found real drift between the presets and their benchmarks (#259 to #263), and a reader checking a preset against its benchmark needs it as much as whoever fits one. So the site serves it.

  • Page. The plot moves from tools/ into site/ as presets.html, beside the guide and the playground, and each page's nav links it. A short intro says what it draws: a preset's run against its benchmark's 20 workers, a collection at a time.
  • Data. just site runs the presets under both collectors and writes plot.json into the commit's folder (ADR 0019), so a deploy and each pull request's preview draw the presets as that commit runs them. The file takes a column per series, which shrinks it.
  • Record. An ADR says why just site, which only copied and zipped, now runs the presets, and what that costs a build.

Done when

  • The deployed site's nav links the page, and it draws each of the five presets under each collector against its benchmark's workers.
  • just check passes.

issues.title: Release v0.2.0
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
pyproject.toml has said version = "0.1.0" since #11, and v0.1.0 matched it by chance. Since v0.1.0, four milestones have closed: First presets, Playground, Guide and Review fixes.

Done when

  • pyproject.toml says version = "0.2.0".
  • The merge commit carries an annotated tag v0.2.0, and a GitHub release gives its notes by milestone, as v0.1.0's does.

issues.title: Check the prose the Review fixes milestone wrote
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Before Review fixes closes, check the prose its pull requests wrote: the lines that #244 to #250 added, and their descriptions.

The prose: the ADR and CONTEXT.md lines, the comments and docstrings in src/, site/, tests/ and tools/, and the messages a reader sees. Check each against the /stop-slop rules, CONTEXT.md's terms and Avoid words, and the code as it stands.

Done when

  • The prose passes all three checks, just check passes, and nothing but prose has changed.

issues.title: Escape the request's values in the Python source
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
toSource in site/source.js writes the request's values into the Python source as they stand. A structure's root, cycle_share, long_share and long_lived_ratio go between quotes unescaped, and py() turns any string it gets into source with String(value). A link can put code in any of these.

holdsCode in site/link.js looks only for own shapes, so that link shows no held note. It runs at once as JSON and fails on the wrong type. If you then switch to "as Python" and press Run, the code runs in the page's worker, which can fetch from the site's origin and post to the page. The hold exists to stop that.

Done when

  • toSource writes each string as a Python string literal and refuses a value of the wrong type, or holdsCode holds any request whose values are not the types the request takes.
  • A test gives each of those fields a value with code in it and shows the code cannot run without a hold.

issues.title: Clear the charts when a run makes no records
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
In site/gc-widget.js, the run's listener swaps in the new records and figures on the first records message. A run shorter than threshold0, with no full collections and shutdown off, makes no records: the worker sends controls and then done, and nothing between.

fresh stays true, so the charts and figures keep the previous request's run while the legend and controls show the new request. done returns early because the figures are missing.

Done when

  • A run with no records clears the charts and figures and shows that the run made no collections.
  • A Playwright check covers it.

issues.title: Keep the request's own value inside a slider's range
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
_ranged in src/pep848_sim/widget/controls.py rounds the max down to the step. The comments on threshold0, a structure's size and its rebuild interval promise room for the request's own value, but the rounding can put the max below it.

Take a structure of size 12,345, never rebuilt, in a shorter run. Its high end is 12,345 and its step 100, so the max comes out at 12,300. The browser clamps the slider to 12,300 while the output reads 12,345, and when you release the slider the value changes to 12,300.

Done when

  • Each ranged control's range holds the request's value.
  • A test builds each ranged control on a value off its step.

issues.title: Take a collection's work and the real-object ratio from the simulator
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Two places work out again what the simulator already defines.

  • tools/compare_presets.py sets REAL_PER_SIMULATED = 16, the ratio Constants derives from real_object_size. Under other constants, its "examined each" and "yield" columns would still convert at 16 and disagree with the simulator.
  • Figures.add in src/pep848_sim/widget/figures.py sums marked + survived + freed, which CollectionCounts.work defines. Record has no work, so if the definition changed, the widget's peak work and work per MB would keep the old sum.

Done when

  • compare_presets converts through the run's Constants.
  • Record gives its work by the same definition as CollectionCounts, and Figures.add uses it.
  • just check passes.

issues.title: Give work per MB no value until the run has allocated
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Figures.work_per_mb in src/pep848_sim/widget/figures.py divides by allocated. A structure with full_collections=True calls gc.collect() at clock 0, before the workload allocates anything, and with every at 1 that record arrives as a part on its own. row() raises ZeroDivisionError, and the worker reports "division by zero" for the whole run.

binOf in site/panels.js already allows for a gc.collect() at clock 0.

Done when

  • work_per_mb is None until the run has allocated, as yield_ is until the run has examined an object, and the page shows it as it shows a yield of None.
  • A test runs a request whose first record comes at clock 0.

issues.title: Refuse an every below 1
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
run() in src/pep848_sim/run.py yields the records every at a time and never checks every. With 0 or less, len(records) - sent >= every holds for good, and run() yields empty parts without end.

request.parse takes any every, and link.decode checks only the top-level keys, so a link can carry one. The worker then posts empty records, never sends done, and keeps both runs going until you stop them.

Done when

  • run() raises ValueError on an every below 1, and parse refuses the request with a message the page shows.
  • Tests cover both.

issues.title: Have the incremental collector clamp a threshold1 below 1 to 1
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
IncrementalCollector.__init__ makes -(-threshold1 // 2) aging spaces, which is none for a threshold1 below 1. The first young collection then fails on self.aging.pop() with IndexError.

Only request.parse in the widget guards against it. run(), the tools and the tests can still build the collector with CollectorSettings(threshold1=0).

The reference branch clamps instead of refusing: for the incremental collector, gc_set_threshold_impl raises a threshold1 of 0 or less to 1 (Modules/gcmodule.c:174), and the legacy collector keeps the value as given. The simulator should do the same. The clamp leaves the PEP's pseudocode as it stands (ADR 0003).

Done when

  • IncrementalCollector runs a threshold1 below 1 as 1, and the legacy collector still takes 0.
  • parse drops its own check, and a request with a threshold1 of 0 runs under both collectors.
  • The threshold1 slider in src/pep848_sim/widget/controls.py starts at 0, since its floor of 1 only followed the request's refusal.
  • A test covers it.

issues.title: Check the prose the Guide milestone wrote
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Before Guide closes, check the prose its pull requests wrote: the lines in main that one of its 24 merged pull requests, #152 to #234, changed last, and all of site/guide.json, the steps' text and notes. The First presets pass, #124, left these lines to this one.

The prose: the ADRs and CONTEXT.md, the README and CONTRIBUTING.md, the site's text and comments, and the docstrings and comments in src/, tests/ and tools/. Check each against the /stop-slop rules, CONTEXT.md's terms and Avoid words, and the code as it stands, with every number a step quotes run again. The pseudocode's comments stay verbatim (ADR 0003), as does the wording CONTRIBUTING.md keeps exact.

PR #231's description says the guide has 65 steps. It has 56; the pass corrects it.

Done when

  • The prose passes all three checks, just check passes, and nothing but prose has changed.

Settled

#236 holds the pass. It covers 1,195 lines of prose in 37 files, which git blame gives to the milestone's 24 pull requests, plus all 56 steps in guide.json, with each step's request run again. It changed prose in 15 files:

  • Nine step notes or texts quoted their runs wrong. The worst was the work budget's first sweep: the old collection at 38 MB sets the budget to zero rather than spending it.
  • Other docs and comments against the code: ADR 0008's columns below 700 px, ADR 0018's nursery teal, the test-pyodide time in ADR 0007 and CONTRIBUTING.md, the README's guide line, and six code comments.
  • Against CONTEXT.md and /stop-slop: bare "garbage", "node", "section", "kept", "simulation", and "step" outside the guide's sense; Wh- openers, passives and two adverbs.

PR #231's description now says 56 steps.

issues.title: Fit the guide's rail and charts on a phone
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #220. On a phone, the guide's rail sticks to the top of the screen with the step's text and its notes, and takes about 350 px of an 800 px screen. The charts below get less than half of it, and the two columns sit side by side at about 150 px each.

The change

  • The rail takes less of a phone's screen: its notes fold behind a toggle, or show on the badges alone, or the rail docks at the foot.
  • The charts get the room the rail gives up.

Open questions

  • Which way the rail gives up its room. A prototype on #220's branch can compare them at 375 px.
  • Whether a phone shows the two columns side by side or one collector at a time, with a switch between them.

Done when

  • At 375 px, a step's text, its notes and the panels it marks fit the screen together, in light and dark mode, and just check passes.

Settled

  • #234 builds variant C from the prototype on prototype/guide-phone, with variant B's dock. The commit there records all three variants and why A and B lost.
  • Two columns or one: one collector at a time on a phone, through two tabs that stick to the top. Each tab carries its marks' numbers, and a step opens on the collector of the first panel it marks.
  • The rail's room: the step docks at the foot with its title and text, in 204–271 px. Its notes move into the widget, under each marked panel's title, or under the figures for a figure.
  • The widget's side: a narrow attribute brings the tabs, the notes and a scroll that brings each new step's first mark into view above the dock. The page's scroll-padding-bottom tells the widget what the dock covers. An entry can carry notes beside marks.
  • What fits: on all 56 steps at 375×800, the first mark stands wholly in view with the step's text. 19 steps also mark a figure or panel out of view, most often a figure about 700 px above the marked panel, and the reader scrolls to it.

issues.title: Fit the guide's widget in one window
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
At 1440×900 the guide's widget runs past the window. The page's heading and intro take 240 px, and the widget 1,076: its settings 70 to 90, its figures 100, and its heap, work and budget panels 440, 200 and 150. A reader steps through a chapter and scrolls to see the panel a note names.

The prototype on prototype/guide-fit compared three arrangements (95a3008) and settled B, with changes from review.

The change

  • The intro becomes a strip over the guide that the reader closes, and stays closed. The page's heading goes: the nav marks the page.
  • The widget's settings move to the rail, in a block at its foot that the reader collapses. The block stays as the reader left it for every step. Open, it keeps the height of the tallest chapter's settings; collapsed, its heading's.
  • The rail's head holds the chapter's name on one line beside small ← and → buttons and the step count, in place of Back and Next.
  • The step's box keeps the height of the guide's longest step, and the chapters' list fills the rail between the step and the settings, scrolling to keep the chapter shown in view. Nothing in the rail moves from one step to the next, or from one chapter to the next.
  • The compact widget sizes its charts so that it ends at the window's foot, and sizes them again as the window changes.
  • The collector constants' toggle keeps the reader's choice for every entry after.

The widget renders its controls into a <gc-controls> element the page places, with the widget's own styles, so the guide still reaches nothing inside the widget's shadow root. ADR 0020 records the layout, and ADR 0017 the toggle.

On a phone the layout stays as it is; #229 fits it.

Done when

  • At 1440×900 the widget ends inside the window on every step, and stepping through every chapter moves nothing in the rail, with the settings open or collapsed. just check passes.

Settled

  • #233 builds layout B. The prototype stays on prototype/guide-fit.
  • The widget takes a fit attribute, and the guide sets it at 900 px wide and up. The plots scale between 0.3 and 1.3 of full size, and the axes, legends and lane spacing stay. panels.js holds the sums (fitted, heapHeight, laneTicks).
  • <gc-controls for="guide"> takes the widget's controls, styled the way the widget styles its own. With nothing left in it, the compact widget's top row drops its margin.
  • Open, the Settings block reserves 182 px: the tallest chapter's 174 px of controls plus 8 px of padding. Collapsed, it keeps only its summary line.
  • Beside the widget, the step box keeps the guide's longest step's height through CSS, with no JS. On a phone each chapter keeps its own height.
  • Once the reader opens or closes the constants toggle, it stays that way on every entry (ADR 0017).
  • Checked at 1440×900 across all 56 steps, with settings open and collapsed. The arrows, list and settings stayed at 45, 451 and 678 px with settings open, and 45, 451 and 860 px collapsed. The widget ended at 887 px, and the page had no scroll.

issues.title: Show the guide a step at a time beside one widget
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The guide reads as an essay with eight widgets in it. Each section runs four or five paragraphs, and the prose spends most of them telling the reader which control to move and which figure to read after: "Move Churn that starts a cycle to 10%, and … Peak uncollected garbage reads 1.9 MB against 0.8." A reader who came for the charts scrolls past the prose, and a reader who reads it has to scroll back to the widget to check it.

The change

  • The guide shows one chapter at a time, as a list of steps, with Back and Next between them, in the layout the prototype settled (A, below): a rail beside one widget.
  • Each step holds a sentence or two and the widget's request: the preset, the settings, the values of the controls. Next applies the step's request, and the charts redraw with the change the sentence names. The kept runs (#135) draw a step the reader has seen at once.
  • The controls stay live within a step, so a reader can try a value of their own.
  • Each step has an address, so the browser's Back button and a link reach it.
  • Each step outlines the panels and figures its text talks about, with a numbered badge whose note in the rail says what to see there. The figures it names get their numbers tinted, and each figure that moved since the last step notes what it was.
  • The widget learns these as its own: a compact view without the object graph, marks on an entry, and notes on the figures that moved. The guide reaches nothing inside the widget's shadow root.
  • The steps live as JSON beside the page, which the tests read.
  • This issue moves the young generation's chapter. The others follow, a chapter an issue: #221 to #228. Until they land, the chapter list links each to its section in the long form, the guide as it stands, which moves to site/guide-long.html. #229 fits the rail and the charts on a phone.

ADR 0009 says the guide embeds a widget in each of its sections, and CONTEXT.md's Guide says each section embeds one. Both change with this, and a new ADR records the step-through layout.

Done when

  • The young generation's chapter steps through on the guide at 1440 px and 375 px, in light and dark mode, its figures read as its notes say, and just check passes.
  • A test checks the figures the chapter's text and notes rest on.

Settled

  • site/guide.json lists the chapters. A chapter with steps runs them on the guide, and one without links to its section in the long form, site/guide-long.html, the guide as it stood. Each step's entry takes the name <chapter id>-<n>, so guide.html#guide=the-young-generation-3 reaches the third step.
  • The widget takes three things from the guide: a compact attribute, which leaves out the object graph, its legend and the select; marks on an entry, as collector.panel or figure.name, which it outlines with numbered badges; and a changes attribute, which notes under each figure what it read before the last runs it asked for. The guide reaches nothing inside the widget's shadow root.
  • The young generation's chapter runs eight steps: the prototype's seven, after a first that says what the young generation holds and how big it is at a threshold0 of 1,000 kB.
  • Back and Next walk every chapter's steps in turn, and the arrow keys step too, unless a slider or a panel has focus.
  • tests/test_guide.py runs each step's request, checks its marks against the widget's names, and checks the figures the chapter's text and notes rest on.
  • ADR 0020 records the layout. ADRs 0008 and 0009 point to it, and CONTEXT.md gains Chapter, Step and Mark.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html:
A prototype on prototype/guide-steps shows the young generation's chapter as seven steps on json_loads, around the real widget, in three layouts:

  • A. A rail beside the widget: Back and Next, the step's text and notes, and the chapter's list of steps. On a phone the rail sticks to the top.
  • B. The widget at full width, and the step in a caption fixed over its foot.
  • C. Step cards that scroll past a pinned widget, with no buttons.

On that branch, run poetry run just serve and open http://localhost:8000/prototype-guide.html?variant=A. The bar at the top or the [ and ] keys switch layouts, and the arrow keys step.

Verdict: A (7721a70 on prototype/guide-steps). What it settled:

  • Each step is one of the widget's entries. The page steps by writing the entry into the URL fragment, which the widget already follows, so the browser's Back button steps back and a link reaches a step. Kept runs draw a step seen before at once.
  • Back and Next sit above the step's text, and the text box keeps the longest step's height, so neither moves between steps.
  • Each step outlines the charts and figures its text talks about. A numbered badge sits on each outline, and a note under the step's text, behind the same number, says what to see there: "Three bars, at 12, 14 and 16 MB, examine each object once."
  • The figures a step names get their numbers tinted, and each figure that moved since the last step notes what it was, as soon as the widget writes it.
  • The current step in the chapter's list takes a filled background, since bold alone read too close to the rest.
  • The guide's widget drops the object graph and its legend. With them, the charts fall below the fold in every layout, and a step's text never sits beside the panel it talks about.

B's caption covered half a phone's screen, and C's cards covered the charts as they passed.

Still open: on a phone, A's sticky rail with its notes takes about 350 px of an 800 px screen. Folding the notes behind a toggle at phone width, or showing them on the badges alone, would give the charts more room. The compact widget keeps the two columns side by side on a phone, about 150 px each.

issues.title: Write the guide's section on uncollected garbage and peak memory
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Section 5 of the guide's outline (#176).

The section

The incremental collector scans old objects at a lower rate, so cyclic garbage can wait there longer. The PEP expects about the same peak memory overall: more for small, short-lived programs, whose young generation can hold up to about 24 MB, and less for large, long-lived ones.

  • Widget: a preset chosen as for section 4. Control: churn that starts a cycle.
  • In the panels: the heap's uncollected garbage band, and peak uncollected garbage beside work per MB.

Depends on

  • #178, the guide's page.
  • #177, so that the page's widgets start their runs as a reader comes to them.
  • #117, which calibrates the presets: the section waits on it, as its point depends on a preset's numbers.

Done when

  • The section is on the guide's page, its widget runs the preset chosen for it with its controls, and its prose says what the panels show.

Settled

  • Where the garbage waits: no preset puts cyclic garbage in the old generation, and churn's cycles die young, so the section shows the PEP's case for small programs: the incremental collector examines nothing until an object has aged through the 24 MB young generation, where the legacy collector's gen 0 collections take the nursery every 2 MB.
  • The preset: json_loads at a threshold0 of 2,000 kB, whose 21 MB run ends before the incremental collector examines a young object. Controls: Churn that starts a cycle and threshold0. Peak uncollected garbage reads 0.8 MB in both columns at 0%, start-up's tree at shutdown; 1.9 against 0.8 at 10%, 5.0 at 25%, and 10.1 against 1.0 at 50%. Work per MB stays lower for the incremental collector: 174 against 229 at 10%. At 1,000 kB the young generation fits in the run, and the incremental collector's peak falls to 1.1 MB.
  • Large programs: a playground link runs async_tree_io_tg with a tenth of its churn starting cycles and its churn living 10 MB on average. There the legacy collector's peak uncollected garbage reads 7.6 MB against 2.6, and its work per MB 1,563 against 954.
  • The guide's opening no longer says more sections follow: with this one, every section of the outline (#176) is on the page.

issues.title: Write the guide's section on the work budget
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Section 4 of the guide's outline (#176).

The section

The work budget starts at -100,000 real objects. Each young collection adds its survivors, and each increment takes off its candidates and gives back twice what it freed, so a heap full of garbage sweeps faster.

  • Widget: a preset whose cyclic garbage reaches the old generation, chosen while writing the section. None of the five may leave any there until calibration, and a sixth preset may suit it better. Controls: the freed-credit multiplier and the initial work budget, the collector constants ADR 0017 unlocked.
  • In the panels: the budget's step line and its negative stretch, and the sweeps figure.

Depends on

  • #178, the guide's page.
  • #177, so that the page's widgets start their runs as a reader comes to them.
  • #117, which calibrates the presets: the section waits on it, as its point depends on a preset's numbers.

Done when

  • The section is on the guide's page, its widget runs the preset chosen for it with its controls, and its prose says what the panels show.

Settled

  • The preset: async_tree_io_tg as calibrated, with the initial work budget and the freed-credit multiplier as its controls. No preset's old collections free anything, as none of the nine benchmarks' did: gcmon recorded 6,919 old collections on the reference branch, and none freed an object. Churn can't put cycles there either, since a cycle's lifetime is never a long one.
  • The freed credit changes no record at any initial budget, and the section says so. A playground link runs the preset with each task linking back to its parent, where the old collections free whole trees: 9 sweeps and three of the four trees at a multiplier of 2, 6 sweeps and two trees at 0.
  • The initial budget moves the first old collection that works from 38 MB to 50 MB at -200,000 and to 26 MB at 0, with 15, 14 and 17 sweeps. Above zero it buys one empty sweep.
  • The constants show at once: a widget that offers no collector settings opens the constants' toggle, with no settings heading over it. ADR 0017 says so now.

issues.title: Check the prose the First presets milestone wrote
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Before First presets closes, check the prose its pull requests wrote: the lines in main that one of its 38 merged pull requests, #99 to #216, changed last. The Playground pass, #166, covered c689813..7578d68, which holds none of them. Lines a Guide pull request rewrote since wait for the Guide milestone's own pass, though a paragraph that mixes the two gets read whole.

The prose: the ADRs and CONTEXT.md, the README, the site's text and comments, the docstrings and comments in src/, tests/ and tools/, and the yield findings in the presets' Records comments. Check each against the /stop-slop rules, CONTEXT.md's terms and Avoid words, and the code as it stands, the numbers the site quotes included. The pseudocode's comments stay verbatim (ADR 0003), as does the wording CONTRIBUTING.md keeps exact.

Done when

  • The prose passes all three checks, just check passes, and nothing but prose has changed.

Settled

The pass read 1,232 lines of prose in 44 files, which git blame gives to the milestone's 38 pull requests, and re-ran every number the site quotes from them.

Against the code:

  • The guide's section on a large increment said halving the graph halves its largest increment. The increments grow 7,608, 16,518 and 32,520 simulated objects, and a graph half the size has loaded before the second, so peak work falls from 32.5K to 8.5K.
  • The guide's section on the legacy collector: "well below the gen 2 bar" is now "about three fifths of" it, 54,519 against 90,156.
  • ADR 0012 said the figures count a full collection like any other. Since #137, peak work leaves it out.
  • ADR 0011: a json_loads preset's heap under the incremental collector holds 18,528 real objects, so "about 18,300" is now "about 18,500". Placeholder comments name no source, which the ADR now says.
  • presets.py's docstring said a placeholder waits for its preset's issue. #121 and #122 have closed and left two placeholders open.
  • CONTRIBUTING.md said Node's tests run against panels.js alone. They also cover graph.js, editor.js, source.js, link.js and kept.js.
  • The README said the site runs one widget and the guide comes next.
  • CONTEXT.md's Preset said every workload parameter is chosen by hand. ADR 0011 takes them from the code and the records.
  • xml_etree_parse's tree is two levels deep except for a chain of 50 elements, not "nearly all" of it. create_gc_cycles' rings come to 131 simulated objects, each a ring of its own, plus the list.

Against CONTEXT.md: "promote" (Survived), "sweep" for a pointer's move (Sweep), "keep" for what survives, bare "garbage" and "parameters", and "exit" or "process" for a worker.

Against /stop-slop: adverbs ("well", "just", "nearly", "freshly", "evenly"), passives ("gets made", "is examined", "are marked", "is built"), and openers with "Where", "When" or "What".

issues.title: Keep each widget entry's records, so picking it again draws at once
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Once a widget offers several entries (#134), picking one runs both collectors on it from the start, every time. A preset's two runs take a few seconds under Pyodide, so switching back to an entry the reader has seen makes them wait for charts they saw a moment ago.

The change

  • The widget keeps the records and figures of each entry's runs, under the request that made them, while the page stays open.
  • Picking an entry whose request matches kept runs draws them at once and asks the worker for nothing.
  • Moving a control makes a new request, so the widget runs it as it does today and keeps the result beside the others.

Open questions

  • How many requests' runs the widget keeps, and which it drops first. A preset's records run to a few thousand, so a page that keeps every request a reader tries can grow large.
  • Whether runs cut short by a switch are kept, to resume or redraw in part, or dropped.

Done when

  • Picking an entry seen before, with the same control values, draws its charts and figures at once, with no request to the worker, in light and dark mode, and just check passes.

Settled

  • How many, and which go first: each widget keeps the runs of its last 16 requests whose runs finished, across its entries, and drops the runs it found or kept longest ago. A preset's two runs come to at most about 250 kB as JSON, create_gc_cycles' at the shortest threshold0 its slider allows, so a widget holds at most about 4 MB.
  • Runs cut short: dropped. A widget keeps runs once both finish. The worker ends a widget's runs when the widget asks for others, so nothing remains to resume, and picking that entry again runs it from the start.
  • The key: the request and the paths of the controls the widget asked for, whose ranges the kept controls hold. The worker writes a share in lowest terms, as "1/4", and the sliders and the legend in thousandths, as "250/1000", so the key reduces each.
  • Controls: a slider or a legend field moved back to a value tried draws at once too, as the lookup sits where every request starts.
  • Entries a link brought with code still wait for Run, and Run always asks the worker.

issues.title: Retire the stand-in once every preset runs
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The home page's one widget offers the stand-in beside the presets through #134's picker. #188 takes the stand-in page away and checks the digests under Pyodide in CI, which leaves the stand-in workload in the home page's widget.

The change

  • The stand-in stays in the widget's list, labelled as a stand-in, until all five of this milestone's presets run: create_gc_cycles, json_loads (#119), xml_etree_parse (#120), async_tree_io_tg (#121) and connected_components (#122).
  • Then the stand-in leaves the list, and the page's text describes the presets in place of the stand-in.
  • The README no longer calls the site's workload a stand-in.

Settled

The widget opens on xml_etree_parse, on the home page and in the playground, and the other presets follow in this milestone's order. Its runs finish drawing first: 3.9 s from a fresh load under Pyodide, where the stand-in took 4.7. Its legacy collector's peak work, 2,142 simulated objects, is about twice the incremental collector's 1,000, and its work per MB, 423, about ten times the incremental collector's 40. A link that names the stand-in opens xml_etree_parse.

The playground drops the stand-in too. A playground link carries its whole request (ADR 0016), so a link to the stand-in's workload still opens it.

The ADRs keep their mentions. ADRs 0016, 0017 and 0019 cite the stand-in in the context of what they decided, and that stays true of the site they describe. "Stand-in" for the worst pause or for overhead, in CONTEXT.md, the collector and the home page's figures, is another sense and stays.

Done when

  • The home page's one widget offers every preset that exists, no page, doc or comment outside the ADRs mentions the stand-in, and just check passes.

issues.title: Add the json_loads preset
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
json_loads decodes three JSON strings twenty times each in every loop: a dict of 32 keys that holds a list of seven strings, a list of 20 ints with a 60 beside it, and a list of three copies of the first dict whose values are all strings. The benchmark drops each result as json.loads returns, and refcounting frees it, since it holds no cycle. In the pyperformance-ms-inc-2 trace, its automatic collections find no cyclic garbage, and a worker allocates about 20 MB over 10 automatic collections. It is the smallest of the five, with no structure of its own beyond start-up, so it tests the churn and the start-up heap (#118) on their own.

The worker

Part of the worker What the code does In the preset Numbers from
start-up and imports the interpreter, pyperf, json and random the start-up the five presets share (#206) records
module globals DICT, TUPLE, three mutated copies of DICT and the three JSON strings part of the start-up structure code
each loop 60 calls to json.loads, each result 2 to 4 dicts and lists, and for each call two match objects and two tuples in the decoder, all dropped at once churn: transients with lifetimes of about 1 kB, and no cycles code
between loops pyperf's timer nothing: no churn outlives a collection records: each legacy gen 0 collection past start-up examines 2 to 6 real objects
shutdown the frames return and the modules go; three full collections start-up's tree with parent pointers turns into cyclic garbage once sys lets go of it; three full collections code

A loop makes about 400 real objects, about 25 kB at 64 B each. The trace gives about 20 kB a loop, start-up included: a worker's 10 automatic collections over its 1,024 loops.

The change

  • The json_loads preset, as the table lays it out.

Settled

A run's length comes from the worker's 10 automatic collections in #117's rerun: 10 gen 0 collections under the legacy collector, and 5 young and 5 old under the incremental one. The run ends about halfway to the next, at 21,000 kB.

No churn outlives a collection. Past start-up, each legacy gen 0 collection examines 2 to 6 real objects, 65 at the last, and the heap holds 18,890 real objects at each, give or take 4. The placeholder's long-lived churn, 1/50 of it living 100 to 1,000 kB, made those collections examine 80 to 256. Without it they examine 16, the one simulated object of churn alive as each comes. The legacy collector's yield comes to 1.1%, as its benchmark's does.

The guide. The section on the young generation no longer says a few objects stay alive between loops. Lower threshold0 and the legacy collector's work per MB holds near 190 down to about 160 kB, where it used to climb. Below that, a gen 2 collection fits in the run and examines the long-lived objects again: at 150 kB, the legacy collector's work per MB comes to 248.

Left open

The 65 real objects the last gen 0 collection examines: a one-off that churn cannot make.

Done when

  • The preset passes its digest and yield tests, a widget runs it by name, and just check passes.

issues.title: Add presets, starting with create_gc_cycles
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
A preset is a named workload that models one worker of a pyperformance benchmark, with its own seed and a run length chosen by hand (CONTEXT.md). The simulator has none yet. This issue adds the first, and what every later preset needs. It builds on #117, which loads the benchmarks' collections, and #125, which lets a workload call gc.collect(). ADR 0011 says where a preset's numbers come from: shapes and counts from the benchmark's code, lengths on the allocation clock from gcmon's records, and the rest fitted by hand.

Every worker starts and ends the same way:

  • Start-up and imports. The interpreter, pyperf and the benchmark's imports fill module globals with classes, functions and data, all under the module root. In the pyperformance-ms-inc-2 trace, each worker's first collection finds about 12,600 real objects in the heap, and the benchmark's own imports and data grow it from there.
  • Shutdown. finalize_modules takes each module out of sys.modules and runs two full collections. A module's functions hold its globals, and its globals hold its functions, so whatever hangs off a module turns into cyclic garbage that those two collections free. connected_components' graph goes this way: its explicit collections' yield in the trace is 97%.

pyperf never calls gc.collect() itself. Outside create_gc_cycles, a worker's only full collections come at its shutdown. The trace holds at most one of the two for each worker, and none for most json_loads and xml_etree workers.

The worker

create_gc_cycles builds 100 rings of 21 Node objects, each node linked to the next and back, and holds them in a list. Each loop calls gc.collect(), builds the rings, drops the list and calls gc.collect() again, timing only the second call.

Part of the worker What the code does In the preset Numbers from
start-up and imports the interpreter, pyperf and gc the start-up the five presets share (#206) records
each loop gc.collect(); 2,100 nodes in 100 rings; the list dropped; gc.collect() a repeating structure of rings under a frame root, 132 kB, with a full collection (#125) before its build and after its drop code
between loops pyperf's timer, whose floats the collector does not track nothing: a loop allocates its rings alone records: the heap at each gc.collect()
shutdown the frames return and the modules go; three full collections start-up's tree with parent pointers turns into cyclic garbage once sys lets go of it; three full collections code

A loop allocates 132 kB, less than threshold0, and calls gc.collect() twice, so no automatic collection falls inside one: in #117's rerun, each incremental worker has two automatic collections, both at start-up, and 1,024 calls to gc.collect(). The code's counts set a loop's length on the clock (ADR 0011).

The change

  • A preset in the simulator: its name, its benchmark, its workload parameters with their seed, and its run length. The collector settings stay the PEP's defaults, which the benchmarks run with.
  • A run ends as a worker does: the workload lets go of what hangs off the module root, leaving it as cyclic garbage, and shutdown's full collections follow (#125).
  • A shape of rings: a list that holds them, each ring's objects linked to the next and back. Neither Chains nor Tree builds rings. A ring of 21 real objects comes to about 1.3 kB, so the shape decides how coarse its rings get (ADR 0002). The shape can land in a pull request of its own that names this issue with #n.
  • A script in tools/ that runs a preset under both collectors and prints its yields, its collections by kind and its heap sizes beside its benchmark's, as #117 loads them (ADR 0011).
  • Each workload parameter's comment names its source: the benchmark's code, or the record it was fitted to.
  • A test pins each preset's records digest under each collector, as ADR 0007 asks.
  • A test holds each preset's yield to its benchmark's as #117 loads it, per collector, generation and kind of collection, within the tolerance #117 sets.
  • A widget runs a preset by naming it, so a preset's numbers live in one place.
  • The create_gc_cycles preset, as the table above lays it out.

Settled

A run's length is the worker's own on the allocation clock (ADR 0011): start-up, then 512 loops, the last ending with its second gc.collect().

A loop is its rings' build, 132 kB. At each gc.collect() the heap holds 18,291 or 20,391 real objects in every worker, the rings' 2,100 apart, so nothing else outlives a loop. Without the placeholder's 8 kB of churn a loop, each call examines 4,760 real objects to the benchmark's 4,755 under the incremental collector, and 19,352 to 19,340 under the legacy one.

512 loops, from the incremental workers' 1,024 calls. pyperf calibrated the legacy workers to 64 loops a value, not 128, so they ran 256. A widget runs one workload under both collectors, and the yields do not depend on the count.

The churn is start-up's build churn alone, with a lifetime of 1 kB, as json_loads' churn has. A lifetime of 4 kB moves what the first collection examines by 0.2%.

Done when

  • The create_gc_cycles preset passes its digest and yield tests, a widget runs it by name, and just check passes.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html: Reopened: #126 recorded ADR 0011 for this issue, and its merge message closed it by mistake. The preset, the rings shape, the script in tools/ and the run-length question remain.

issues.title: Add the connected_components preset
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
networkx_connected_components loads the Amazon co-purchasing graph from SNAP, about 262,000 products, into a networkx Graph while the script's module globals load, before pyperf starts: G = nx.read_adjlist(...). It keeps the graph until shutdown: a dict of attributes and a dict of neighbours for each node, and for each edge a data dict that its two ends share. pyperf runs one loop per value, four per worker. Each loop counts the graph's connected components with a breadth-first walk that makes a key iterator over each node's neighbours, a list for each level and a set for each component, all short-lived.

In #117's rerun, a worker makes 99 automatic collections under either collector, and its heap tops out at about 1,465,000 real objects after the 61st. While the graph loads, the branch's old collections examine it in increments: 231,870, 89,717 and 85,797 real objects in the largest three, identical in all 20 workers. Once the module holds it, they go idle.

The worker

Part of the worker What the code does In the preset Numbers from
start-up and imports the interpreter, pyperf, networkx the start-up the five presets share (#206) records
loading read_adjlist: the graph, and as it goes a list for each line, a tuple for each edge and a throwaway dict or two for each edge a graph of 89,007 simulated objects, built in a frame and then held by sys (#210) code for the shape and the size; records for the frame
each loop the walk: an iterator for each node, a list for each level, a set for each component churn: transients with short lifetimes, and no cycles code
shutdown the graph and the modules let go; two full collections the graph turns into cyclic garbage with its module code

The change

  • A graph shape: many objects, each linked to a handful of others, under the module root: Graph.
  • The connected_components preset, as the table lays it out.
  • The guide's sections that run connected_components say what the incremental collector does with a graph a frame holds while it loads, and the section on a large increment runs it.

Settled

The graph is built in a frame. read_adjlist's frame holds the graph until it returns, and only then does the module's global take it. The branch marks from sys alone, so its old collections examine the graph in increments while it loads. Under sys from its first object, the preset's old collections marked it and examined 223 real objects each, to the benchmark's 19,952; built in a frame, they examine 22,664. A frame root for good would match the run, but at shutdown _Py_Finalize's collection would free the graph, where the benchmark's finalize_modules frees it once the module goes.

The load's churn stays out. The heap tops out about 118 MB after start-up, so read_adjlist's lists, tuples and throwaway dicts come to about 0.3 kB for each kB of graph. A build's churn comes in whole kB, and 1 kB would double the load, so the preset leaves it out and its load ends about 29 MB early.

A loop's length comes from the 99 automatic collections, the run ending about halfway to the next, as json_loads' does: 26,342 kB a loop, where the placeholder was 26,500.

The guide. The section on a large increment runs connected_components: while the graph loads, each increment is about twice the last, and the incremental collector's peak work, 32,520 simulated objects, passes the legacy collector's 24,000. The section on the old generation runs async_tree_io_tg instead, whose tree sys reaches, to show marking and the work budget's pacing. The playground link #209 put in the section on a large increment goes, with its test.

Left open

The preset's largest increment, 520,320 real objects, is about twice the benchmark's 231,870, and comes later in the load: the benchmark's load runs longer, with the churn the preset leaves out. The churn that outlives a collection stays a placeholder.

Done when

  • The preset passes its digest and yield tests, a widget runs it by name, and just check passes.

issues.title: Let a frame hold a module-rooted structure while it builds
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
A structure under the module root hangs off sys from its first object. That models module globals that a module defines statement by statement, as start-up's are. It misses a module-level X = build(): the function's frame holds what it builds until it returns, and only then does a global take it.

connected_components loads its graph that way, G = nx.read_adjlist(...). In #117's rerun, the branch's old collections examine the graph in increments while it loads, up to 231,870 real objects in one, identical in all 20 workers, and mark it once the module holds it. The preset hangs the graph off sys from the start, so its old collections mark it and examine 223 real objects each, where the benchmark's examine 19,952 (#122).

A frame root for good fits the run but not shutdown: _Py_Finalize's collection would free the graph, where the benchmark's finalize_modules frees it once the module goes. Holding every module-rooted structure in a frame while it builds would not do either: sys reaches async_tree_io_tg's tasks through the event loop as each is scheduled, and its old collections would examine 20,104 real objects each again, where the benchmark's examine 643 (#121).

The change

  • A structure's workload parameters gain built_in_frame, false by default and only for a structure sys holds: a frame holds the structure while it builds, and sys takes it once the build ends, its churn included.
  • A request may leave the field out, so links written before it still open. A request the simulator writes spells it out.
  • The playground's legend offers it as a third choice under Held by: a frame, then sys. The workload source writes it as built_in_frame=True, and the legend reads held by a frame while built, then by sys.
  • CONTEXT.md names it among the workload parameters.
  • No preset takes it yet; #122 moves connected_components' graph onto it.

Done when

  • A structure built in a frame hangs off sys from its build's end and not before, under both collectors; the legend, the workload source and links carry the field; and just check passes.

issues.title: Add the async_tree_io_tg preset
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
async_tree_io_tg runs a tree of asyncio tasks six levels deep, with six branches at each level and each level under a TaskGroup: 55,987 tasks, whose 46,656 leaves each sleep 50 ms. pyperf runs the tree once per value, four times per worker. Each run builds the whole tree, and lets each task go as it finishes. Each task brings a coroutine and its frame, and each sleep a future and a timer handle.

In #117's rerun, a worker makes 261 automatic collections under either collector, and its heap peaks at 857,000 to 866,000 real objects, about 15 a task. Its collections find no cyclic garbage beyond start-up's, so refcounting frees all of the tree.

The worker

Part of the worker What the code does In the preset Numbers from
start-up and imports the interpreter, pyperf, asyncio the start-up the five presets share (#206) records
each run the task tree: 55,987 tasks with their coroutines, frames, groups, futures and timer handles, under the event loop a tree with six branches under sys, about 53 MB at its peak, built and let go each run code for the shape; records for the size and the root
each run the event loop's own objects: handles, callbacks, the ready queue build churn placeholder
shutdown modules let go; two full collections as #118 adds code

A run allocates about 130 MB on the clock, more than twice the tree's peak. Leaves finish and free their tasks while others are still being built, and the event loop's churn fills the rest.

The change

  • A tree shape with six branches and no links back to the parents: Hierarchy.
  • The async_tree_io_tg preset, as the table lays it out.
  • The guide's section on a large increment, which ran async_tree_io_tg on the premise that sys does not reach its tree, says what the benchmark shows, and links to the playground for the PEP's large increment.

Settled

The tree hangs off sys. The branch marks from interp->sysdict alone (seed_reachable_space in Python/gc.c), as the PEP's pseudocode does. Its old collections spend their whole budget and examine 643 real objects each on average, so sys reaches the tree, through the event loop that runs it. Under a frame root the preset's old collections examined 22,972 each; under sys they examine 397.

The run's length comes from the 261 automatic collections, the run ending about halfway to the next, as json_loads' does: 129,594 kB a run, where the placeholder was 130,000.

15 real objects a task stays: the peak heap less start-up's, over the tasks.

The large increment. With the tree under sys, the incremental collector's peak work is 2,035 simulated objects to the legacy collector's 12,003, and none of the five benchmarks keeps a large structure in the old generation that sys does not reach. The guide keeps the PEP's point with a playground link that opens the same workload with the tree under a frame root, where the incremental collector's peak work passes the legacy collector's more than three times over. A test holds the link's workload to the preset's.

Left open

The young collections examine other amounts than the benchmark's: the preset's examine 25,982 real objects each against 19,942 under the incremental collector, and 12,991 against 16,606 in each legacy gen 0. That points at the event loop's churn and how long a task lives, which no target fixes yet.

Done when

  • The preset passes its digest and yield tests, a widget runs it by name, and just check passes.

issues.title: Add the xml_etree_parse preset
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
xml_etree's script runs four benchmarks, each in workers of its own, and pyperf's --worker-task=0 is parse. For each value pyperf takes, bench_etree builds a tree of 5,103 elements, serialises it and writes it to a temporary file. It then runs bench_parse once per loop: 30 times, it parses the file and parses the same bytes, and each new tree replaces the last of its kind. An element holds its children and nothing points back up, so a tree holds no cycle, and refcounting frees each tree it replaces. bench_etree drops the tree it built when it returns.

In #117's rerun, a parse worker makes 51 automatic collections under either collector. Its collections free 249 real objects a worker, all of them start-up's: 129, 84 and 36 under the legacy collector, 129 and 120 under the incremental one. The 2.3% cyclic garbage that xml_etree's young collections find across its four tasks comes from iterparse, whose young collections find 6.05% under the incremental collector.

The worker

Part of the worker What the code does In the preset Numbers from
start-up and imports the interpreter, pyperf, xml.etree.ElementTree with its C accelerator, tempfile the start-up the five presets share (#206) records
each value build_xml_tree: a root with 50 children of 100 subchildren each, and a chain of 50 under deepchildren, 5,103 elements in all a tree under a frame root, 322 simulated objects, built at each value's start and dropped at its end code
each loop 60 parses, half from the file and half from the bytes two repeating trees of the same shape and size under frame roots, one per source, each dropped when its next build ends code
each loop the parser's own objects churn without cycles records
shutdown modules let go; two full collections as #118 adds code

pyperf ran one loop per value and four values per worker, so a worker builds 244 trees. Its 51 automatic collections put its end between 102,000 and 104,000 kB, and the preset ends about halfway, as json_loads' does. Less start-up's 4,624 kB, that comes to 403 kB a tree on the clock, so the parser allocates about 81 kB beyond each tree's 322.

The change

  • A tree shape without parent pointers, as build_xml_tree builds it: Hierarchy.
  • The xml_etree_parse preset, as the table lays it out.
  • just compare prints the real objects one collection examines on average, beside its benchmark's, so a fit can see more than yield.

Settled

No cycles in the churn. The preset's churn made a fiftieth of its allocations into cycles, for the 2.3% this issue first quoted. Its incremental collector's young collections found 25.8% cyclic garbage, where its benchmark's find 0.6%. Without cycles they find 0.5%, and the legacy collector's find 0.0% against 0.0%.

The churn's lifetime stays open. A mean of 1 kB and one of 4 kB make the same collections, so the preset takes 1 kB, as json_loads does.

What the collections examine, in real objects, the benchmark's then the preset's: 1,500 and 1,564 in each young collection, 13,267 and 12,303 in each legacy gen 0, and 25,324 and 22,672 in each legacy gen 1. A legacy gen 0 collection meets about 2.6 live trees' worth of objects in the benchmark and 2.4 in the preset. No target depends on it.

Done when

  • The preset passes its digest and yield tests, a widget runs it by name, and just check passes.

issues.title: Fit the workers' start-up to the rerun
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Every preset begins with start-up: the interpreter, pyperf and the benchmark's imports. Each preset still has #118's placeholders there, 350 chains and 350 tree objects under sys with 6 kB of churn after each. Their first collections examine 4,600 to 6,100 real objects, where their benchmarks' examine 8,100 to 8,800. #117's rerun shows the five workers start up alike, so one fit serves the five presets (#118, #119, #120, #121, #122).

The rerun

Medians over each benchmark's 20 workers, in real objects:

Benchmark Heap at the 1st collection (2,000 kB) Legacy 1st examines / frees Legacy 2nd (4,000 kB) examines / frees
create_gc_cycles 12,212 8,413 / 129 6,348 / 84
json_loads 12,602 8,696 / 129 6,095 / 84
xml_etree_parse 12,661 8,747 / 129 5,855 / 84
async_tree_io_tg 12,480 8,141 / 129 6,352 / 48
connected_components 12,814 8,845 / 91 5,658 / 44

Where the records show start-up's end, in create_gc_cycles and json_loads, it comes between 4,000 and 6,000 kB and leaves 18,291 to 18,890 objects that the collections examine.

  • Untracked tuples. A collection untracks a tuple that holds only objects it never sees, without examining it. About 4,000 of the first heap go that way at the first collection, and about 11,000 by start-up's end. The simulator has no untracking, and the PEP's pseudocode has none (ADR 0003).
  • Objects sys does not reach. Under the incremental collector, each of create_gc_cycles' gc.collect() calls examines and keeps 3,705 objects besides the rings, and every benchmark's first shutdown collection examines 3,900 to 4,500. A full collection marks what sys reaches, so something else holds these.
  • Start-up's cyclic garbage. The legacy collector's first three collections free 129, 84 and 3, 216 in all, and create_gc_cycles' first gc.collect() under the incremental collector frees the same 216.
  • Shutdown. Where gcmon caught finalize_modules' first collection, it frees 12,637 to 12,995 of start-up's objects.

The change

  • One start-up, shared by the five presets, in four structures: a tree of 13 objects that start-up lets go of once built; chains of 121 and a tree of 790 under sys; and chains of 232 under a frame root. Each object comes with 3 kB of churn, which takes in the untracked tuples.
  • ADR 0011 says the objects the legacy collector's first collection examines set start-up's size, and the untracked tuples count as churn.
  • just compare prints the objects the first collection examines in place of the first heap.
  • The presets that pass their yield tests with it lose their strict xfails.
  • The guide and the home page say what the new start-up changes, and the widgets' sliders follow each preset's structures to their new places.

Settled

Untracked tuples count as churn. Untracking in the simulator would need a workload parameter and a step the PEP's pseudocode does not have. Fitting start-up to the first heap instead would give it about 29,500 real objects, and create_gc_cycles' gc.collect() yield would land near 3.4% against its benchmark's 5.4%, outside the tolerance. The cost: the branch's incremental collector keeps the tuples tracked until a collection examines them, so a json_loads worker's heap holds 29,700 real objects all run, where its preset's holds about 18,300.

What passes. With the new start-up, create_gc_cycles passes under both collectors (gc.collect() 21.9% against 22.1% and 5.4% against 5.4%; gen 0 1.3% against 1.4%), and so does json_loads under the legacy collector (1.0% against 1.1%). connected_components passes under the incremental collector too: its old collections now examine the frame-held chains and free nothing, 0.0% against 0.0%. Its benchmark's old collections examine about 20K objects each to the preset's 3.7K, which stays #122's to look into. xml_etree_parse still misses under both (#120).

Done when

  • The five presets share the start-up, their first collections under the legacy collector examine within a tenth of their benchmarks', the yield tests pass for every preset the fit settles, and just check passes.

issues.title: Load the benchmarks' collections from gcmon's CSV
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Each preset is checked by yield against its benchmark: collected over candidates, which leaves scale out. gcmon traces pyperformance's workers and records every collection with the runtime's counters, so the targets come from its traces. No number from a trace is typed into the repo: a fresh trace, loaded again, moves every target.

The change

  • gcmon extracts a trace into a CSV file, one row per collection, with the columns below, and a metadata file beside it (sergey-miryanov/gcmon#228).
  • A loader in tools/ reads those files and gives each benchmark, per collector and generation, the collections, candidates, collected and yield of its automatic collections, and of the gc.collect() calls it makes before shutdown. The tests read it; sim.zip never ships it.
  • Rerun pyperformance under gcmon's latest version on the reference branch, sergey-miryanov/cpython@incremental-gc-update-2, at a commit the metadata records: once with the incremental collector and once with -X gc=legacy. Done on 2026-10-26 at revision 5542f2021c2: pp-inc.csv and pp-legacy.csv, each with its .meta.json.
  • The CSV and metadata files from the rerun live in the repo under data/, as gcmon wrote them. The mock files and tools/mock_data.py go.
  • The loader takes each worker whole up to shutdown: interpreter start-up, imports, the benchmark's loops and pyperf's bookkeeping alike. pyperformance's benchmarks are no GC benchmarks, and their timed part means nothing to the collector, so a preset models a worker's object graph and how the collector processes it, never one part of the worker.
  • A collection is explicit when its auto_collect is 0, whoever started it: the benchmark, pyperf or the interpreter shutting down.
