  • Shutdown's collections set no target, in the loader or in the simulator's tally. gcmon reads a process from outside, once a tick, and a process can exit before the next tick. Shutdown's rows come last, so a lost one has no later row to fold into: in the rerun, most workers lack at least one of their three.
  • The loader leaves out pyperf's calibration workers and the processes with no benchmark name, which are not workers.
  • The yield test runs. The presets whose yields still miss their benchmark's fail it as strict xfails, each naming the issue that fits it: create_gc_cycles under both collectors (#118), json_loads under the legacy one (#119), xml_etree_parse under both (#120) and connected_components under the incremental one (#122).

Settled

Shutdown's first collection. finalize_modules' two collections carry reason 1, and _Py_Finalize's carries 2, as a gc.collect() call does. The loader takes a worker's last reason-2 row for shutdown's, unless an automatic collection follows it. In the rerun no automatic collection follows any worker's last reason-2 row.

  • Of the five benchmarks, only create_gc_cycles calls gc.collect(): 1,024 times a worker under the incremental collector and 512 under the legacy one, since pyperf calibrated 128 loops a value against 64. In the other four, every reason-2 row is shutdown's, and the rule leaves them no explicit target.
  • Where gcmon lost all three of shutdown's rows, the rule leaves out the benchmark's last call instead: 11 of create_gc_cycles' 20 workers under the incremental collector, 15 under the legacy one. Its yield moves by under 0.01 points: 22.0747% against 22.0833%.
  • An exact rule would need gcmon to read the interpreter's finalizing flag at each collection.

The tolerance. A preset's yield passes within a fifth of its benchmark's or half a point of the objects examined, whichever is wider. A benchmark's 20 workers agree to within 0.01 points, so their spread cannot set it. Most targets sit at 0.05% or under, where a share of the target leaves no room, and half a point keeps a preset that finds no garbage apart from a benchmark whose collections find 1.4%. The old 5 points was wider than every target but one.

Columns

Needed:

Column What it holds
benchmark pyperformance's name for it, such as json_loads or xml_etree_parse
pid, pid_epoch the process: with benchmark, they name one worker in the file
calibration 1 for pyperf's calibration workers, which the loader leaves out
ts when the collection started, in ns, to order a worker's rows
generation 0, 1 or 2, as the runtime files it
auto_collect 1 for a collection the runtime started on its own, 0 for gc.collect() and for shutdown's
reason the branch's _PyGC_Reason: 0 for heap, 1 for shutdown, 2 for manual (sergey-miryanov/gcmon#229). Shutdown runs three full collections: PyGC_Collect() in _Py_Finalize, which carries 2, then finalize_modules' two, which carry 1
collections, candidates, collected the runtime's running totals for the worker and generation, as read; the loader takes differences, and a row gcmon lost folds into the next one it read, except a worker's last, which has none to fold into

Wanted:

Column What it gives us
heap_size, heap_size_stop objects in the heap before and after: how large each structure is beside the rest
old_work the work budget, to hold the incremental collector's budget against the simulator's
increment_size objects in each increment an old collection forms: how far the object graph's links reach
survivor_count survivors of the collection

No column gives the allocation clock. CPython's allocator does not report the bytes it has allocated, and RSS samples cannot stand in for them, so a preset's length still comes from its automatic collections, each threshold0 kB after the last (ADR 0011).

Metadata: the trace and its hash, the Python build with its revision, pyperformance's and pyperf's versions, and the date. The collector and the thresholds come as columns, gc_type (1 legacy, 2 incremental) and threshold0 to threshold2. The loader skips gcmon's version.

Done when

  • The loader reads the rerun's files and gives each of the five benchmarks its yield per collector and generation, for its automatic collections and for its gc.collect() calls before shutdown, the yield test runs with the unfitted presets as strict xfails, and just check passes.

issues.title: Scale the work panel to the runtime's own collections
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The work panel's y-scale takes in shutdown's work, so where shutdown takes a large heap, the runtime's own collections shrink to slivers.

Why

Since #200, shutdown's first full collection takes the whole heap while the modules still hold it, and the second frees what they held. In connected_components both fall in the last bin, about 180K objects, so the scale runs to 200K where the runtime's largest collection in a bin is about 28K. The guide's sections on the legacy collector, the old generation and tuning all run connected_components, and point the reader at the bars of the runtime's own collections: the gen 1 and gen 2 spikes, and the incremental collector's steady bars. At this scale those bars are hard to read, and the peak work figure carries the comparison alone.

The change

  • The work panel's y-scale ends past the most work a bin holds without shutdown's, with ADR 0008's room above it.
  • The scale keeps the work of gc.collect() calls. create_gc_cycles' start-up collections reach 291 objects, and its calls do most of its work, so a scale fit to the runtime's own collections alone would cut every bar of its calls.
  • A bin whose work reaches past the end is cut there, with a mark that says so, and the hover still gives its whole work.
  • A run whose only work is shutdown's keeps a scale that fits it.
  • ADR 0008 says how the scale ends.

Each guide and home widget at its settings, the largest bin over both columns:

Widget Runtime's own Without shutdown Shutdown's bin Scale before Scale after
Legacy collector (connected_components, 1,000) 89,713 89,713 179,071 200K 100K
Old generation, tuning, home (connected_components, 2,000) 28,000 28,000 179,067 200K 30K
Young generation (json_loads, 1,000) 710 710 1,063 1,200 800
Home json_loads (2,000) 301 301 1,053 1,200 400
Large increment, home (async_tree_io_tg) 41,251 41,251 2,990 50K 50K
gc.collect() and shutdown, home (create_gc_cycles) 291 23,054 8,035 25K 25K
Home xml_etree_parse 2,843 2,843 2,019 3,000 3,000

Done when

  • In the guide's connected_components widgets, the runtime's own bars fill the panel, shutdown's bin shows as cut, its hover gives its work, and just check passes.

issues.title: Write the guide's section on tuning with gc.set_threshold()
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Section 8 of the guide's outline (#176).

The section

The API stays, and its meaning changes: threshold0 is the size of a half-space in kB, threshold1 the number of aging half-spaces, rounded up to even, and threshold2 goes unread. In the legacy collector that 3.15 ships, threshold0 counts net objects, threshold1 gen 0 collections before a gen 1, and threshold2 gen 1 collections before a gen 2. The young generation comes to threshold0 × (threshold1 + 2) kB, 24 MB at the defaults, which the PEP bounds as the extra memory a small program pays. Even the legacy collector now starts a collection by the memory allocated since the last one, not by the net count of objects, and -X gc=legacy picks it.

  • Widget: connected_components at the PEP's defaults. Controls: threshold0, threshold1.
  • In the panels: the young generation's notes under the thresholds, and the figures: collections, peak work and work per MB.

json_loads, the other candidate, runs these controls in the young generation's section already, and at the defaults its incremental collector examines nothing. connected_components shows the trade threshold0 makes:

threshold0, threshold1 Collections Legacy peak work, work per MB Incremental peak work, work per MB
500, 10 402 89.7K, 2,512 1.0K, 1,756
1,000, 10 202 89.7K, 2,208 2.0K, 1,751
2,000, 10 102 24.0K, 1,764 4.0K, 1,751
8,000, 10 27 89.7K, 1,764 16.0K, 1,692
2,000, 2 102 85.8K, 2,093 4.0K, 1,751
2,000, 20 102 44.0K, 1,774 4.0K, 1,751

The incremental collector's peak work follows threshold0 while its work per MB holds, and threshold1 changes nothing for it here, since the graph outlives any young generation. The legacy collector's work per MB rises as threshold0 falls, and its peak work jumps whenever one of its collections takes the whole graph: a gen 2 at 500 and 1,000 kB, a gen 1 at 8,000. The section points to the young generation's section for objects that die young, where threshold1 matters.

Depends on

  • #178, the guide's page.
  • #177, so that the page's widgets start their runs as a reader comes to them.

Done when

  • The section is on the guide's page, its widget runs the preset with its controls, and its prose says what the panels show, without figures that calibrating the preset (#117) would move.

issues.title: Write the guide's section on gc.collect() and shutdown
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Section 7 of the guide's outline (#176).

The section

gc.collect() with no argument collects the whole heap under either collector, and the PEP deprecates passing any argument: 0 asks for a young collection and 1 for an increment of the old generation. Every collection, a full one included, resets the countdown to the next one the runtime starts. Shutdown's three full collections free what the frames left, then, once the modules go, the cycles the modules' globals leave behind (#197).

  • Widget: create_gc_cycles at the PEP's threshold0 of 2,000 kB, which calls gc.collect() 1,024 times, so the runtime starts none of its own once the loops begin. Control: threshold0.
  • In the panels: the gc.collect() ticks and the shutdown rule in the heap panels, the full collections' faded work, the heap falling at shutdown, and the figures: work per MB the same in both columns, yield apart, and peak work from start-up alone.

At 2,000 kB the gaps between calls, a ring build of 132 kB and then 8 kB, never reach threshold0, so the runtime starts only start-up's collections. Each call takes the whole heap, about 830 objects, and the call after each drop frees the loop's rings. Work per MB comes to 10,296 legacy and 10,288 incremental. Yield reads 8.6% and 97.3%: the incremental collector marks what sys reaches, and yield leaves marked objects out. Shutdown's first collection frees nothing, since the last loop freed its rings; once the modules go, the second frees the start-up tree, 350 objects, and the third nothing. At a threshold0 of 130 kB the runtime's own collections come back inside each build: the legacy collector's 549 examine rings still being built, 68,000 objects in all, and free nothing, while 13 of the incremental collector's 549 do any work, since each gc.collect() takes its young generation with it.

Depends on

  • #178, the guide's page.
  • #177, so that the page's widgets start their runs as a reader comes to them.

Done when

  • The section is on the guide's page, its widget runs the preset with its control, and its prose says what the panels show, without figures that calibrating the preset (#117) would move.

issues.title: Run shutdown's first full collection before the modules go
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
On the reference branch a worker's shutdown runs three full collections, and the simulator runs two (ADR 0012).

Why

_Py_Finalize calls PyGC_Collect() once the worker's frames have returned. Then finalize_modules takes the modules out of sys.modules and calls _PyGC_CollectNoFail twice (Python/pylifecycle.c on incremental-gc-update-2). Workload.shut_down lets go of the frame roots and of the modules, and only then runs its two. So the simulator frees in one collection the cyclic garbage the frames left and the cyclic garbage the modules left, where the branch frees them in two.

The first collection carries _Py_GC_REASON_MANUAL and the last two _Py_GC_REASON_SHUTDOWN. In gcmon's xml_etree_parse-inc.csv extract, every process whose full collections gcmon caught holds them in that order, and in an xml_etree_parse worker the first examines 3,902 objects and frees 14. No capture can check the simulator's counts for these collections, though: a process can exit between gcmon's ticks, and its last rows go with nothing after them to fold into (#117).

The change

  • Workload.shut_down lets go of every frame root, runs a full collection, lets go of the modules, then runs the two it runs now. All three record as shutdown.
  • ADR 0012, ADR 0005's mention of shutdown, and CONTEXT.md's Shutdown and Full collection say three.
  • The pinned digests of the presets that end in shutdown move: pin them again.

Done when

  • A run that ends in shutdown records three full collections, the first before the modules go, and just check passes.

issues.title: Write the guide's section on a large increment
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Section 6 of the guide's outline (#176).

The section

An increment is a transitive closure, so when one object of a structure reaches all the rest and sys does not reach the structure, an increment that starts from that object takes everything of the structure in pending. The old collection examines it whole, however little of the work budget is left. The PEP's future work names the cost: long pause times when the transitive closure an increment needs is large.

  • Widget: async_tree_io_tg at the PEP's threshold0 of 2,000 kB, whose task tree makes the incremental collector's peak work pass the legacy collector's. Control: the tree's size, labelled Hierarchy size.
  • In the panels: the incremental column's tallest bars, the increments that start from a tree's root, each larger than the last while a tree grows; the peak work figure; and the work budget, which drops far below zero after each large increment.

A frame holds the task tree, so marking from sys leaves it in pending, and the oldest pending object, the tree's root, reaches all of it. At 2,000 kB the first tree's increments examine 7,550, 16,251 and 32,251 objects as it grows, and the largest over the run's four trees examines 33,251. The legacy collector's largest collections are gen 1 collections of 12,004, and its one gen 2 collection, at 266 MB, comes just after a tree has gone and examines 1,253. The tree's size turns the comparison: at 20,000 the legacy collector's peak work passes the incremental collector's, 12,003 to 8,251; at 35,000 the incremental collector's passes, 16,251 to 12,003; and at 65,000, the largest, a gen 2 collection comes while a tree lives, and the legacy collector's passes again, 66,252 to 49,251. The section is titled "A large increment": the largest increment holds the tree, not the whole heap.

Depends on

  • #178, the guide's page.
  • #177, so that the page's widgets start their runs as a reader comes to them.

Done when

  • The section is on the guide's page, its widget runs the preset with its control, and its prose says what the panels show, without figures that calibrating the preset (#117) would move.

issues.title: Write the guide's section on the old generation
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Section 3 of the guide's outline (#176).

The section

An old collection runs between young ones and takes pending objects in two ways. It marks what sys reaches, moving it to visited unexamined, then takes increments of what is left: everything reachable from the least recently scanned pending object, examined together for cycles. The work budget sets how much each takes, so the collector scans the old generation as fast as young collections move objects in. When pending empties, the two spaces swap and a new sweep starts.

  • Widget: connected_components at the PEP's threshold0 of 2,000 kB. Control: the graph's size.
  • In the panels: pending and visited swapping at each sweep, each sweep longer than the last; steady bars of work where the legacy column rises at each gen 1 collection; the work budget lifted by each young collection and spent by the old one after it; and the old collections going idle once the graph stops growing.

xml_etree_parse cannot show an old collection: at every threshold0 its work budget never turns positive, so every old collection is idle, as gcmon's capture of the real worker shows too. connected_components at 2,000 kB ends four sweeps, at 34, 42, 58 and 90 MB. Each young collection moves 4,000 objects of the graph in and the old collection after it marks 4,000, where the legacy collector's gen 1 collections examine 24,000 and it runs no gen 2. Once the graph stops growing, near 118 MB, the old collections go idle and the last sweep leaves 25,492 objects in pending. Work per MB comes out close, 1,315 legacy and 1,302 incremental, shutdown included. sys reaches the whole graph, so the old collections only mark and no increment forms; the section says so, and leaves increments to #184. The graph's size moves the sweeps: none at 5,000 kB, two at 20,000, five at 150,000, while the incremental collector's largest collection stays at 4,000 from 20,000 up.

Depends on

  • #178, the guide's page.
  • #177, so that the page's widgets start their runs as a reader comes to them.

Done when

  • The section is on the guide's page, its widget runs the preset with its control, and its prose says what the panels show, without figures that calibrating the preset (#117) would move.

issues.title: Write the guide's section on the young generation
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Section 2 of the guide's outline (#176).

The section

The nursery, five aging spaces by default, and a young collection that takes the oldest aging space. A survivor gets scanned once before it reaches the old generation, where the legacy collector scans it twice.

  • Widget: json_loads, all transients and no cycles, starting at a threshold0 of 1,000 kB. Controls: threshold0, threshold1.
  • In the panels: the long-lived objects in the aging lane of both heap panels; the legacy column's work while the worker builds them and at its gen 1 collection, against the incremental column's idle stretch and its young collections; the notes under the thresholds; and work per MB, legacy beside incremental.

At the PEP's settings the preset's 21 MB run ends before an object can cross its 24 MB young generation: every incremental collection is idle, and the legacy collector runs 10 gen 0 collections and no gen 1. At a threshold0 of 1,000 kB the run's 700 long-lived objects reach the oldest aging space at 12 MB, and young collections at 12, 14 and 16 MB examine each of them once. The legacy collector examines each in a gen 0 collection as the worker builds them, and again in its gen 1 collection at 12 MB: 1,621 work against 700 before shutdown. A lower threshold0 raises the legacy collector's work per MB before shutdown, 86 at 300 kB and 132 at 100, while the incremental collector's holds at 33. A threshold1 past 18 puts every young collection that would do work after the run's end. The nursery's sawtooth shows only while the worker builds its long-lived objects. The incremental collector's old collections stay idle all run, since its work budget never turns positive; the work budget's section (#182) takes that up.

Depends on

  • #178, the guide's page.
  • #177, so that the page's widgets start their runs as a reader comes to them.

Done when

  • The section is on the guide's page, its widget runs the preset with its controls, and its prose says what the panels show, without figures that calibrating the preset (#117) would move.

issues.title: Write the guide's section on the legacy collector
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Section 1 of the guide's outline (#176).

The section

The legacy collector's three generations: the nursery at 2,000, the aging generation on every 10th collection, and a full collection of the old one only after 100 collections and once new objects pass a quarter of it. On a large heap that rule lets cyclic garbage pile up, and each gen 2 collection is one long pause.

  • Widget: connected_components, its 89,007-object graph alive to the end, starting at a threshold0 of 1,000 kB. Controls: threshold0 and threshold2.
  • In the panels: the legacy column's work spikes at each gen 2 collection, and the peak work figure.

At the PEP's settings the preset's legacy run makes 99 collections and no gen 2 collection before shutdown: with threshold1 and threshold2 at 10, the first gen 2 comes at the 133rd collection. At a threshold0 of 1,000 kB it comes at 133 MB and examines the whole graph, 89,709 objects, where a gen 1 collection examines 12,000 at most and the incremental collector's largest collection 2,000. threshold2 brings the gen 2 collection earlier and moves the legacy column alone. No gen 2 collection in any preset frees anything, so the section states the PEP's point about cyclic garbage piling up in the old generation without pointing at the panels for it; the uncollected garbage section (#183) takes that up.

Depends on

  • #178, the guide's page.
  • #177, so that the page's widgets start their runs as a reader comes to them.

Done when

  • The section is on the guide's page, its widget runs the preset with its controls, and its prose says what the panels show, without figures that calibrating the preset (#117) would move.

issues.title: Keep a survivor that refcounting frees during a collection out of the spaces
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Hypothesis found a run whose record counts a freed object in the spaces. test_each_record_holds_the_heap_and_its_reachable_part_before_and_after fails with (16, 4, 11, 4) != (16, 4, 10, 4): after an old collection, the record's spaces hold 11 objects and the heap 10.

Why

Collector.collect_cycles lists the survivors among the objects it examined before it clears the garbage. Clearing a garbage object can free, by refcounting, an object outside the examined ones, and that can free a survivor whose only outside reference it held. The survivor stays on the list, and the caller puts it in a space: the old collection appends it to visited, so visited holds an object the heap has freed, and survived counts it. CPython's collector unlinks an object from its list as it deallocates it, so its survivors hold only live objects.

Reproduction

The incremental collector at gc.set_threshold(1, 1, 0) with the work budget starting at 0, as the test's collector starts it, 16 kB, seed 0, churn without cycles, and two structures held by sys: a one-object tree, kept to the end, and an own shape of 6 objects with a lifetime of 1 kB, rebuilt every 6 kB, whose links(i) gives [(0, i)] for every object but object 5, which gives [(0, 5), (0, 0), (5, 3)]. At 15 kB the old collection examines objects 2, 5 and 6, and collect_cycles returns 5 as a survivor, which the clear has freed.

from fractions import Fraction

from pep848_sim.collectors.collector import CollectorSettings
from pep848_sim.collectors.heap import Heap
from pep848_sim.collectors.incremental import IncrementalCollector
from pep848_sim.structures import Own, StructureParameters, Tree
from pep848_sim.workload import ChurnParameters, Workload, WorkloadParameters

table = {i: [(0, i)] for i in range(1, 40)}
table[0] = []
table[5] = [(0, 5), (0, 0), (5, 3)]
code = f"TABLE = {table!r}\ndef links(i):\n    return TABLE.get(i, [(0, i)])\n"
churn = ChurnParameters(Fraction(0), 1, 1, Fraction(0), (1, 1))
structures = (
    StructureParameters(Tree(), 1, "module", None, None, 0, False),
    StructureParameters(Own(code=code, line=1), 6, "module", 1, 6, 0, False),
)
collector = IncrementalCollector(CollectorSettings(1, 1, 0))
collector.work_to_do = 0  # so that old collections run within 16 kB
heap = Heap(collector)
Workload(heap, WorkloadParameters(churn, structures, 0)).run_to(16)
print([x for x in collector.space_of if heap.is_freed(x)])  # [5]

The change

  • collect_cycles returns only the survivors still alive after the clear, and counts only those as survived.
  • A test pins the example.

Open questions

  • Whether an object refcounting frees during the clear counts as freed. CPython's collected counts only the unreachable objects the collection found.
  • Whether a preset's run meets the case: the pinned digests say.

Done when

  • No space holds a freed object after a collection, the example passes, and just check passes.

issues.title: Start the guide's page with why a cycle collector
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Section 0 of the guide's outline (#176), and the page the other sections land on.

The change

  • A guide page of its own, in every page's nav, beside the home page. The home page keeps its widget and its reading notes, and points to the guide.
  • Section 0, Why a cycle collector: refcounting frees most garbage the moment it goes, and the collector exists for cycles, which are rare among live objects, so a collector that scans early wastes work. The section sets the two collectors side by side on one allocation clock, and points to "Reading the widget" on the home page. It has no widget.
  • CONTEXT.md's Guide entry names where the guide lives, if the page's place needs a word.

Done when

  • The guide's page is in the nav of every page, with section 0, in both themes and at a phone's width.

issues.title: Show each check as a job of its own in CI
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
CI runs just check as one step of one job, so a pull request's checks list shows one check. A failing check sends you to the log to learn whether ruff, mypy, pyrefly, pytest, tsc, the widget's tests or the Pyodide check broke. The first failure stops the rest, so a second waits for the next push.

The change

  • CI runs each recipe just check runs as a job of its own, named for the recipe: lint, typecheck, test, check-ts, test-js and test-pyodide. The checks list names the one that failed, and a failing job leaves the others to finish.
  • Branch protection requires a check named check, so a last job of that name passes once every recipe's job passes, and the protection stays as it is.
  • Codecov's upload moves into the test job.
  • A test fails when CI's jobs and the recipes just check runs drift apart.
  • CONTRIBUTING.md says how CI runs the recipes.

Done when

  • A pull request's checks list shows a check for each recipe and check, a failing recipe fails check, and just check passes.

issues.title: Check the digests under Pyodide in CI, and retire the stand-in page
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
ADR 0007 makes a run depend only on its inputs, so the record digests the tests pin under CPython hold under Pyodide too, and it asks whoever bumps Pyodide to check them there by hand. The stand-in page does that check in a browser for one workload, the fixed one tests/test_run.py pins, beside two widgets readers don't need, behind a link in every page's nav. The presets' pins go unchecked under Pyodide. The check belongs in CI, where nobody has to remember it, over every pinned run.

The change

  • A check that loads Pyodide in Node, from the pyodide npm package at the version the site's worker loads (314.0.7), runs the fixed workload and each preset under both collectors through pep848_sim.widget.request, the worker's own path, and compares each records digest with its pin.
  • The pins move out of the tests' parameter lists into one file, tests/digests.json, which pytest and the Node check both read.
  • A test keeps the npm package's version and the worker's CDN version in step.
  • just check runs the check as a recipe of its own, so CI runs it on every pull request and push to main, and a local check matches CI's.
  • widget.html and stand-in.js go, with every nav's link to them and the home page's paragraph about them. The stand-in workload stays in the home page's widget until #123.
  • ADR 0007 records the check in CI in place of the hand check, and CONTRIBUTING.md names the recipe and the npm package.
  • #123 drops its items on the stand-in page and a digest page.

Open questions

  • How long the check adds to just check: Pyodide's start in Node and ten preset runs, which a browser runs in about half a second each.

Done when

  • CI fails when a run's digest under Pyodide differs from its pin, the site has no stand-in page and no link to one, and just check passes.

issues.title: Start a widget's runs when a reader comes to it
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The guide embeds a widget in each of its sections, eight in all (#176). A widget asks the page's one worker for its two runs as soon as it connects (ADR 0009), so the guide's page would start sixteen runs on load, and a reader at the top would wait behind the runs of every section below.

The change

  • A widget asks for its runs once it first comes within about a screen of the viewport.
  • A widget the reader scrolls past keeps the runs it started.
  • A link that names a widget in its fragment starts that widget's runs at once.
  • The home page, the playground and the stand-in page, whose first widget sits near the top, draw as they do now.

Done when

  • On a page with several widgets, only the widgets a reader has come near ask for runs, and the first widget's charts draw as soon as they do on a page with one widget.

issues.title: Serve each page the scripts it was deployed with, past the browser's cache
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
GitHub Pages tells browsers to keep every file for 10 minutes (Cache-Control: max-age=600). A reader who had the site open before a deploy can get one deploy's HTML with another's scripts until the copies expire. After #172 deployed, a browser kept the old home page and playground, without the theme switch, and the old gc-widget.js, which ignored the switch, while the stand-in page loaded fresh.

The change

  • just site stamps the files it copies with the deploy, the commit or a hash of their contents, so each page fetches the scripts, the stylesheet and sim.zip it was deployed with.
  • site/ stays hand-written and runs as it is under just serve, as CONTRIBUTING's "There is no build step" asks. An ADR records the stamp.

Open questions

  • How the stamp reaches the modules a script imports. gc-widget.js imports six modules by relative URL, runs.js starts worker.js, and the worker fetches sim.zip. A query string on a page's script tag stops at the first import; a directory per deploy, or an import map, carries it through.
  • What a page cached from the deploy before asks for. With a directory per deploy, the old directory has to stay on gh-pages for 10 minutes or more, or the old page's scripts 404.

Done when

  • After a deploy, a browser that held the previous deploy's pages gets each page with the scripts, the stylesheet and the simulator it was deployed with.

issues.title: Fit the widget to a phone's width
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
ADR 0008 laid the widget out for the desktop and left the phone layout to the Guide milestone. At 375 px, on the home page and the playground, three parts of the widget break:

  • The row of figures keeps its six columns, and their values push it to 744 px inside a 343 px widget, so the page scrolls sideways to 760 px.
  • The top row gives the object graph its 320 px minimum and leaves the select, the controls and the legend a column 0 px wide. They spill under the graph, which covers them.
  • The two columns of panels split 343 px between them. Each chart keeps 120 px of margins, which leaves a plot about 36 px wide.

The change

  • The figures wrap to as many columns as fit, each with legacy beside incremental.
  • Where the graph and the controls can't sit side by side, the top row stacks: the select and the controls, then the graph and its legend.
  • Where a chart's plot has too little room to read, the columns of panels stack, legacy above incremental.
  • No page scrolls sideways at 375 px.

Open questions

  • Whether stacked columns keep #116's crosshair across both, with one a screen below the other, or a narrow widget shows one collector at a time behind a switch.
  • At what width each part stacks.

Done when

  • At 375 px and 768 px, the home page, the playground and the stand-in page show every part of the widget with no overlap and no sideways scroll, in both themes.

issues.title: Switch between a light and a dark theme, in gruvbox colors
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The site follows the system's color scheme and offers no way to change it, and its colors come from the dataviz skill's reference palette.

The change

  • A button at the end of each page's nav switches between the light and the dark theme. A page starts in the system's scheme, and keeps the reader's choice across pages and visits.
  • The pages and the widget take their colors from gruvbox: its medium background and text, its grays for secondary and muted text, the grid and the zero lines, and its neutral accents for the panels' eight series.
  • Each series keeps its gruvbox hue and moves only as far as the dataviz validator needs for its neighbors in each panel to pass, in both themes. Survived, which gruvbox has no hue for, takes a muted violet between its blue and its purple. In the dark theme aging darkens to a mustard, to stay apart from pending.
  • One stylesheet holds the colors for every page and the widget.

Done when

  • The button switches every page and the widget, charts included, without a reload, and the next page keeps the choice.
  • The palette passes the validator for the heap's lanes and stack and for the work stack, in both themes.

issues.title: Read a panel's values from the keyboard
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
#115 shows a panel's values under the pointer. A reader without a pointer can't reach them: no panel takes focus, and the tooltip shows only on hover.

The change

  • Each panel with a tooltip takes focus with Tab: the heap, work and work budget panels in both columns.
  • On focus, the crosshair or outline and the tooltip show at the first collection or bin, or where the pointer last rested in that panel.
  • The left and right arrow keys step to the previous or next collection on the heap panel and the work budget, and to the previous or next bin on the work panel. Home and End go to the first and the last.
  • Leaving the panel hides them, as the pointer leaving does.
  • A focused panel shows a focus ring in the text colors.

Open questions

  • Whether a screen reader hears each step. A live region would announce every value the arrows reach, and every redraw's while runs stream.
  • Whether #116's crosshair across both columns follows the keyboard too.

Done when

  • Tabbing to any panel in either column and stepping with the arrow keys shows the values hover shows, in light and dark mode.

issues.title: Give every widget entry the collector's thresholds and constants, apart from its workload
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The home page's widget gives each entry its own sliders, and only the stand-in and json_loads get threshold0. The thresholds belong to the collector, not the workload, so every entry should offer them, in one place apart from the workload's sliders. A reader should also be able to move the collector constants there and watch what they change.

The change

  • The widget's sliders come in two groups: the workload's, which each entry lists as now, and the collector's, which the widget's JSON lists once for every entry. The widget tells them apart by path: settings.* and constants.* go to the collector's group.
  • The collector's group shows threshold0, threshold1 and threshold2, with threshold2 marked as the legacy collector's alone. The threshold0 and threshold1 sliders also say what they make: the nursery's size, two half-spaces of threshold0 kB, and the aging generation's spaces and size. Nothing new reaches the simulator: the sizes follow from the thresholds, as in the PEP.
  • Under them, a toggle, closed at first, opens sliders for the collector constants: the initial work budget in real objects, the freed-credit multiplier and the long-lived ratio.
  • pep848_sim.widget.controls gives ranges for the new paths: threshold1 from 1, threshold2 from 0, the budget in real objects, the multiplier from 0, the ratio as a share. Each range widens to take in the request's own value. The budget needs a unit for a plain count.
  • The real object's size stays on the playground: it sets the simulator's scale, and moving it would change what every other slider's units mean.
  • CONTEXT.md: the playground stops being the one page that unlocks the collector constants, and a control can move one. A new ADR records the two groups, the shared list and the constants' place on the home page.

Done when

  • Every entry on the home page shows the collector's group, each slider runs both collectors again with its new value, the threshold sliders show the sizes they make, and just check passes.

issues.title: Check the prose the Playground milestone wrote
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The Playground milestone wrote ADRs 0013 to 0016, amended others, added terms to CONTEXT.md, and put prose into the playground's page, the home page and the README, and into the docstrings, comments and messages of the editor, the source, the link and the simulator. Before the milestone closes, check all of it.

Scope

What changed from c689813, before #158, to the milestone's last merge: git diff c689813 main, Markdown, HTML, JavaScript and Python. The First presets milestone's prose stays with #124.

The check

  • /stop-slop on every paragraph, docstring, comment and message the milestone wrote or changed.
  • CONTEXT.md's terms, and its Avoid words. Many carry a qualifier ("bare", "when the two could be confused"), so each hit needs judgment.
  • The code as it stands: each claim in an ADR, a docstring or a comment still holds.
  • The pseudocode's comments stay verbatim (ADR 0003).

Done when

  • One pull request fixes what the check finds, just check passes, and the milestone closes.

issues.title: Link the playground from the top of every page
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The home page links to the playground once, in the More section at its foot, under the widget and every workload's description. A reader who wants to change a workload scrolls past all of it before learning the playground exists, and the paragraph there predates the source view, the constants and the link.

The change

  • A row of links above each page's title: the home page, the playground, the stand-in page and the repository on GitHub, with the current page marked. It scrolls with the page, so it never covers the widget.
  • The home page's introduction names the playground and what it adds.
  • The More section says what the playground does now.

Done when

  • Each page shows the row, the home page's introduction links to the playground, and just check passes.

issues.title: Share a playground run by its link
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
A reader who finds a workload worth showing has no way to send it. The playground's editor holds the whole request, so a link can carry it.

The change

  • The playground's address holds the editor's request: the workload, the collector settings and constants, and any shape's code. Opening the link fills the editor and starts the runs.
  • A link that carries code fills the editor and waits for the reader to press Run. Code in Pyodide can reach the page through js, so a link that ran code on open would let anyone run a script on the site's origin.
  • A button beside the editor copies the link.

Open questions

  • How long a link gets: plain JSON, or compressed with the browser's CompressionStream and base64url.
  • Whether a link names its preset and carries only the fields the reader changed. It would then follow the preset's numbers when the rerun (#117) changes them, where a full request keeps the old ones.

Done when

  • A copied link opens the same editor and the same runs in another browser, a link with code waits for Run, and just check passes.

issues.title: Unlock the collector constants and the real object's size on the playground
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
CONTEXT.md makes the playground the one page that unlocks the collector constants, and the place a reader can change the 64 B the simulator assumes for a real object. Today all four sit in the code:

  • the incremental collector's initial work budget, the pseudocode's -100,000 real objects (collectors/incremental.py:39);
  • its freed-credit multiplier, 2 (collectors/incremental.py:132);
  • the legacy collector's long-lived ratio, a quarter (collectors/legacy.py:75);
  • the 16 real objects to a simulated one (ADR 0002), which divides each count the PEP gives in real objects.

The change

  • A request carries the collector constants and the real object's size beside the collector settings. Their defaults stay the PEP's and the reference branch's (ADR 0003, ADR 0004), so every preset keeps the digests ADR 0007 pins.
  • The playground shows them apart from the collector settings, under a heading that says no Python API changes them.

Open questions

  • Which numbers follow the real object's size: only the counts the PEP gives in real objects, such as the initial work budget, or the presets' sizes too, which ADR 0011 derives from real-object counts in the records.

Done when

  • Changing each constant or the real object's size on the playground changes the runs, the defaults reproduce the pinned digests, and just check passes.

issues.title: Switch the playground's editor to Python source
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The prototype for #153 on prototype/playground tried the workload as Python source beside the widget, its layout C. D won as the playground's default, and C stays one switch away for a reader who wants to compute a size, loop over structures or keep several shapes of their own in one place.

The change

  • A switch on the playground between the legend editor (#153) and the source.
  • The source spells out the workload the legend editor holds: the churn, each structure, the run length, the collector settings and shutdown, in kB, with the prototype's names: Structure, Churn, Settings and a class for each shape.
  • Run and Ctrl+Enter run it. An error shows under the box with its line.
  • Switching back fills the legend editor with the workload the source made. A shape of your own written as a function in the source (#155) carries its code back.

Open questions

  • Whether the source keeps the widget beside it, as in the prototype, or above it, since the panels squeeze at that width.
  • How the request carries the source: in a field of its own, as the prototype's did, or as the spelled-out workload, with the source written again on each switch.
  • The box: a textarea, or CodeMirror from jsDelivr, the choice #155 makes too.

Done when

  • A reader can switch from the legend editor to the source and back without losing a change, run the source, and see an error under the box for a line that fails, in light and dark mode, and just check passes.

issues.title: Write a shape of your own on the playground
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The five shapes model the presets. A reader who wants a doubly linked list, a cache whose values hold their keys, or a graph with a cycle through every node needs a shape the simulator lacks.

A shape is one function. links(i) gives the links object i brings, by index among the structure's objects, and Build.add calls it once per object (structures.py). A reader can write that function.

The change

  • The playground's editor offers a sixth shape, the reader's own: a code box for links(i). The worker's Pyodide runs it (ADR 0009), at about the cost of the five built-in shapes.
  • Before the runs start, the simulator calls the function on the structure's first objects and refuses a link that points past object i or below 0, or anything but pairs of ints. The error and its line show under the box.
  • The simulator counts the cyclic garbage a drop leaves from the shape's links: what sits on a cycle or hangs from one. The built-in shapes declare that count in cyclic_garbage.
  • The object graph samples the reader's shape four children and three levels deep, with a field to change both.
  • A Stop button ends a run stuck in the reader's code, by ending the worker and starting a new one.

Open questions

  • What the reader writes: a bare links(i), or a class whose parameters the editor shows as fields, as the built-in shapes have a width or a length.
  • The code box: a textarea, or an editor such as CodeMirror from jsDelivr at an exact version, as CONTRIBUTING.md asks of every library.
  • How the request carries the code, and whether parse compiles it or hands it to a module of its own.
  • The reader's code runs on the site's origin and can reach the page through Pyodide's js module. That's fine for code the reader wrote. #156 decides what a shared link may run.

Done when

  • A reader can write a shape, see its sample in the object graph with its cycles marked, run it under both collectors, and see an error under the box for a link that points past object i, in light and dark mode, and just check passes.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html: The prototype on prototype/playground (#153) runs a shape of your own in each layout: pick "Your own" as a structure's shape, or write Own(f) in C's source. It counts the cyclic garbage a drop leaves by refcounting the shape's own links, samples the shape three children and four levels deep, and shows a bad link as the simulator's error: links(0) gives (0, 1): a link joins two of objects 0 to 0.

issues.title: Edit a whole workload on the playground
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The home page's widget gives each entry one or two controls: json_loads moves threshold0, xml_etree_parse the size of its parse tree. A reader who wants a bigger tree in async_tree_io_tg, a second graph in connected_components or churn without cycles has no way to ask. CONTEXT.md promises a playground for that: the page with one widget and every control unlocked.

The widget already runs a full workload. parse in pep848_sim.widget.request takes one in place of a preset's name. The site has no page to write one on.

The change

  • A page of its own, site/playground.html, with one widget, linked from the home page. It loads its own Pyodide (ADR 0009).
  • The reader starts from any preset or the stand-in, and the editor fills in its workload, run length and collector settings.
  • Each structure: its shape, one of the five with its own parameter (a chains' width, a hierarchy's branches, a graph's edges a node, a ring's length), its size, root, lifetime, rebuild interval and build churn, and whether it calls gc.collect(). The reader can add, remove and reorder structures.
  • The churn: its lifetime mean, its long-lived share and their lifetimes, its cycle share and cycle size.
  • The run length and the three thresholds.
  • A workload the simulator refuses, such as a build that outlasts its rebuild interval, shows the simulator's words beside the field and starts no run.
  • The object graph and the charts draw as they do on the home page.

Open questions

  • The layout: the editor beside the widget, above it, or in a drawer. A prototype on a branch of its own compares them first.
  • Whether an edit starts the runs again, as a control's release does, or waits for a Run button, since a reader may change several fields before one run.
  • Whether the playground keeps sliders for the fields a slider suits.

Done when

  • Starting from each preset, a reader can change any field, add or remove a structure and see both runs and the object graph again, in light and dark mode, and just check passes.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html:
A prototype on prototype/playground compares four layouts around the real widget:

  • A. A form beside the widget, run with a button.
  • B. A table of structures above the widget, with the churn and the run as sentences of fields. Each change runs both collectors again.
  • C. The workload as Python source beside the widget, run with a button or Ctrl+Enter.
  • D. The editor in the widget's legend, beside the object graph. Each line opens its fields, and each change runs both collectors again.

On that branch, run poetry run just serve and open http://localhost:8000/prototype-playground.html?variant=A. The arrow keys switch layouts.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html: Verdict: D, with C one switch away (fa8949b on prototype/playground). The editor sits in the widget's own legend, beside the object graph, and each change runs both collectors again, as a control's release does. Each structure's numbered line opens its fields under it. A squeezed the code box into a narrow column and the widget beside it, and B pushed the widget down under a table. #157 takes C, the workload as Python source, as a view the reader can switch to.

issues.title: Draw the selected preset's object graph
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
A preset's workload parameters say which structures it builds, what holds each one and which of its links lie on cycles, but the widget shows none of that: it draws only what the collectors did. A reader who picks connected_components sees the heap climb to 90 MB without seeing that it is a graph in a module's globals, whose only cycle runs through the module's functions.

The heap holds too many objects to draw: 89,007 for connected_components' graph, 52,487 for async_tree_io_tg's tree. A sample of each structure, built by the same Shape.links the simulator uses, can show its shape without drifting from the model.

The change

  • The worker answers a request for a preset's sample: for each structure, its first objects and their links as its shape builds them, its root, its size, its lifetime and rebuild interval, and which links lie on a cycle.
  • The widget draws the selected entry's sample: sys and the frame roots, each structure under its root, laid out by its shape, with the links on cycles drawn apart from the rest. Each structure carries its full size, and churn shows as short-lived objects, with the cycles it makes.
  • One drawn object stands for one simulated object, 16 real ones (ADR 0002).

Open questions

  • Where it goes: a panel in the widget, or a figure beside each preset's paragraph under "The workloads".
  • How it lays out: a fixed layout for each shape, or a force layout over them all.
  • How many objects of each structure to sample.
  • Whether a later step colours the sample by the space each object sits in at the clock under the pointer.

A prototype on a branch of its own compares the layouts first.

Done when

  • Picking any preset draws its sample in light and dark mode, each structure under its root with its cycles marked, and just check passes.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html: A prototype on prototype/object-graph compares three ways to draw a preset's sample on the home page, switched by ?variant= and a floating bar: A, a small diagram for each structure in the widget, grouped by what holds it; B, a force-directed diagram after each preset's paragraph; C, a row for each structure in the widget, its diagram beside its builds on the allocation clock. tools/prototype_object_graph.py writes the samples from the presets' real shapes. Verdict to follow.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html: Verdict from the prototype: E (238bed3 on prototype/object-graph). The selected preset's sample as one force-directed graph at the widget's top right, beside the select and the controls, with its legend under them. sys and the frames sit at the top with dashed links to what they hold, links on a cycle stand apart, and the layout fits itself into its frame. It moves the figures down about 150 px; D, the same graph under the controls, moved them 330 px, and B, a graph after each preset's paragraph, sat far down the page.

issues.title: Span the crosshair across both columns
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
#115 draws a crosshair across one column's lanes at the pointer's clock. The two runs share the allocation clock, so a crosshair across both columns lets you compare the legacy and incremental collectors at the same point in the same allocations.

This builds on #115 and lands after it.

The change

  • Hovering any panel in either column draws the crosshair at the same clock in every panel of both columns.

Open questions

  • Whether the column the pointer is not in shows its tooltip too, or the crosshair alone.

Done when

  • Hovering a panel in either column draws the crosshair at the same clock across both columns, in light and dark mode, and a redraw costs about what ADR 0008 records.

issues.title: Show the tooltip once the pointer rests
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
#115's tooltip shows as soon as the pointer enters a panel and follows it, so it covers the plot while you sweep across it.

A prototype compared three ways to show what a panel reads: the tooltip once the pointer rests, the values in each panel's legend row with no tooltip, and the tooltip at once, as now. It lives on prototype/hover-readout (a7e8d36), out of main. The rest delay won, with Escape to hide the tooltip. A sweep across a panel leaves the plot in view, and readers already stop to read. The legend row kept the plot clear too, but each legend had to keep two lines' height so its readings never pushed the charts under the pointer, and the readings shifted sideways as their widths changed. A key held down to show the tooltip lost before the prototype: no reader would find it, and touch has no keys.

The change

  • The crosshair and the work panel's outline follow the pointer at once, as now.
  • The tooltip shows once the pointer has rested 350 ms. A move of more than 3 px hides it until the pointer rests again, so a hand's tremor doesn't.
  • Escape hides the tooltip until the pointer moves on.
  • While runs stream, a shown tooltip holds through redraws, as now.
  • The home page's "Reading the widget" and ADR 0008 say so, and ADR 0008 lists the legend row and the held key among the options turned down.

Done when

  • Sweeping across any panel in either column shows the crosshair or outline and no tooltip, resting shows the tooltip, and Escape hides it, in light and dark mode.

issues.title: Show a panel's values under the pointer
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
You can read the widget's values only off the axes: no chart says what sits under the pointer.

The change

  • The heap panel: at the pointer's clock, a crosshair across the column's four lanes, and a tooltip with the heap, its reachable part, the uncollected garbage and each space, in MB.
  • The work panel: a tooltip on each bar, with the bin's clocks and its marked, survived and freed objects.
  • The work budget: a crosshair, and the budget at the pointer's clock.
  • A record holds the heap before its collection and after it, at one clock (ADR 0010), so a tooltip at a collection's clock shows both.
  • Tooltip text wears the text colors, never a space's or a part's, and each hit target is larger than the mark it covers.

Open questions

  • Plot rebuilds every chart on each redraw while runs stream (ADR 0008), so a tooltip Plot draws vanishes at the next frame. Either hover waits for the runs to finish, or the widget keeps the pointer's clock and draws the tooltip again on each redraw.
  • Each lane is a chart of its own, and Plot's pointer works within one chart, so the widget has to share the pointer's clock across the lanes.

Not here

  • A crosshair across both columns: #116 takes it, once this lands.

Done when

  • Hovering any panel in either column shows the values under the pointer, in light and dark mode, and a redraw costs about what ADR 0008 records.

issues.title: Test the widget's JavaScript in just check
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Nothing runs the widget's JavaScript in CI: tsc checks its types and no more. #110's bug, a line the legend named nursery that traced the whole heap, passed every check, and only a Playwright script outside the repo could measure it.

gc-widget.js cannot load under Node as it stands: it imports Observable Plot from jsDelivr and defines <gc-widget> as it loads. The functions that turn records into a panel's data, heap(), work() and ceiling(), need neither Plot nor the DOM.

The change

  • Move those functions into a module of their own that imports neither Plot nor the DOM, and let gc-widget.js import it.
  • Test them with Node's built-in runner, node --test, so no new package comes in.
  • Keep the tests out of site/: just site copies that folder whole, and the deploy would publish them.
  • A just recipe runs them, and just check runs that recipe, so CI and the deploy gate on it.
  • tsc checks the tests as it checks the site.
  • CONTRIBUTING.md names the recipe and lists the tests under Checks.

Done when

  • just check fails on a bug planted in heap(), such as the nursery's lane holding the whole heap as before #110, and passes on the code as it stands.

issues.title: Show pyrefly's warnings in just typecheck
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
just typecheck runs pyrefly check at its default level, which prints errors alone and exits 0 on a warning. The warning #108 fixed stood unseen for that reason, behind a line saying "1 warning not shown". With --min-severity=warn, pyrefly prints each warning and exits 1: planting #108's warning back for one run shows both.

The change

  • just typecheck runs pyrefly check --min-severity=warn, so a warning fails just check, CI and the deploy.
  • CONTRIBUTING.md's Checks says a pyrefly warning fails the check too.

Done when

  • just check fails with #108's warning planted back, and passes on the code as it stands.

issues.title: Say that BAR caps a bar's width
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The comment above BAR in site/gc-widget.js reads "The tallest a bar of work grows". The work panel insets each bar by (binPx - BAR) / 2 on either side, so BAR caps how wide a bar grows. A bar's height comes from its work.

The change

  • The comment says BAR caps a bar's width.

Done when

  • The comment matches what BAR does, and just check passes.

issues.title: Mark full collections in the widget
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
#125 added full collections: the calls to gc.collect() a structure asks for, and shutdown's two. The widget draws each like any other collection, so a reader can't tell them from the ones the runtime starts, and the work panel can put one in the wrong bin.

  • The work panel puts each collection's work in the bin that holds its clock less threshold0, since an automatic collection covers the threshold0 kB before it. A full collection can come any number of kB after the last one, so its bar can land a bin before the one it ran in.
  • A full collection marks or examines the whole heap in either collector, so its bar can dwarf the automatic collections' around it, with nothing to say gc.collect() ran it.
  • Peak work stands in for the worst pause, and a run that calls gc.collect() will usually find its peak in one of those calls, where both collectors take the whole heap.
  • The heap panel shows the uncollected garbage falling to 0 at each one, and the incremental collector's budget drops to 0, with no mark to say why.

No page runs a workload that calls gc.collect() until #118 adds the first preset.

The change

  • The work panel bins a full collection by its own clock, and sets its work apart from the automatic collections'.
  • The charts mark the clock of each full collection, and say whether gc.collect() or shutdown ran it.

Open questions

  • How to mark them: a rule across every panel at each one, a color or pattern of their own in the work panel, or both. create_gc_cycles calls gc.collect() twice a loop, about every 130 kB, so a rule for each call would crowd a run of many MB.
  • Whether peak work counts full collections, or a figure of their own reports them.

Done when

  • A widget running a preset that calls gc.collect() shows where each full collection ran and what it did, apart from the automatic collections, in light and dark mode, and just check passes.

issues.title: Let a widget offer several presets and show one at a time
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The home page runs two widgets, the stand-in and create_gc_cycles (#133), and #119 to #122 add four more presets. Every widget on a page starts its runs as the page loads, and they all share the page's one Pyodide worker (ADR 0009), so each widget a page adds delays the rest. Readers compare the two collectors within one widget, never across widgets, so stacking widgets adds scrolling and little else.

The change

  • A widget's JSON can hold a list of entries in place of one request. Each entry has a name, a title, its own request (a preset by name, or a workload spelled out) and its own controls.
  • The widget shows a select of the entries' titles and runs one entry at a time.
  • Picking an entry drops the runs under way, as requestRuns already does for a new request, removes the last entry's controls, clears the figures and charts, and starts the new entry's runs with its own controls.
  • The widget keeps each entry's control values while the page stays open, so picking an entry again restores what the reader set.
  • The URL fragment names the widget, by its id, and the entry it shows, by the entry's name, so a link opens a given preset in a given widget. A page with several widgets keeps a pair for each.
  • A widget with one entry shows no select and works as it does today, as the guide's sections need: one preset, and a control or two.
  • CONTEXT.md's Widget says a widget offers one preset or a choice of several.

Not here

  • Keeping each entry's records, so that picking it again draws at once instead of running again: #135.

Done when

  • A widget that lists the stand-in and create_gc_cycles shows one at a time, each with its own controls, which keep their values across switches. A link with a fragment opens a given entry in a given widget, and a widget with one entry shows no select. All of it works in light and dark mode, and just check passes.

issues.title: Let a workload call gc.collect()
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Most of the five benchmarks' cyclic garbage goes in full collections, not in the collections the runtime starts on its own. create_gc_cycles calls gc.collect() twice a loop, 1,024 times per worker. The other four never call it, and pyperf never does either: their full collections come at shutdown, where finalize_modules runs two once it has let go of the modules. A module's functions hold its globals and its globals hold its functions, so whatever hangs off a module turns into cyclic garbage there, and those two collections free it (#118).

In the pyperformance-ms-inc-2 trace, young and old collections find almost none: their yield stays under 0.1%, but for xml_etree's young collections at 2.3%. Full collections free 22% to 97% of the objects they examine. The simulator collects only at multiples of threshold0, so no preset can match its benchmark's yield (#117).

The change

  • A workload parameter that calls gc.collect() at points on the allocation clock, as create_gc_cycles does before each build of its rings and after each drop (#118).
  • A run that ends as a worker does: once the workload lets go of what hangs off the module root (#118), two full collections follow, as finalize_modules runs them.
  • Each collector runs a full collection at those points: the legacy collector a gen 2 collection, the incremental collector what gc.collect() does in it.
  • A full collection leaves a record of its own, and the figures and the work panel count it like any other collection.
  • CONTEXT.md gains an entry for a full collection, which it names today only under Avoid, as gc.collect().
  • A workload that asks for neither runs as before, so the pinned digests hold.

Open questions

  • What the incremental collector's full collection does to its spaces, the sweep and the work budget. The PEP's text comes first and the reference branch where the PEP says nothing (ADRs 0003 and 0004). Whatever we settle goes into an ADR.
  • How the widget marks a full collection on the clock, beyond its work.
  • Whether the parameter takes a period in kB, or ties the calls to a structure's build and drop, as create_gc_cycles makes them.
  • Whether a full collection's record says what started it, gc.collect() or shutdown, as sergey-miryanov/gcmon#229 will let #117 tell them apart in the benchmarks' records.

Done when

  • A workload that calls gc.collect() and a run that ends with a shutdown's two full collections both run under both collectors, each full collection leaves its own record, the pinned digests hold for workloads that ask for neither, and just check passes.

issues.title: Split the heap panel into lanes on one clock
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The heap panel stacks the spaces, the old generation at the bottom and the nursery on top, and draws a line along the top of each band. The nursery's band sits on top, so its line traces the whole heap: it climbs to 48 MB in the home page's legacy run and to 50 MB in its incremental run. The records never hold more than 2 MB of nursery in the first run and 4 MB in the second.

Split the panel into lanes that share the allocation clock:

  • the whole heap, its reachable part, and the gap between them shaded as uncollected garbage;
  • the nursery;
  • the aging generation;
  • the old generation. In the incremental column its pending space and visited space stack, since together they make the old generation and the edge between them shows how far the sweep got.

Every lane in both columns has the same height and one y-scale, so a height reads as the same MB in any lane. Only the top lane's axis names the unit, and the lanes' colors and the legend name what each shows.

ADR 0008 calls the panel stacked, so the change amends it, along with the home page's text on reading the widget.

No test runs the widget's JavaScript, so a Playwright script outside the repo checks the drawn panel: how high the line in the nursery's color reaches.

issues.title: Annotate recording as a generator
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
pyrefly warns on Collector.recording (collector.py:145): annotating a @contextmanager function's return as Iterator[None] is deprecated, and it asks for Generator[None]. just check hides the warning, since pyrefly shows errors alone by default, so it has stood since the recording came in.

The change

  • recording returns Generator[None], imported from collections.abc.

Done when

  • pyrefly check --min-severity=warn reports no warnings, and just check passes.

issues.title: Hold an increment in a space of its own
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
An old collection takes an increment out of pending into a plain list: pending_space.pop(0) takes its first object, and form_transitive_closure takes the rest with pending_space.remove(target). While collect_cycles runs over the increment, no space holds its objects, so when the heap frees one, Collector.remove finds no space and has to check for that. Requiring a space there fails six tests with KeyError, all on old collections.

The reference branch keeps an increment in a list of its own. gc_collect_incremental_old starts one, PyGC_Head increment, and moves the first pending object there with gc_list_move(first, &increment); expand_incremental_region moves each pending object it reaches there the same way.

The change

  • form_transitive_closure returns the increment as a Space, so appending an object to it takes the object out of pending. A plain list keeps the walk's order, since a space cannot grow while it is iterated.
  • Collector.remove(x) drops its check and removes x from space_of[x], and its docstring stops explaining a missing space.
  • The PEP names form_transitive_closure without defining it, so holding the increment in a space keeps to the pseudocode (ADR 0003).

Builds on #105, which names the map space_of.

Done when

  • The tests pass unchanged, the two pinned digests included. The space keeps the order the walk reached, so survivors reach visited in the order they do now.
  • Every object the heap frees sits in a space when it goes.

issues.title: Let a space move its own objects
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Space and Collector reach into each other. Space.append, pop and remove call Collector._place, and _place edits the _objects of the old space and the new one. Two places record where an object sits, space._objects and Collector._spaces, and only _place, in the other class, keeps them in step. The name _spaces reads as the collector's spaces, but it maps each object to its space.

The map stays. It plays PyGC_Head's part: it keeps each object in one space and lets an append take the object out of the space it was in. It stays on the collector's side, not in SimulatedObject, since the heap owns an object's record and the collector owns its space, as gc.c alone reads and writes PyGC_Head.

The change

  • Space moves its objects itself. It holds the collector's map, and append, pop and remove take an object out of the space it sits in, editing another Space's _objects from within the class.
  • Collector._spaces becomes space_of, which only spaces write.
  • Collector._place goes. Collector.remove(x), which the heap calls when it frees x, takes x out of its space if it has one: an old collection takes objects out of pending before collect_cycles frees some of them.
  • Space(collector) and the list methods the pseudocode reads stay as they are.

Done when

  • The tests pass unchanged, the two pinned digests included. No test reads _spaces or _place.
  • Neither Space nor Collector touches a private member of the other.

issues.title: Count each collection in the base collector
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The legacy collector's _collect and the incremental collector's young_collection count a collection the same way: they take the number of objects to examine, call collect_cycles, and append CollectionCounts(kind, 0, survived, freed). old_collection sums survived and freed over its increments itself. Moving _collect into Collector would serve the young collection alone, since an old collection calls collect_cycles once per increment.

The change

  • collect_cycles adds the objects it examined and freed to running totals on the collector, so a test can still call it outside a collection.
  • recording(kind) takes the totals' difference across the collection and writes the CollectionCounts and the Record. The legacy collector takes the kind from select_generation, the incremental one from young_next.
  • old_collection adds the objects scan_reachable marked, the one count the base cannot see.
  • The legacy _collect goes, and each collect_generationN calls collect_cycles itself. The legacy collector keeps the reference branch's functions (ADR 0004).
  • young_collection reads as the PEP's pseudocode, and old_collection returns at the swap as the pseudocode does, dropping its break (ADR 0003).
  • The Collector docstring says where a record's counts come from.

Done when

  • The tests pass unchanged, the two pinned digests included.
  • Neither collector builds a CollectionCounts.

issues.title: Remove a closed pull request's preview completely
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Closing #99 removed its preview but left one empty file on gh-pages: pr-preview/pr-99/.nojekyll. When the deploy action clears a folder, it deletes everything but a .nojekyll or CNAME the incoming folder lacks (src/git.ts, v4.9.0). Each preview copies site/.nojekyll into its folder, so each closed pull request would leave one behind.

Pages reads .nojekyll at the branch's root, and the deploy from main puts one there.

The change

  • The Preview workflow deletes _site/.nojekyll after just site, so a preview's folder never holds one.
  • One commit on gh-pages deletes pr-preview/pr-99/.nojekyll.

Done when

  • The pull request for this issue gets a preview with no .nojekyll in its folder.
  • Closing it leaves nothing of it under pr-preview/.
  • gh-pages holds no pr-preview/pr-99/.

issues.title: Preview each pull request's site
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The site deploys only from main, so a pull request's changes to the pages or the widget can be seen only after it merges, or by building it locally.

Give each pull request a preview under the published site, at pr-preview/pr-N/, linked from a comment on the pull request and removed when it closes. Pages then serves a gh-pages branch instead of the artifact actions/deploy-pages uploads: a merge to main publishes to the branch's root after just check, as it does now, and leaves the previews alone. The site's paths are relative, so it runs the same in a subfolder. A pull request from a fork gets no preview, since its token cannot write to the repository.

The live site must not go down during the switch. CONTRIBUTING.md's Publishing says how the site and the previews deploy.

Done when this issue's own pull request shows a working preview, and the site still deploys from main after the merge.

issues.title: Show the widget on the home page
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The Simulator and Widget milestones built a widget that runs both collectors in the browser, and every merge publishes it, but the home page still says the project "is still being designed" and links nowhere near it. The widget lives on widget.html, which no page links to.

Put the stand-in widget, with its controls, on the home page, under a few lines that say what each part shows: the row of figures, the heap by space with its reachable line, work in bins, and the work budget. Say what the workload is, that it stands in for the presets to come, and that the guide comes after them. Link widget.html, with its second widget and the digests, at the foot of the page beside the source. The README's line about the site says the same.

The Guide milestone writes the real text and the phone layout; this page only has to show the widget and say what a reader is looking at. Its prose goes through /stop-slop and uses CONTEXT.md's terms. After the merge, v0.1.0 tags it.

Done when the published home page runs the stand-in widget and its text matches what the widget shows.

issues.title: Check the prose the Widget milestone wrote
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The last issue under Widget has closed. Before the milestone closes, check the prose it wrote since the last pass, #79:

  • CONTEXT.md: the new "Control" entry;
  • ADR 0007: the clause on how the thresholds are built;
  • CONTRIBUTING.md: npm ci and Node in the setup, the check-py and check-ts recipes, tsc under Checks, and The package;
  • the site: the text of widget.html, the widget's labels and messages, and the comments in gc-widget.js, runs.js, worker.js and stand-in.js;
  • the docstrings and comments in src/pep848_sim/widget/, the package __init__ files, and the new ones in workload.py;
  • the docstrings and comments in the tests the milestone added or grew: test_controls.py, test_figures.py, test_parts.py, test_request.py and test_workload.py;
  • the comments in justfile, the two tsconfigs, the setup action, dependabot.yml and .pre-commit-config.yaml.

Check each against three things:

  • the /stop-slop rules, as Prose in CONTRIBUTING.md says;
  • CONTEXT.md's terms and its Avoid words. Many of those words are avoided only bare or in one sense, so a grep finds candidates and each needs a reading. Most hits so far are code names or allowed senses ("kind" in Record.kind, "cycle" as a reference cycle, "step" as a slider's), but "threshold" alone in workload.py's comments, meaning a lifetime threshold, deserves a look beside the collector's three;
  • the code as it stands. The widget grew figures and controls over the milestone, and two comments look older than the code: gc-widget.js opens by describing the figures and panels but not the controls, and stand-in.js speaks of "one widget's two runs" on a page that now holds two widgets beside its own digest runs.

The pseudocode's comments stay verbatim (ADR 0003), as does the wording CONTRIBUTING.md keeps exact. Merged pull requests, closed issues and commit messages stay as they are.

Done when the prose passes all three checks, just check passes, and nothing but prose has changed.

issues.title: Build geometric lifetimes for large means without the wait
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
geometric_thresholds takes 0.52 s for a churn lifetime mean of 1,000 kB and 5.65 s for 3,000 kB under CPython. Each run builds its own thresholds before its first record, so a widget's two runs wait twice that, and longer under Pyodide. It builds about 22 thresholds per kB of mean, and its two ints grow with each one, so the time grows faster than the square of the mean.

A control on the churn lifetime mean (#83) would make a reader wait that long after each release. Either build the thresholds faster, keeping them exact (ADR 0007), or cap the mean a control can reach.

Done when the thresholds for the largest mean a control allows take a few milliseconds, they equal what geometric_thresholds gives today for every mean, and the pinned digests in tests/test_run.py stay as they are.

issues.title: Re-run a widget when a reader releases a control
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
A widget shows the controls its page names, each a workload parameter or a collector setting. Moving a control starts nothing. When the reader releases it, the widget cancels its two runs and starts both again with the new value. The re-run reuses the page's Pyodide (ADR 0009); in prototype #7 the first chart came 80 to 115 ms after Pyodide was ready.

  • The page names the controls in the widget's markup, and a widget the page gives none shows none. The playground, with every control and the collector constants, belongs to the Guide milestone.
  • Each control's range keeps the workload valid: StructureParameters refuses a build that outlasts its rebuild interval, for one.
  • Two widgets on one page share the worker (#80). Releasing a control in one leaves the other's runs going.

Done when the stand-in page holds two widgets with a few controls each, and releasing a control re-runs its own widget and no other.

issues.title: Split the package into the collectors, the workload and the widget
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
src/pep848_sim holds nine modules side by side. They already import one way, and three parts would show it:

  • pep848_sim.collectors: the heap, the collector base, and the incremental and legacy collectors. ADRs 0003 and 0004 govern this part. The heap and the collectors import each other, so they share it.
  • pep848_sim itself: the workload, its structures and a run.
  • pep848_sim.widget: what the page's worker calls, request and figures. Its JavaScript stays in site/.

The collectors import nothing else from the package, and only the widget imports the widget.
