A test reads each module's imports and fails on one against that direction, so the split holds as the package grows. The tests stay in one folder: six of them import strategies from one another. The worker's pyimport paths and the comments in site/runs.js follow the move, and CONTRIBUTING.md names the parts.

Done when the modules sit in their parts, the pinned digests hold, and the import test fails on a planted import against the direction.

issues.title: Lead the widget with a row of figures
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
A row of figures leads the widget, above the panels (#81), each legacy beside incremental (ADR 0008):

  • peak work;
  • peak uncollected garbage, which comes as a collection starts (ADR 0010);
  • work per MB;
  • yield, over the whole run;
  • collections;
  • sweeps for the incremental run, gen 2 collections for the legacy one.

The figures come from the records alone, and they update as the records stream in. This issue's seams settle where the figures are derived: in Python, where the tests reach them, or in the widget's JavaScript. Either way, only correctly rounded arithmetic derives them (ADR 0007).

Done when the stand-in page shows the six figures for both runs as they stream, and a test or a worked example in the pull request checks each one.

issues.title: Type check the site's JavaScript in just check
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
CONTRIBUTING.md says the site's JavaScript has no tooling in CI: each file starts with // @ts-check, and only an editor checks it. The site now holds four scripts, and #80 and #81 each found type errors by running tsc by hand. Let just check run tsc too, so CI and the deploy gate on it.

  • just check-py runs ruff, mypy, pyrefly and pytest, and just check-ts runs tsc. just check runs both.
  • TypeScript 7.0.2, pinned in a private package.json and locked in package-lock.json. It checks the scripts from their JSDoc in strict mode, with no build step and nothing emitted.
  • site/tsconfig.json checks the page's scripts against the DOM, and site/tsconfig.worker.json checks worker.js against a web worker's globals.
  • The CI setup action installs Node 24 with actions/setup-node, then runs npm ci. Dependabot moves the npm packages with the same 7-day cooldown as the rest.
  • CONTRIBUTING.md names tsc in its setup, its recipes and its Checks.

Done when just check fails on a type error planted in a page script and on one planted in the worker, and passes on the scripts as they stand.

issues.title: Draw the heap, work and work budget panels in `<gc-widget>`
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
<gc-widget>, one Web Component in site/, draws the runs the worker streams (#80) as ADR 0008 lays them out: two columns, legacy on the left and incremental on the right, each with three panels whose y-scales the columns share.

  • The heap by space, stacked, with the reachable line on top, from both readings in each record (ADR 0010). The gap between the stack and the line is the uncollected garbage.
  • Work, binned into about forty bins a run, each a whole number of collection intervals, stacked as marked, survived and freed.
  • The work budget as a step line, with a bold zero line and the negative stretch shaded. The legacy column shows a line saying it keeps none.

Observable Plot loads from jsDelivr at an exact version. The x-axis spans the run length from the start. The widget redraws at most once an animation frame, with the records that have arrived, and each y-scale grows to the next of 1, 1.2, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 times a power of ten. Prototype #9's variant C, on the prototype/09-widget-layout branch, is the starting point. The layout is for the desktop; the Guide milestone takes up the phone.

Done when the stand-in page draws both runs in the three panels as they stream, and the pull request records how long a redraw takes at the stand-in's count of collections. Prototype #9 fit about 600 collections a run in a 60 Hz frame.

issues.title: Stream both runs to the page from one worker
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
A page makes one worker as it loads, and every widget on the page runs its runs there (ADR 0009). This issue builds that worker and the Python it calls, with a bare page to watch the records arrive.

  • site/worker.js starts Pyodide 314.0.7 from jsDelivr, fetches and unpacks sim.zip, and imports the simulator.
  • A module in pep848_sim takes a workload, collector settings, a run length and every as JSON values, and returns the two runs, legacy and incremental. It imports nothing from the browser, so the tests run it under CPython.
  • The worker alternates the two runs. After each part it posts the records as the run yielded them, then returns to its event loop on a MessageChannel it makes for that yield (ADRs 0006 and 0007).
  • Each request names its widget. A widget's new request drops that widget's runs still going.
  • site/widget.html, which index.html does not link to, sends a stand-in workload and shows each run's records arriving. The stand-in is not a preset, and it goes when First presets brings the first one.

Done when:

  • just check passes with the new module covered;
  • the stand-in page, served by just serve, shows both runs' records arriving;
  • in the worker, the two runs tests/test_run.py pins give the digests it pins (ADR 0007);
  • the pull request records the µs per kB both runs take under Pyodide. On a workload like prototype #6's, with 8 MB of module globals and a 20 MB tree rebuilt every 80 MB, the simulator takes 2.3 to 2.6 µs per kB under CPython, about twice the prototype's time. ADR 0006 cites 1.3 to 1.7 µs per kB under Pyodide. If the new figure changes what ADR 0006 decides, amend it.

issues.title: Check the prose the Simulator milestone wrote
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The last issue under Simulator has closed. Before the milestone closes, check the prose it wrote since the last pass, #42:

  • CONTEXT.md: the new "Churn lifetime" and "Alive" entries, and the reworded "Workload parameter" and "Sweep";
  • ADR 0010;
  • the docstrings and comments in src/pep848_sim/ and in the tests.

Check each against three things:

  • the /stop-slop rules, as Prose in CONTRIBUTING.md says;
  • CONTEXT.md's terms and its Avoid words. Many of those words are avoided only bare or in one sense, so a grep finds candidates and each needs a reading. Three look real so far: "node" in Tree, "least recently scanned" in two comments in test_incremental.py, and "random steps" in test_heap.py;
  • the code as it stands. Names and owners moved during the milestone: the collector took over freeing cyclic garbage, the heap became a dict, and collect came back as the heap's call. A docstring written before a move can describe the old code.

The pseudocode's comments stay verbatim (ADR 0003), as do the C field names in the struct maps and the wording CONTRIBUTING.md keeps exact. Merged pull requests, closed issues and commit messages stay as they are.

Done when the prose passes all three checks, just check passes, and nothing but prose has changed.

issues.title: Runs that stream their records
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
One run of a workload by one collector under one set of collector settings, as the worker will drive it, over #25 to #29.

  • A run is a generator that yields its newest records every few collections (ADR 0006). It keeps its state in the generator, none at module level, and owns its random.Random(seed) (ADR 0007). It runs from an empty heap to the run length on the allocation clock, which it takes as an input.
  • One record per collection, of ints and strings: the allocation clock, which collection it was, marked, survived and freed, the work budget, the sweep, the heap by space, and its reachable part. Decide here, with an ADR, whether a record holds the heap before its collection as well as after it. #9 found the nursery near zero in a heap read after a collection, and uncollected garbage, whose peak is one of ADR 0008's figures, is highest just before one.
  • The records carry what ADR 0008's figures need: peak work, peak uncollected garbage, work per MB, yield, collections, and sweeps or gen 2 collections.
  • The two runs of a workload, one per collector, allocate the same objects in the same order.

Tests: the two collectors' runs allocate the same objects at the same points on the allocation clock; yielding in parts of any size gives the same records as one part; a test pins the records digest of one fixed workload per collector under CPython (ADR 0007). The presets bring their own digests.

Done when just check passes with the digests pinned.

issues.title: Run a workload by one collector, streaming its records
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #30, after #74.

  • A run is one workload by one collector under one set of collector settings, from an empty heap to a run length on the allocation clock, which it takes as an input. It is a generator that yields its newest records every few collections, and the rest at the end (ADR 0006). It keeps its state in the generator, none at module level, and its workload owns the run's random.Random(seed) (ADR 0007).
  • A run that ends on a collection boundary collects there as well, as one that went on would at its next allocation.
  • The two runs of a workload, one per collector, allocate the same objects in the same order: the workload's draws never depend on what a collector does, and both collectors collect at the same boundaries (ADR 0004, ADR 0005).

Tests: the two collectors' runs allocate the same objects at the same points on the allocation clock; yielding in parts of any size gives the same records as one part; a test pins the records digest of one fixed workload per collector under CPython (ADR 0007). The presets bring their own digests.

Done when just check passes with the digests pinned. With #74, this finishes #30.

issues.title: Record each collection, with the heap before and after it
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #30. The run generator builds on it.

  • Each collection leaves one record of ints and strings (ADR 0007): the allocation clock; which collection it was, young or old, or gen 0, 1 or 2; marked, survived and freed; the work budget after it; the sweep; and, before the collection and after it, the heap by space and its reachable part.
  • The record holds the heap before its collection as well as after, as the reference branch's struct gc_generation_stats keeps heap_size_start and heap_size_stop. A heap read after a collection alone shows the nursery near zero (#9), and uncollected garbage, whose peak is one of ADR 0008's figures, peaks just before one. An ADR records the decision.
  • The heap's trigger calls one base-class method around each collection, which notes the heap before and after; each collector's own collect stays as the pseudocode or the branch writes it.
  • Each collector names the spaces it reports, in the order a stacked chart draws them: the incremental collector the nursery, aging, pending and visited, with reachable, sys and the marking worklist, among the visited; the legacy collector the nursery, aging and old. The legacy collector keeps no budget and runs no sweeps, so its records hold 0 for both; the figure of gen 2 collections counts the records of that kind.
  • The records carry what ADR 0008's figures need: peak work, peak uncollected garbage, work per MB, yield, collections, and sweeps or gen 2 collections.

Tests: the records of hand-built runs under each collector, field by field, before and after a collection that frees garbage; the sweep moves on at each swap; under Hypothesis, each record's heap before and after adds up to the alive objects, its reachable part to what the tests' walk reaches, and the uncollected garbage before one collection is never below the uncollected garbage after the one before.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Legacy collector after the reference branch
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The three-generation collector the reference branch keeps behind -X gc=legacy (ADR 0004), over the heap of #25, with the collect_cycles of #27.

  • It runs every threshold0 kB allocated, gross, as the branch counts them, where CPython 3.15 counts net objects. Both runs of a widget then collect at the same boundaries, as ADR 0005 requires.
  • Lay out the spaces as the reference branch's GC state for the legacy collector does, and link its struct fields in the pull request.
  • A gen 0 collection takes the nursery and moves its survivors to the aging generation. A gen 1 collection takes the nursery and aging, a gen 2 collection takes the whole heap, and both move their survivors to the old generation.
  • The collector picks the oldest generation whose count is over its threshold, as CPython's collect_generations does. It holds a gen 2 collection back until the objects that survived gen 1 collections since the last gen 2 reach 25% of those the last gen 2 left: the long-lived ratio, a collector constant. Check each rule against Python/gc.c on incremental-gc-update-2 and link the lines in the pull request.
  • Its work is survived plus freed. It marks nothing and keeps no work budget.

Invariants, under Hypothesis: no reachable object is ever freed; every live object sits in exactly one space; a gen 2 collection leaves no uncollected garbage.

Done when example tests walk a hand-built heap through each collection, the invariants hold, and just check passes.

issues.title: Incremental collector after the PEP's pseudocode
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The collector PEP 848 proposes, over the heap of #25. It follows the PEP's pseudocode over the reference branch (ADR 0003).

  • collect() runs every threshold0 kB and alternates old and young collections, starting with an old one. The nursery is two half-spaces, and the aging generation is threshold1 / 2 aging spaces, rounded up. The first young collections take empty aging spaces, so they are idle. The collector ignores threshold2, as the PEP says.
  • The heap triggers each collection, for both collectors, through the Collector base: at the start of an allocation, allocate or allocate_unseen, it checks whether the clock sits on a threshold0 boundary, collects if so, and only then moves the clock on. The workload has let go of that kB's lifetimes by then, so ADR 0005's order holds. CPython sets a flag that the eval loop checks later, which can delay a collection past its threshold; the simulator collects at the boundary and leaves that delay for later. A run that ends on a boundary collects there as well (#30).
  • Write the collector as the pseudocode reads, as close as Python lets it: its names, its functions and their lines in the same order (#66). A comment maps each name to its field in the reference branch's GC state, and the pull request links those fields. The collector's behaviour follows the pseudocode (ADR 0003).
  • A young collection takes the oldest aging space, credits the work budget with its survivors and moves them to the visited space. The nursery becomes the newest aging space: the collector puts its nursery first among its aging spaces and starts an empty one, as the pseudocode does (#34).
  • An old collection runs while the work budget is positive. First it marks what the module root reaches and debits what it marked. Then it collects increments, each the transitive closure of the least recently scanned pending object, debiting what the increment examined and crediting twice what it freed. Once pending runs empty, the collector swaps pending and visited, puts sys back to be marked, sets the budget to 0, and ends the sweep.
  • The pseudocode's visited.remove(sys) comes after the swap, when sys sits in the new pending_space: read it as taking sys out of the space that holds it. Read the bare pending and visited as pending_space and visited_space (#67).
  • collect_cycles finds the unreachable objects among those it examines (#51) and frees them with the heap's free_cyclic_garbage (#36, #49), which takes them off the uncollected garbage count. The legacy collector reuses it.
  • Each collection counts marked, survived and freed, and its work is their sum.
  • Collector constants: the initial work budget of -100,000 real objects, -6,250 at 64 B (ADR 0002), and the freed-credit multiplier, 2. CONTEXT.md lets the playground change the 64 B, and 1024 / 48 is not an integer; the size stays at 64 B until the playground, which settles a rounding rule.

Invariants, under Hypothesis: no reachable object is ever freed; every live object sits in exactly one space; the work budget moves by exactly what the counters say, the swap's reset to 0 aside; cyclic garbage wholly in the old generation when a sweep starts is freed by its end, unless newer garbage holds it, which leaves it for a later sweep (#67).

Done when example tests walk a hand-built heap through the pseudocode line by line, the four invariants hold, and just check passes.

issues.title: Incremental collector: old collections
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #27, after #66.

  • old_collection follows the pseudocode line by line (ADR 0003). While work_to_do is positive: if reachable holds anything, scan_reachable marks it, moving it to visited_space and what it references from pending_space onto reachable, and debits what it moved. Otherwise it takes the least recently scanned pending object, forms the transitive closure of pending objects from it, debits the increment's size, collects its cycles (#65), moves the survivors to visited_space and credits twice what it freed. Once pending_space runs empty, it swaps the two spaces, puts sys back on reachable, sets work_to_do to 0 and ends the sweep.
  • The pseudocode's visited.remove(sys) comes after the swap, when sys sits in the new pending_space; read it as taking sys out of the space that holds it. Read the bare pending and visited in scan_reachable and in forming the increment as pending_space and visited_space.
  • Each old collection counts marked, survived and freed, and its work is their sum.
  • The freed-credit multiplier is 2, the pseudocode's.

Tests: a hand-built heap walks through old_collection line by line, a swap included; under Hypothesis, #27's four invariants: no reachable object is ever freed; every alive object sits in exactly one space; work_to_do moves by exactly what the counters say, the swap's reset to 0 aside; cyclic garbage wholly in the old generation when a sweep starts is freed by its end, unless newer garbage holds it. An increment follows references forward, so an older cycle that a newer one holds survives its increment and waits for a later sweep; an example pins that.

Done when just check passes. With #65 and #66, this finishes #27.

issues.title: Incremental collector: spaces, alternation and young collections
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #27, after #65.

  • The code reads as the PEP's pseudocode does, as close as Python lets it: its names (nursery, aging, pending_space, visited_space, reachable, work_to_do, young_next), its functions (collect, young_collection, old_collection, scan_reachable), and their lines in the same order. A comment maps each name to its field in the reference branch's GC state, and the pull request links those fields.
  • reachable is a space like the others, and sys starts on it, as the pseudocode starts it.
  • aging holds ceil(threshold1 / 2) spaces, 5 at the default threshold1 of 10, as the PEP's prose and #27 set it; the pseudocode starts it as [[]].
  • collect() alternates young and old collections, starting with an old one (young_next = False).
  • A young collection takes the oldest aging space, collects its cycles (#65), credits work_to_do with the survivors, moves them to visited_space, puts the nursery first among the aging spaces and starts a new one. The first ceil(threshold1 / 2) young collections take empty spaces and are idle.
  • Each collection counts survived and freed. old_collection does nothing until #67.
  • A real object stays at 64 B until the playground, so work_to_do starts at -6,250 (ADR 0002) and no rounding rule is needed yet.

Tests: a hand-built heap walks through young_collection line by line; the first young collections are idle; under Hypothesis, no reachable object is ever freed, and every alive object sits in exactly one space.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Free cyclic garbage in the collector, as CPython's delete_garbage does
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Follows #65; before #66.

free_cyclic_garbage sits on the heap, but freeing cyclic garbage is the collector's work. CPython's delete_garbage calls each unreachable object's tp_clear, which lets go of the object's references, and refcounting deallocates what reaches zero; the runtime keeps refcounting and memory.

  • The heap gives up free_cyclic_garbage and gains clear(x), after tp_clear: it lets go of every reference x holds, and refcounting frees what that leaves at zero, x too once nothing holds it. Only a collection clears, and only objects it found unreachable, so whatever a clear frees comes off the uncollected garbage count (#36).
  • collect_cycles frees what it finds (#51) by clearing each unreachable object the cascade has not freed yet, as delete_garbage does.
  • The heap's check that nothing outside a group holds it goes. The group now comes from find_unreachable in the same method, and #51's property shows that nothing outside holds what it finds. The heap keeps its own asserts on counts.

Tests: a clear frees what the object alone held and lowers the count by what it freed; an object that something still holds stays alive after a clear, holding nothing; collect_cycles frees a group with what it alone holds, and leaves a cycle the group held alive and counted; #36's state machine frees its dropped cycles through collect_cycles.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Trigger collections at threshold0 boundaries, and collect cycles
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #27. The legacy collector (#28) builds on it too.

  • A collection reads references and counts and frees what it finds, so it needs the heap: Heap(collector) hands the collector itself.
  • At the start of each allocation, allocate or allocate_unseen, the heap checks whether the clock sits on a multiple of threshold0, the start of the run aside. If it does, it calls collector.collect(), and only then moves the clock on. The workload has let go of that kB's lifetimes by then, so ADR 0005's order holds (#61). Both collectors take the trigger from the Collector base, with one threshold0 in kB (ADR 0004).
  • collect_cycles(objects) in the Collector base finds the unreachable objects among objects (#51), frees them with the heap's free_cyclic_garbage (#36, #49), and returns the survivors in their order and the number freed, as the pseudocode's collect_cycles does. Both collectors call it.

Tests: a stub collector records each collection: one at each multiple of threshold0, from either kind of allocation, before the clock moves and after the workload's let-gos for that kB; collect_cycles returns the survivors in order and the number it freed, and the uncollected garbage count drops by that number.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Structures and their shapes
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Objects a workload builds in one shape, hangs off one root and drops together, over the heap of #25 and the churn of #26.

  • Workload parameters: a structure's shape, size, root (module or frame), lifetime and rebuild interval, and the build's churn: the churn allocations after each built object.
  • A build allocates the structure in the order its shape gives, with the build's churn after each built object. The workload builds a long-lived structure once and never drops it. It rebuilds a repeating structure every rebuild interval, and the builds never overlap: the simulator refuses a workload whose build outlasts its interval.
  • Each built object comes held by its allocating frame (#35). The build lets go of that frame root once it has linked the object into the structure; the structure's root keeps its own until the structure's lifetime ends.
  • At the end of a structure's lifetime, its root lets go. A structure whose shape has cycles becomes cyclic garbage, and refcounting frees one without on the spot.
  • A workload is its background churn and its structures, seed included.
  • Two shapes to start, the ones the prototypes used: chains of module globals, and a tree with parent pointers off a frame root. The First presets milestone adds the shapes its presets need.

Tests: a dropped tree with parent pointers becomes cyclic garbage; refcounting frees dropped chains on the spot; builds start where the rebuild interval puts them on the allocation clock. Under Hypothesis: for any workload, builds never overlap.

Done when a test can run a workload of churn and both shapes to any point on the allocation clock, and just check passes.

issues.title: A workload of churn and structures, run to any point
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #29, after #60.

  • A workload is its background churn, its structures and its seed (#26, #60). run_to(clock) runs it one kB at a time, as churn alone does.
  • Churn and structures share one schedule of let-gos, so each kB keeps ADR 0005's order: the clock moves, the workload lets go of each lifetime that ends there, then a collection runs if the kB is a boundary. Churn gains a one-kB step, so that a build puts its churn allocations after each built object.
  • The workload builds its long-lived structures first, one after another, from the start of the run. Each repeating structure falls due at the multiples of its rebuild interval, and a build due while another runs waits for it to finish. Builds then never overlap, and a workload with one repeating structure builds where its interval puts it.

Tests: builds start where the rebuild interval puts them on the allocation clock; the build's churn follows each built object; under Hypothesis, for any workload, builds never overlap, run_to(c) leaves the clock at c, and the uncollected garbage count equals what the tests' walk does not reach.

Done when a test can run a workload of churn and both shapes to any point on the allocation clock, and just check passes.

issues.title: Structures: two shapes, built, dropped and rebuilt
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #29, after #59.

  • StructureParameters: the shape, the size, the root (module or frame), the lifetime and rebuild interval, and the build's churn, the churn allocations after each built object. A long-lived structure has no lifetime and no rebuild interval.
  • Two shapes to start, the ones the prototypes used, each an allocation order and the links each new object gets:
    • chains of module globals: the structure's root, a module, holds width chains, a shape parameter (64 in the prototype), and each new object goes on the end of the next chain in turn;
    • a binary tree with parent pointers: node i links to node (i - 1) // 2, and that node links back.
  • A structure builds one object per kB, in its shape's order. Each built object comes held by its allocating frame (#35), and the build lets go of that root once it has linked the object in. A frame-rooted structure's root keeps its allocating root until the structure's lifetime ends; a module-rooted one hangs off sys and lets go of its own.
  • When its lifetime ends the structure drops: the workload lets go of its frame root, or cuts sys's reference to it (#59). A shape with cycles declares its size as uncollected garbage (#36), and refcounting frees one without on the spot.
  • The simulator refuses a repeating structure whose build, size × (1 + build_churn) kB, outlasts its rebuild interval. Putting the build's churn between built objects falls to the workload.

Tests: a dropped tree with parent pointers becomes cyclic garbage, its whole size counted; refcounting frees dropped chains on the spot, from either root; a build allocates and links in its shape's order; a structure whose build outlasts its interval is refused.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Cut a reference between two objects
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #29. The structures build on it.

  • heap.unlink(source, target, leaves_unreachable=0) takes away one reference from source to target, as a program does when it rebinds a global or removes an item from a container. The target's count drops, and refcounting frees whatever that leaves at zero, as letting go of a frame root does.
  • A structure rooted on a module hangs off sys, so the workload drops it by cutting sys's reference to its root. As with let_go_frame_root, the workload says how many objects the cut leaves unreachable: a shape with cycles leaves its whole size (#36).
  • The heap refuses to cut a reference that source does not hold. Where source holds target more than once, the cut takes the first, and the rest keep their order.

Tests: cutting a chain's last reference frees it whole; cutting one of two references to a target leaves it held by the other, and the source's remaining references in order; a missing reference is refused and changes nothing. Under Hypothesis, the random heap and #36's state machine gain cuts: each count still equals the references and roots, refcounting still frees no reachable object, and the uncollected garbage count still equals what the tests' walk does not reach.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Background churn
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The objects a workload allocates outside any structure, over the heap of #25.

  • Workload parameters: the fate mix (the share of churn allocations that start a cycle, the rest transient), the cycle size, and the transients' lifetimes.
  • Lifetimes are geometric in whole kB: a bisect into exact integer thresholds built with fractions. ADR 0007 rules out log, exp, pow, ** with a float, and expovariate. The prototypes gave a small share of transients a long lifetime, past the young generation, so that some reached the old generation.
  • The workload allocates a cycle in one go, holds it by a frame root, and lets go of it when its lifetime ends. From then on the cycle is cyclic garbage.
  • Each new object comes held by its allocating frame (#35). The workload lets go of that frame root once it has linked or rooted the object where it belongs; a cycle keeps its first object's root as the frame root that holds it.
  • A transient that the workload lets go of at or before the next collection boundary moves the allocation clock and makes no object (ADR 0005). Within each kB the clock moves, the workload lets go of each object whose lifetime ends there, and then a collection runs if the kB is a boundary. This issue takes the boundaries as an input: one every threshold0 kB, which both collectors share (ADR 0004).
  • Each run owns its random.Random(seed), and no draw depends on what a collector does.

CONTEXT.md names the fate mix and the cycle size as the churn's workload parameters, and has no term for the transients' lifetimes. Add one in the same change.

Tests: the lifetime thresholds equal their fractions values, and a long draw lands within a stated tolerance of the fate mix and the lifetimes the workload asks for. At every boundary the heap holds the same objects as a run that makes every transient.

Done when a test can run churn over the heap to any point on the allocation clock, and just check passes.

issues.title: Churn over the heap, with lazy transients
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #26, after #53.

  • run_to(clock) moves the allocation clock one kB at a time. In each kB the churn allocates one thing, a transient or the next member of a cycle it is building, then lets go of each lifetime that ends at the new clock value, as ADR 0005 orders it. A run can stop at any point on the allocation clock, and runs of different lengths agree on the kB they share.
  • The fate mix, the Fraction of churn allocations that start a cycle, decides whether an allocation starts a cycle of cycle_size objects. The workload builds the cycle as a ring. Each new member gets a link from the one before, and the workload lets go of the member's allocating root; the first member keeps its root, which holds the cycle. When the cycle's lifetime ends, the workload lets go of that root and declares the cycle's objects uncollected garbage (#36). A collection in #27 can land while a cycle is half built, as in CPython.
  • A transient whose let-go comes at or before the next collection boundary, the first multiple of threshold0 at or after the kB it was made in, moves the clock and makes no object (ADR 0005). A flag makes every transient from the same draws, for the test below.
  • Each run owns its random.Random(seed), and no draw depends on what a collector does.

Tests: a long seeded run lands within a stated tolerance of the fate mix; at every boundary the heap holds the same objects as a run that makes every transient, comparing objects by their place in the nursery; under Hypothesis, run_to(c) leaves the clock at c, and the uncollected garbage count equals the alive objects the tests' walk does not reach.

Done when a test can run churn over the heap to any point on the allocation clock, and just check passes.

issues.title: Keep the heap's records in a dict of alive objects
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Follows #47 and #50.

The heap keeps one record per object in a list that the object's int indexes, and freeing an object leaves None in its place. The list grows with every object a run makes, freed or not: a million allocations leave a million entries, 8.45 MB of them, however few objects stay alive. frame_roots() walks all of it, holes included, and so would any later pass over the heap.

  • Keep the records in a dict from each alive object's int to its record. A counter hands out the ints in allocation order, the dict iterates in insertion order (ADR 0007), and no int serves twice.
  • Freeing deletes the record. is_freed(x) asks whether the dict lacks x, and len(heap) is the dict's size, so the separate alive count goes.
  • The public methods and what they return stay the same, so the existing tests cover the change.

Cost, in a microbenchmark of a million allocations, links and frees: the dict took 349 ms where the list took 262 ms, about 90 ns more per object, and ended with 2,000 entries in 0.15 MB where the list had a million in 8.45 MB.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Lifetimes for background churn, drawn exactly
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #26. The churn over the heap builds on it.

  • A lifetime is geometric in whole kB, on 1, 2, 3 and up, with a mean the workload sets. The workload draws one with a bisect of getrandbits(32), one word of the generator, into integer thresholds built from exact ratios of integers. ADR 0007 rules out log, exp, pow, ** with a float, and expovariate. Plain ints build the same thresholds as Fraction about 2.5 times faster, since they skip its gcd at every step; 2**-32 is finer than any chart or statistic the demo shows.
  • A small share of transients draws a long lifetime instead, uniform over a range of kB with randint, so that some outlive the young generation and reach the old generation. The prototype for #8 drew 0.2% of its transients from 30,000 to 300,000 kB.
  • A cycle draws its lifetime from the geometric alone, as in the prototype.
  • Shares are Fractions, drawn with randrange(denominator) < numerator.
  • CONTEXT.md has no term for the transients' lifetimes. Add one in the same change.

Tests: for a mean of 4 the thresholds equal 2**32 - 3**l * 2**(32 - 2*l) for l up to 16, where no rounding enters; a long seeded draw lands within a stated tolerance of the mean and of the long share.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Find the unreachable objects among those a collection examines
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #27, after #49. #28 reuses it.

  • A collection examines some of the heap's objects: an aging space or an increment, or for the legacy collector one or more generations. Among them it finds the unreachable ones as CPython's deduce_unreachable does. Each object's count starts at its reference count, and the references from other examined objects come off it. An object left above zero has a holder outside the examined objects, so it survives, with everything it reaches among them. The rest is unreachable.
  • What it finds is the group that free_cyclic_garbage takes (#36, #49): cyclic garbage, and whatever that garbage alone holds. No object in the group has a holder outside it, which the heap asserts.
  • Garbage that other garbage holds from outside the examined objects survives, as in CPython, until a collection examines its holder too.
  • It reads the heap's references and reference counts and changes nothing. Freeing, counting the work, and moving survivors stay with #27 and #28.

Tests, under Hypothesis:

  • Over the random heap of the heap's tests, with its two-way links and the cycles they close, take any subset of the alive objects. What it finds equals the subset less what the tests' walk reaches from the roots and from every object outside the subset.
  • In #36's state machine, finding over every alive object gives the objects of the dropped cycles that no collection has freed, and freeing what it finds brings the uncollected garbage count to 0.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Free a group of cyclic garbage outright, in the group's order
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Follows #36.

free_cyclic_garbage has each member of the group let go of its references, as CPython's tp_clear does, and leaves refcounting to free the members in whatever order their counts reach zero. Partway through, a member can sit alive with its references cleared. The loop skips members the cascade freed before their turn, and you have to trace the counts to see that the whole group goes. The method also iterates set(group), which ADR 0007 rules out: sets serve membership alone.

  • Free the members first, in the group's order, then let go of their references to objects outside the group, so refcounting frees what the group alone held. One method frees an object, whether refcounting or a collection frees it.
  • The heap asserts that nothing outside the group holds a member, in place of the ValueError it raised. A collection never hands over such a group: CPython's collector counts a reference from outside the collected objects as a root, so a cycle that other garbage holds survives until a collection takes its holder too. A group with a holder outside it is a collector's bug, like a negative count.
  • The state machine checks that freeing a group frees every object built with its cycle. Until now only an example test caught a free that keeps the references leaving the group.
  • An example test covers a group that holds another cycle: freeing the group leaves that cycle alive and counted.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Uncollected garbage, counted as it changes
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #25, after #35.

  • The heap counts uncollected garbage as it changes. A walk at every collection would take longer than most collections, which examine a fraction of the heap. Letting go of a cycle, or of a structure with cycles, adds its objects to the count, since the workload knows how many it lets go of (#26, #29), and freeing them takes them off. The prototypes counted the same way.
  • Freeing what a collection found: given a group of cyclic garbage, the heap frees it, lets go of the group's references to objects outside it, and takes the group off the count.
  • The heap's reachable part, which the records carry (#30), is its live objects less the uncollected garbage.

Tests: under Hypothesis, over random allocations, links, frame roots, and cycles let go of and freed, the count equals the live objects the tests' walk from the roots does not reach, after every operation.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Refcounting frees what it can, on the spot
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #25, after #33 and #34.

  • Letting go of an object's last reference frees it by refcounting on the spot: the heap has the collector remove it from its space (#34), the object lets go of its own references, and refcounting frees whatever those leave at zero, in turn.
  • A new object comes held by its allocating frame, as in CPython: allocate takes a frame root on it, and refcounting frees it once the workload lets go of that root and nothing else holds it.
  • Objects in a cycle keep each other's counts above zero, so a dropped cycle stays, as cyclic garbage, until a collection frees it.
  • The tests walk the heap from its roots to find its reachable part. The simulator keeps a count instead (#36).

Tests: refcounting frees an acyclic drop whole, and leaves a dropped cycle whole, along with whatever it holds. Under Hypothesis, over random allocations, links, and frame roots taken and let go: refcounting never frees a reachable object, every object it leaves unreachable lies on a cycle or is reachable from one, and every live object sits in exactly one space.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Spaces, each live object in exactly one
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #25, after #31.

  • The collectors own every space, the nursery included. A Collector base holds the nursery; the incremental collector (#27) adds its aging, pending and visited spaces, and the legacy one (#28) its aging and old generations. A collector may replace its nursery.
  • The heap holds its collector and hands it each new object with add, which puts the object last in the nursery. #35 adds remove, for an object refcounting frees. The heap touches spaces nowhere else.
  • The collector records each object's space and moves objects between spaces, as CPython's collector does with its generation lists. A space keeps its objects in the order they entered, so that an old collection can take the least recently scanned pending object first.

Tests: under Hypothesis, over random allocations through the heap and moves through the collector, every live object sits in exactly one space, and each space keeps the order objects entered it.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: The module root and frame roots
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #25, after #31.

  • The module root: sys, an object the interpreter holds from the start and never lets go of. Module globals hang off it.
  • Frame roots: references a running frame holds. A workload takes one on an object and lets go of it later. A frame root counts in the object's reference count, as a reference from another object would, though no object holds it.
  • The heap records its roots, sys and how many frame roots each object has, so that the tests can walk the heap from them.

Tests: taking and letting go of frame roots moves the reference counts and the heap's record of its roots. The heap refuses to let go of a frame root an object does not have.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: The allocation clock
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #25.

  • The allocation clock counts kB of real objects allocated since the run began, as the collectors' trigger counts them, at allocation.
  • Allocating a simulated object moves it by 1 (ADR 0002), and so does a kB for a transient the simulator never makes (ADR 0005).

Tests: after any mix of allocations and kB without an object, the clock reads their total.

Done when just check passes.

issues.title: Simulated objects and their references
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Part of #25.

  • A simulated object is an int indexing the heap's lists, so the simulator makes no reference cycles of its own for the host's collector to chase. The prototypes handed a freed object's int out again, which kept the lists short.
  • Each object holds its references to other objects in a list, in the order the workload made them, and a count of the references into it.
  • Linking one object to another adds a reference and raises the count. An object may hold the same reference more than once, and each counts.
  • Lists and dicts give every order the heap keeps. Sets serve membership tests, and id() and hash() order nothing (ADR 0007).

Tests: reference counts follow links, repeated ones included.

Done when just check passes.

Put it in CONTRIBUTING.md, which is the process, and point to it from CLAUDE.md. Say what wins when the skill's rules clash with the glossary's terms or with wording the repo keeps exact.

issues.title: Measure cold start to the first chart
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Throwaway code. Time from page load to the first chart: Pyodide 314.0.7 starting in a Web Worker, fetching and unpacking sim.zip, importing it, the first records of both runs, and the first Plot render. Runs stream their records (ADR 0006, #20), so time the full chart too: until both runs have finished and the last redraw is done. Measure with a cold and a warm browser cache.

#6 saw 2.3 to 3.1 s from starting the worker to a ready Pyodide, in a fresh browser profile and so with a cold cache, on a desktop.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html:
Findings

Prototype on the throwaway branch prototype/07-cold-start. It is never merged; its README has the tables, the method and the commands. The page makes the worker first and then imports Plot; the worker starts Pyodide 314.0.7, fetches and unpacks sim.zip (#8's simulator, 4.6 KB), imports it and streams both runs (ADR 0006); the page draws ADR 0008's layout from what has arrived, once a frame. Headless Chrome 155 on a desktop, a cold load in a fresh profile (renderer already started) and two warm loads after it, three rounds each.

Verdict: about 2.7 to 2.8 s to the first chart cold and 1.3 to 1.5 s warm, nearly all of it Pyodide starting.

Run lengths below are on the allocation clock: the MB of simulated objects a run allocates, computed in the browser. Over the network a load moves Pyodide, Plot and sim.zip, nothing else; the records go from the worker to the page inside the browser, about 55 KB as JSON for both runs of 1 GB.

150 MB, cold warm 1 GB, cold warm
Pyodide ready 2719 ms 1184-1268 ms 2611 ms 1327-1442 ms
first chart on screen 2832 ms 1266-1350 ms 2704 ms 1412-1534 ms
full chart on screen 3377 ms 1679-1774 ms 6340 ms 5223-5532 ms
  • Pyodide starting is 1.1 to 1.4 s warm (WebAssembly compiled and instantiated, the standard library unpacked, Python started) and 2.6 to 2.7 s cold, the difference being 6.2 MiB of downloads: pyodide.asm.wasm 3.3 MiB, python_stdlib.zip 2.4 MiB, Plot about 250 KiB. A warm load transfers nothing.
  • After Python is ready, the first chart is on screen 80 to 115 ms later: sim.zip, unpacking and import about 15 ms, the first records of both runs 30 to 45 ms, the first redraw 30 to 50 ms.
  • Plot loads in 0.6 to 1.2 s cold, alongside Pyodide, off the critical path.
  • The full chart is the runs, computed in the worker: 0.4 to 0.5 s more for runs of 150 MB on the allocation clock, 3.6 to 4.0 s more for runs of 1 GB.
  • Yielding with setTimeout(0) costs 4 to 7 ms a yield in a worker; a MessageChannel message (one per yield) saved 80 ms over 22 parts and 1.0 s over 144, alternated in the same sessions. A message from the page runs between parts either way: a ping waited about 10 ms at the median, 50 ms at p95, about 100 ms at worst, which is how soon a changed control could cancel a run.

Suggested for the site: one Pyodide per page, in one worker made at page load and shared by every widget, so it is ready before the reader reaches the first one; a re-run never restarts Pyodide, so after a control changes the first chart is about 100 ms away; yield with a MessageChannel; preloading the two big files from the page's head might shorten the cold start (not measured).

Not measured: the site's own round trips (here the page, widget.js, worker.js and sim.zip came over loopback; from GitHub Pages each costs one), a laptop, a slow network (only the bytes), a phone, Firefox and Safari, several widgets on a page, cancelling a run, preloading.

issues.title: Mock the widget layout with Plot
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Throwaway code, on mocked data shaped like the simulator's output (one record per collection), at realistic sizes: a few hundred to a few thousand collections per run.

Draw the four panels: the heap by space with the reachable line on top, the collection bars stacked marked / survived / freed with idle collections as markers, the work budget with a bold zero line and the negative region shaded, and the summary numbers. Two columns, legacy and incremental, with a shared y-scale. Desktop only: the phone layout is postponed to the Guide milestone.

Record how long a redraw takes and whether the panels read clearly.

Records stream in as the runs go (ADR 0006, #20), so also time a redraw while both runs grow, at most one per animation frame: that time sets how many collections a run yields at a time. Check that the shared y-scale still reads well while it grows.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html:
Findings

Prototype on the throwaway branch prototype/09-widget-layout. It is never merged; its README has the tables, the method and the commands. Three variants of the four panels on real records from #8's simulator (75 to 2000 collections per run), switchable via ?variant=:

  • A, Columns: the layout this issue describes, two columns of heap by space, work per collection as stacked bars, work budget and summary tiles.
  • B, Overlay: one column, both collectors on the same axes (incremental in the accent, legacy in gray): heap and reachable with the uncollected garbage shaded between, work per collection as dots, budget, comparison table.
  • C, Summary first: the comparison as figures, then compact columns with work binned into whole numbers of collection intervals.

What reads:

  • Heap: stacked by space (A, C) shows the mechanism (gen 2 piling up; pending and visited swapping each sweep), overlaid (B) shows the comparison (with 100 MB of globals the incremental heap climbs to 300 MB against legacy's 140 MB, the band says why). The nursery hardly shows: records hold the heap after a collection, when it has just been emptied.
  • Work per collection as bars does not survive density: at 500 collections a bar is about a pixel, at 2000 a faint hairline, and marked, survived and freed blur together. Dots (B) carry the peaks at any density (legacy 182K vs incremental 85K); binning (C) brings the composition back.
  • Work budget (step line, bold zero line, shaded negative stretch) and the summary read in every variant; C's figures make the headline first.

Redraw (headless Chrome, desktop; frame = callback to next callback, so style, layout and paint count):

Collections A B C
500 25 ms 16 to 20 ms 14 to 15 ms
600 28 ms 17 ms 16 to 17 ms
2000 82 to 88 ms 44 to 47 ms 39 to 40 ms

Plot rebuilds each chart's SVG, so the cost grows with the records: about 35 µs per collection per run for A, 18 µs for B and C. Against 60 Hz, C fits up to about 600 collections, B is at or a little over, A never fits.

While runs stream: the x-axis spans the run from the start, so charts fill from the left and read well halfway; the y-scales grow (heap 7 to 11 times a run in fine steps), each growth a visible jump. Sending 7 collections per frame took 286 frames and 8 to 15 s for 2000 collections: the redraw, not the yield, paces a stream.

Suggested for the widget: the page draws whatever records have arrived once per frame (the worker yields small); work per collection as dots, with composition binned where yield matters; the comparison as an overlay, the mechanism as a stack by space; records that also carry the heap before each collection; y-scales that grow in fine steps, starting from the previous run's maximum on a re-run.

Which layout the widget takes is open: see the variants.

issues.title: Check that runs are identical under CPython and Pyodide
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Throwaway code. Run one workload with one seed under CPython 3.14 and under Pyodide, and again across two page loads, and compare the per-collection records byte for byte.

Look for anything whose order depends on memory addresses: iterating a set of objects, ordering by id() or by an object's default hash. Close with the rules the real simulator must keep so that every reader sees the same charts.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html:
Findings

Prototype on the throwaway branch prototype/08-identical-runs. It is never merged; its README has the tables, the method and the commands.

Verdict: runs are byte-identical in every environment tried, and six rules keep them so.

  • #6's simulator, its records widened to what the charts read (every space, the live heap, uncollected garbage, the sweep), in four configurations: the default workload, another seed with 7 kB transients, threshold0 700, and 100 MB of module globals.
  • Six environments: CPython 3.14.5 on Windows (two processes, one with a fixed PYTHONHASHSEED), CPython 3.12.3 on Linux with glibc (WSL), and Pyodide 314.0.7 in two fresh headless Chrome 155 page loads and in Edge 155.
  • Every record digest is the same everywhere: straight through, with lazy transients (ADR 0005, which leaves every field of every record as it was), streamed and alternated (ADR 0006), and, in the worker, back to the event loop after each yield, cancelled, restarted in the same interpreter and passed through toJs().

What differs, in the same programs:

  • Iterating a set of objects, sorting by id(), iterating a set of strings and hash() of a string: different in every process and every page load. Pyodide randomizes string hashing too.
  • The C library's log, exp, sin, pow and so expovariate: Windows, Linux and Pyodide each have their own, at most 1 ulp apart, in 0.01 to 3% of results. Pyodide's is the same in every load. int() of #6's lifetimes hid every difference, by luck: about once in 10^17 draws it would not.

The rules for the real simulator

  1. Order comes from insertion only: lists and dicts; sets only for membership; never id() or hash() order. Objects are ints.
  2. No C-library floating point decides a run: no log, exp, sin, pow, no ** with a float, no expovariate or other distributions built on them. Draws are integer-exact; a lifetime is a bisect into exact integer thresholds (geometric lifetimes have rational ones, exact with fractions).
  3. Each run owns its random.Random(seed), and its draws never depend on the collector; a run's state lives in its generator, nothing at module level.
  4. Records hold ints and strings; what charts derive uses only correctly rounded arithmetic.
  5. Python and Pyodide stay pinned, a test pins each preset's records digest under CPython, and a Pyodide bump re-checks the digests under Pyodide before merging.
  6. The worker passes records on as they are, and the digest is checked on the JS side too.

Not tried: Firefox and Safari (not installed here), CPython 3.14 on Linux (WSL had 3.12), and other configurations than these four.

issues.title: Measure two runs against the 1 s budget under Pyodide
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Throwaway code. A rough simulator of realistic size (object graph, background churn, one structure, both collectors in rough form) runs a workload twice, once per collector, under Pyodide 314.0.7 in a Web Worker on a mid-range laptop, and under CPython 3.14 for comparison.

Record the times. If two runs do not fit in 1 s, list what would make them fit: cheaper transient churn, shorter runs, or something else.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html:
Findings

Prototype on the throwaway branch prototype/06-run-budget. It is never merged; its README has the full tables, the method, and the commands to rerun it.

Verdict: two runs fit in 1 s on a desktop, and the budget caps run length.

  • A rough simulator sized and costed like the real one: an int-indexed object graph with reference counts, collections that find survivors from external references, the incremental collector after the PEP's pseudocode, the legacy one with CPython's counts and the 25% ratio. Default workload: 8 MB of module globals, a 20 MB tree with parent pointers rebuilt every 80 MB, churn of 3% garbage cycles and short transients.
  • Pyodide 314.0.7 (Python 3.14.2) in a module Web Worker, headless Chrome 155, i5-11600K desktop; Edge within 5%. Two runs at 150 MB, about three sweeps: 0.61 s best of 7, 0.72 s as a fresh worker's first runs. CPython 3.14 is about 1.3 times faster.
  • The cost is per kB allocated, not per sweep: 1.9 to 2.4 µs/kB under Pyodide. With 100 MB of module globals the cost per kB stays the same, but three sweeps need over 1.2 GB, so such a preset stops short of three sweeps.

What makes it fit on slower machines

  1. Lazy transients: a transient let go at or before the next collection is never made; only the clock moves. Every collection, sweep, work and peak count came out identical to the eager runs, for both collectors at every length, and runs are 26 to 34% cheaper: 150 MB is 0.43 s, 0.48 s first. The condition is that the heap is sampled only at collections, as #9's one record per collection does.
  2. A cap on run length: 250 to 300 MB per run with lazy transients on this desktop, nearer 200 MB on a laptop.
  3. The host's collector off during a run: safe, since the simulator makes no cycles, and 1 to 8% faster.

The rest of the time goes to the workload: about 70% is churn, refcounting and random draws, and 4 to 6% is collect_cycles.

Not measured: a mid-range laptop (scaling by 1.5 gives 1.1 s eager and 0.7 s lazy at 150 MB as first runs), Firefox and Safari (not installed here), and startup (#7; 2.3 to 3.1 s to a ready Pyodide here).

For #8: every collection count and work figure matched between CPython and Pyodide in every run.

thread.author: sergey-miryanov
thread.html:
Decided

After these findings, in #20:

  • Runs are not capped to fit the 1 s budget. They stream their records to the widget as they go, and the charts fill in from the left (ADR 0006). The "cap on run length" above is superseded; a preset's run length stays chosen by hand, aiming at about three sweeps.
  • Only the transients a collection can see are made (ADR 0005).

#20 closes this issue when it merges.

issues.title: Keep Dependabot to typos' own release tags
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
Dependabot's first pull request here, #15, moved the typos hook from v1.51.1 to varcon-core-v5.0.7. crate-ci/typos also tags the other crates it publishes (varcon-core-v*, typos-dict-v*, dictgen-v* and more), and Dependabot reads the highest version among them as a typos release. gcmon got the same pull request (sergey-miryanov/gcmon#225). Both were closed by hand, and every varcon-core release will open another.

varcon-core is the only series numbered above typos' own 1.x, so ignoring >= 2 for typos stops it without hiding a real release. Add to the pre-commit entry in .github/dependabot.yml, with its comment:

  ignore:
    # crate-ci/typos also tags its other crates (varcon-core-v5.0.7, ...),
    # and Dependabot reads those as typos releases. typos itself is at 1.x.
    - dependency-name: "https://github.com/crate-ci/typos"
      versions: [">= 2"]

Revisit it if typos reaches 2.0.

Done when check-dependabot passes and Dependabot's next pre-commit update job leaves typos alone or moves it only to a v1.* tag.

issues.title: Let actionlint accept `$/` self-repository actions
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
GitHub's $/ syntax (changelog, 2026-07-30) points a uses: at an action in the workflow's own repository, at the commit that is running. actionlint 1.7.12 rejects it:

specifying action "$/.github/actions/my-action" in invalid format because ref is missing. available formats are "{owner}/{repo}@{ref}" or "{owner}/{repo}/{path}@{ref}" [action]

This is rhysd/actionlint#711, still open. When the first workflow here uses $/ (say, a composite action that the CI and deploy workflows share), give the actionlint hook gcmon's exception, with its comment:

      - id: actionlint
        # actionlint has no support for GitHub's `$/` self-repository syntax
        # yet; see rhysd/actionlint#711.
        args: ["-ignore", 'specifying action "\$/']

Drop it once an actionlint release supports the syntax.

Done when a workflow that uses a $/ action passes poetry run pre-commit run actionlint --all-files.

issues.title: CI workflow: just check on every pull request
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
.github/workflows/ci.yml runs poetry run just check on Python 3.14 for pull requests to main, with actions pinned by SHA.

Then make it a required check in branch protection for main, so a red pull request cannot be merged.

Upload the coverage to Codecov, which is enabled on the repository, as gcmon does:

  • just test also writes coverage.xml (pytest-cov's --cov-report=xml), ignored by git.
  • A step after just check, with if: always(), uploads it with codecov/codecov-action pinned by SHA and token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}.
  • codecov.yml after gcmon's, with the project target at our 99% gate and a single upload per commit (gcmon waits for three, one per OS).

Once Codecov has reported on a pull request, make codecov/project and codecov/patch required checks on main too, next to the CI check and pre-commit.ci - pr. Codecov reports only after an upload, so the workflow runs on every pull request, with no paths filter: a pull request it skipped could never merge.

issues.title: Run the hooks on every pull request with pre-commit.ci
issues.author: sergey-miryanov
issues.bodyHTML:
The hooks only run where someone ran poetry run pre-commit install, and just check, which CI gates on, covers ruff alone: typos, codespell, check-jsonschema, actionlint, zizmor and the file checks never run in CI. Run them on every pull request with pre-commit.ci, as gcmon does.

  • Give the pre-commit.ci GitHub App (https://github.com/apps/pre-commit-ci) access to this repository.
  • Add gcmon's ci: block to .pre-commit-config.yaml, with its comment: autofix_prs: true, autoupdate_schedule: quarterly, submodules: false. pre-commit.ci's autoupdate pins an annotated tag's own SHA rather than its commit and has no off switch, so it runs at the rarest schedule.
  • .github/dependabot.yml updates the hook pins instead (the pre-commit ecosystem), and, as in gcmon, pip and github-actions too, daily with a cooldown. Add check-dependabot to the check-jsonschema hooks.
  • Make pre-commit.ci - pr a required check on main, next to the one from #4.
  • Say in CONTRIBUTING.md that pre-commit.ci runs the hooks on every pull request and may push fixes to it, and that Dependabot moves the pins.

Done when a pull request with a trailing space gets an autofix commit from pre-commit.ci and a green pre-commit.ci - pr, and main requires that check.

issues.title: Poetry project on Python 3.14 with the check set
issues.author: sergey-miryanov

Make the Getting set up, Commands and Checks sections of CONTRIBUTING.md true.

  • pyproject.toml with [project] metadata, requires-python = ">=3.14", the package at src/pep848_sim, and poetry.lock
  • dev group: pytest, pytest-cov, hypothesis, ruff, mypy, pyrefly, pre-commit, rust-just
  • ruff, mypy and pyrefly targeting 3.14, both type checkers strict; coverage fail_under = 99
  • justfile with check, test, lint, typecheck, site, serve, running under PowerShell on Windows
  • .pre-commit-config.yaml: ruff, typos, codespell, actionlint, zizmor, the whitespace hooks, LF line endings
  • an empty src/pep848_sim with one smoke test

Done when poetry run just check passes on a fresh clone.

273.bodyHTML:
Closes #269

Stacked on #272: it reuses that PR's structure for what a worker allocates before its loops. Merge #272 first.

xml_etree_parse's workers start their collections 2,162 kB apart while they parse, and 2,000 kB apart everywhere else. 2,162 kB is six parses of 360 kB each. The C accelerator parses without returning to the interpreter, so a collection that falls due during a parse waits until the parse returns. Every worker gcmon read whole has 40 such late collections, and the run now has the same 40.

Workers Preset before Preset now
Automatic collections 51 51 51
The first 2,001 kB 2,000 kB 2,000 kB
The last 108,086 kB 102,000 kB 108,406 kB

What changes

  • A build in C (ADR 0022). A structure gets built_in_c. While its build runs, its churn included, the heap holds back an automatic collection that falls due and starts it at the first allocation after the build ends. A collection due as the build starts still runs before it. The budget restarts from the late collection. The workload alone decides when builds run, so both collectors hold back the same collections. Churn treats a held collection's boundary as the next kB, which errs early, and ADR 0005 now says so. The Hypothesis test that compares lazy and eager transients now draws the flag too.
  • The playground. The editor has a box for the flag, the legend says "built in C: a collection due meanwhile waits until the build ends", and the workload source writes built_in_c=True. A link from before the flag opens with it off.
  • xml_etree_parse.
    • A parse's slot is 360 kB: the tree's 322 objects at 72 B an element, then churn for the rest.
    • A value's tree, serialised and written, takes 3,864 kB before the first parse, and a value now spans 71 slots, 25,560 kB. The workers' values run 25,468.
    • The workers' first late collection examines three parsed trees, so it follows their third parse, and their parses start at about 9,150 kB. The 660 kB the workers allocate after start-up, before their first value, get the set-up structure from #272. That structure moves into _StartUp.set_up(), which both presets now call.
    • The run ends where the workers start shutdown, 109,612 kB. That is 2,088 kB past the fourth value, and the run spends it on the start of a fifth. In the workers, that stretch is pyperf's own work and the last value's serialising.
  • The glossary adds "a build in C" under Build, and the home page says a collection that falls due during a parse waits for it.

The legacy gen 0 collections still examine fewer objects than the workers' (#262). That PR comes next, stacked on this one.

How I checked

just check passes, test-pyodide included, with xml_etree_parse's two digests re-pinned. A new test checks that each of the run's collections starts 2,000 kB after the last or at a parse's end, 40 of them late. I rendered the playground in Chrome: the legend line shows, and the page logged no errors.

The workloads

The widget opens on xml_etree_parse, which models a worker of the xml_etree benchmark's parse task. Four times over, it builds a tree of 5,103 elements, then parses it 60 times, from a file and from bytes in turn, and each parsed -tree replaces the last of its kind. No element links back to its parent, so -refcounting frees each tree as the next replaces it, and a collection that -examines a tree finds it alive. Before shutdown, the collections find no +tree replaces the last of its kind. C code parses each one, so a collection +that falls due during a parse waits until it ends. No element links back to its +parent, so refcounting frees each tree as the next replaces it, and a +collection that examines a tree finds it alive. Before shutdown, the collections find no cyclic garbage beyond a few cycles that start-up lets go of. Its workload's slider sets the parsed trees' size.

274.bodyHTML:
Closes #262

Stacked on #273, which holds back xml_etree_parse's collections until each parse returns. Merge #272 and #273 first.

Under the legacy collector, xml_etree_parse's workers examine 15,480 real objects at nearly every gen 0 collection: three parsed trees. A collection that waits for a parse to return finds that parse's tree young, along with the two before it. root1 still holds the oldest of the three until the next assignment. Their gen 0 collections dip during each value's Python phase, where they find part of a tree at most.

What changes

A parsed tree now lives 817 kB, not 720. It goes when the next parse but one returns, two slots on. The collection waiting on that parse still finds it, so the lifetime is one kB longer than that. A value's first parse starts as soon as the value's own tree has built, 96 kB ahead of its slot. Its tree lives that much longer so that it reaches the third parse's return, and the other parsed trees get the same lifetime.

Real objects examined by the legacy collector's gen 0 collections, the run against the workers' medians:

Collection Workers Run
5 to 14, 17 to 26 and so on, as a parse returns 15,479 to 15,483 15,456, and 16,752 to 16,976 at each value's first
15 and 16 1,129 and 4,053 1,200 and 2,688
27 and 28 5,187 and 5,181 1,200 and 2,688
39 and 40 10,343 and 5,181 1,200 and 2,688
3 9,199 3,472

Before this change, the run examined 10,304 at most of its collections, two trees, and its collections fell where the workers' did not.

Two gaps remain:

  • The run's values repeat every 25,560 kB, so its dips repeat exactly. The workers' values run 25,468 kB, so their Python-phase collections fall at different points of each value and find different parts of it.
  • At collection 3 the workers have imported xml.etree, which start-up, shared by all five presets, leaves out.

Gen 0's average goes from 8,754 to 12,700 against the workers' 13,267, and gen 1's from 20,032 to 25,184 against 25,324.

How I checked

just check passes, test-pyodide included, with xml_etree_parse's two digests re-pinned. A new test checks that the 36 gen 0 collections a parse holds back find three parsed trees, and that the on-time ones during each value's Python phase find less than one.

275.bodyHTML:
#261

Stacked on #274. Merge #272, #273 and #274 first.

connected_components' workers import networkx from 4.6 MB to about 14.6 MB, load the graph until about 125 MB, then walk it. The preset loaded the graph straight after start-up and left out read_adjlist's churn, because a build's churn came in whole kB. Its load ended at 94 MB, and its legacy collections went idle from the 49th, where the workers' stay busy to the 63rd.

What changes

  • A build's churn can be a fraction (ADR 0023). By its k-th object a build has made k times the churn, rounded down, so a churn of 1/4 follows every fourth object with one allocation. A request holds a fraction as text, "6/25", and a whole churn as a number, so older links still open. A float is refused. The editor shows the churn to a hundredth, and the workload source writes the text. The glossary's Build says so.
  • connected_components.
    • networkx's imports: 1,425 module-held objects with 6 kB of churn after each, from start-up's end to 14,599 kB. The workers' gen 0 collections there examine 4,400 to 4,800 real objects each, and the run's 4,576 to 4,592.
    • The load takes 0.24 kB of churn for each kB of graph and ends at 124,967 kB.
    • Each walk shrinks to 18,508 kB, so the run still ends at 199 MB.
  • The guide and home page. The graph is now structure 6, so the guide's two steps that resize it point there. Its connected_components steps carry the new numbers, and two of their claims change. The incremental collector's largest increment, 27.9K, now passes the legacy collector's peak of 19.4K, as the home page already said. At threshold1 2, two gen 2 collections fit the run, since the graph keeps loading past the first. The home page says the module imports networkx.

Legacy collector, real objects examined, workers' medians against the run:

Collection Workers Before Now
Gen 0, 4 to 7 (imports) 4,403 to 4,836 32,000 4,576 to 4,592
Gen 0, 9 to 62 (load) 24,719 to 27,641 32,000 to 47, then 16 25,808
Gen 0, 63 (load ends) 12,916 16 12,496
Gen 1, 12 163,036 328,320 162,416
Gen 1, 24 to 48 301,202 to 322,563 346,112 to 384,000 309,680
Gen 1, 60 300,245 16 309,680
Gen 1, 72 62,522 16 64,112

Per collection, gen 0 averages 14,695 against the workers' 14,682, and gen 1 183,160 against 182,947.

Under the incremental collector, the run's young collections now stay busy to the 73rd, at 146 MB, as the workers' do. Before, they stopped at the 55th. The 73rd examines 38,288 against their 37,799. Old collections examine 18,714 each on average, against the workers' 19,952; before, the run's examined 24,667.

What remains

Under the incremental collector, the old collections' work still departs from the workers':

  • At collections 31 to 39, 62 to 78 MB, the workers' young collections examine 6,604 to 13,602 real objects each, and the run's 51,616. The legacy collector's gen 0 collections at the same clocks examine about 26,000 in both, so the workers allocate as much there as anywhere in the load.
  • The run's young collections add more to its budget there, so it recovers sooner than the workers'. At 96 MB it takes the graph's pending part in one increment of 446,256 real objects. The workers' old collections do about 50,000 each from the 50th to the 74th, and the run's do nothing from the 50th to the 64th, then mark up to 51,616 at each to the 74th.

I haven't found what makes the branch's young collections dip there. If it's how they work, ADR 0003 keeps the simulator from following, since its collector follows the PEP's pseudocode. So this PR leaves #261 open.

How I checked

just check passes, test-pyodide included, with connected_components' two digests re-pinned. New tests cover a fraction's spread, the build's length, a whole fraction read as an int, a float or a word refused in a request, and the editor's churn helpers. The Hypothesis test that compares lazy and eager transients now draws churns in quarters.

#263

Stacked on #275, which lets a build's churn be a fraction. Merge #272, #273, #274 and #275 first.

As each run of async_tree_io_tg's task tree ends, its workers' legacy gen 0 collections climb from about 15,300 real objects to 25,600 and up to 39,388, for about 14 MB. The preset built each tree at 1 kB of churn an object, so its gen 0 collections held at 16,000 while a tree grew. Each tree then sat idle until the next run, and the collections in that stretch examined almost nothing.

What changes

  • The tree's churn is now 1.17 kB for each kB of tree, from the records (ADR 0023). The first tree builds from 7,524 kB to 121,420, where the workers' builds from about 7,500 to about 123,000. Its gen 0 collections examine 14,752 to 14,800, against the workers' 15,260 to 15,600.
  • The set-up. The workers' first tree starts 2,900 kB after start-up ends. The set-up structure from #272 now fills that stretch here too.
  • What the finishing tasks keep. A new structure follows each tree and fills the rest of its run. It takes 0.23 kB of churn for each kB it keeps, and goes as the next run starts. The tree now goes 6 MB after it has built, where the workers' heap peaks. Each run is 128,869 kB, so the run still ends at 523 MB.
  • The guide and home page. The guide's async_tree_io_tg steps carry the new numbers. Three of their claims change. The legacy collector's work per MB, 868, now runs well above the incremental collector's, 654. The largest tree the slider allows is now 59,300 kB. With parent links, the old collections free two trees, not three. The home page says the gen 0 collections climb as each run ends, and only the churn's lifetimes remain placeholders.

Legacy gen 0 collections as the first tree ends, real objects examined, workers' medians against the run:

Collection 61 62 63 64 65 66 67 68 69 70
Workers 15,260 22,335 25,603 26,678 39,388 34,086 30,460 17,107 11,018 15,604
Before 80 64 96 64 80 80 64 14,272 16,016 16,048
Now 18,016 26,032 26,032 26,032 26,016 26,016 26,016 26,032 11,904 14,800

The other three runs end the same way, give or take a collection. A simulated object stands for 16 real ones of 64 B (ADR 0002), so a gen 0 collection can examine at most 32,000 real objects of its 2,000 kB. The workers' peak of 39,388 passes that, so the run holds at 26,000, the workers' average through the climb.

Under the incremental collector, the young collections now go idle as each tree ends, from collection 65 to 77, where the workers' do from 69. The tree has gone by the time it would leave the aging generation.

Workers Before Now
Legacy gen 0, examined each 16,575 12,991 15,884
Legacy gen 1, examined each 167,552 160,111 162,493
Legacy gen 2, examined 30,468 35,840 23,776
Incremental young, examined each 19,735 25,784 22,244
Old collections that do any work, each worker 104 86 at 32,000 94
Their average work 22,384 about 29,000 26,930

What remains

  • The old collections' work. Within each build, the workers' young collections examine from 7,500 to 31,000 real objects each, in waves, while their legacy gen 0 collections hold at 15,300. The run's young collections hold at 29,500, so its old collections mark 29,000 to 30,000 each where the workers' spread. The same gap shows in connected_components (#275): the branch's young collections examine less than the run's at some stretches while the allocation stays the same.
  • The heap. The run frees the tree at once, where the workers free it task by task over about 10 MB. Its heap peaks at 935,808 real objects, against the workers' 857,000 to 866,000, since what the finishing tasks keep stacks on the whole tree.

How I checked

just check passes, test-pyodide included, with async_tree_io_tg's two digests re-pinned. The test that checked each tree goes as the next run starts now checks that each tree goes while its tasks finish, and that what they keep goes as the next run starts.
