283.bodyHTML:
#263
#279

async_tree_io_tg's Hierarchy held one simulated object a task. Marking reached a task and its six children in one step, pulled young objects into the old generation 16 times too fast, emptied the aging spaces and stalled. A new shape, TaskGroups, builds the objects asyncio makes, in asyncio's order (ADR 0026).

What the reference build shows

  • sys reaches all 55,987 tasks through the event loop, 7 references down. A first-in, first-out walk from sys scans 16,520 objects before the loop.
  • The loop's ready queue holds a Handle for each task made and not yet run, and its heap of timers holds the sleeping leaves' TimerHandles.
  • A running task that starts a TaskGroup keeps 13 tracked objects, and a leaf 14. Its Handle and TaskStepMethWrapper go as it first runs.
  • Each task links back to its parent through its done-callback and the parent's await, and to itself through the Future it waits on. The tasks cut those links as they finish.

The shape

  • One simulated object stands for an object of one role in each of 16 tasks.
  • A path of 10 objects leads to the loop, which holds the ready queue and the timers.
  • A task's handle leaves the ready queue as the task runs: the shape's unlinks.
  • A new teardown(size) gives the links a drop cuts first, so a dropped tree leaves no cyclic garbage.
  • The preset's tree lives 10 MB after it has built, not 8, at 1.07 kB of build churn a kB, not 1.17.

Fit

Presets page, incremental collector:

Series Before After
gen 0 examined 37% 9%
gen 1 work 25% 10%
gen 1 budget 12% 3%
gen 1 examined 4% 4%

Legacy gen 0 examined falls from 3% to 2%, and gen 1 examined from 4% to 2%. Legacy gen 1 yield stays at 16%.

For #279, legacy collections, real objects examined:

Collection Workers Run
Gen 2, 133rd, 266 MB 30,468 28,176
Gen 1, 193rd, 386 MB 199,934 217,216
Gen 1, 132nd, 264 MB 37,693 64

The 132nd still misses.

The other presets' digests stay the same, connected_components' among them.

Guide and site

  • The tree grows from 52,487 objects to 55,429, and its slider's largest to 62,200 kB.
  • The chapters on the old generation and the work budget take the new numbers: 12 sweeps where there were 9, and old collections that mark about 1,900 objects each.
  • The sweeps no longer run long and short by turns, so that note gives their first five ends.
  • Without the freed credit, the trees with parent pointers now go at 172, 324 and 500 MB, and the sweeps fall from 10 to 6. The note gives those clocks.
  • Requests name the shape task_groups, and a workload source TaskGroups().
  • ADR 0024 points to ADR 0026, and CONTEXT.md's Structure entry allows a shape that cuts its cycles before it goes.

@@ -0,0 +1,92 @@
+# async_tree_io_tg's tasks take asyncio's shape
+
+With the collector following the branch (ADR 0024), async_tree_io_tg's young
+collections examined within 37% of its workers', and its old collections' work
+within 25%. The preset's tree was a Hierarchy of 6 branches at 15 real objects
+a task: 52,487 simulated objects for the benchmark's 55,987 tasks, about one a
+task. An instrumented worker on the reference build shows how far that is from
+what asyncio makes:
+
+- sys reaches the tasks through the event loop, 7 references down. A walk from
+  sys, first in, first out as the branch marks, scans 16,520 objects before the
+  loop and 18,222 before its queue of handles ready to run.
+- The ready queue holds a Handle for each task made and not yet run: 43,796 at
+  the 30th collection, 15,825 at the 50th. The loop's heap of timers holds the
+  sleeping leaves' TimerHandles, 30,831 at the 50th.
+- The branch marks in layers of one type each, breadth first: the Handles at
+  the 22nd collection, the Contexts and TaskStepMethWrappers at the 24th, the
+  Tasks from the 26th to the 30th, then the coroutines and TaskGroups.
+- A running task that starts a TaskGroup holds 13 tracked objects of its own,
+  and a leaf 14. Its Handle and TaskStepMethWrapper go when the ready queue lets
+  go of them, as the task first runs.
+- Each task links back to its parent twice: its done-callback is a method of
+  the parent's TaskGroup, which holds the parent in `_parent_task`, and the
+  parent awaits it. The task also reaches itself through the Future it waits
+  on and that Future's wake-up call. The tasks cut these links as they finish.
+
+At one object a task, marking reached a whole task, with its six children, in
+one step, and pulled the young objects into the old generation 16 times too
+fast. The aging spaces ran empty, the young collections gave no budget, and
+marking stalled.
+
+A new shape, TaskGroups, builds the objects asyncio makes, in asyncio's order.
+One simulated object stands for an object of one role in each of 16 tasks
+that asyncio makes one after another (ADR 0002). A path of 10 objects leads
+from the structure's root to the loop, which holds the ready queue and the
+timers. A parent's step makes each group of 16 tasks with 7 objects: the task,
+its coroutine, two Contexts, its Handle in the ready queue, the Handle's
+TaskStepMethWrapper and the done-callback. When the group first runs, the
+ready queue lets go of its Handle. A group of tasks with children then makes a
+TaskGroup, its list and its set, its children's groups, and 5 objects to wait
+on a Future. A group of leaves makes 9 objects, its timer and the timer's
+arguments among them. The structure holds 55,429 objects, and a larger one
+starts the tree again under the same loop.
+
+A shape can now cut links before a drop: `teardown(size)` gives the pairs, and
+`Build.drop` unlinks them before it lets go of the root. TaskGroups cuts each
+task's links back to its parent and to itself, so a dropped tree leaves no
+cyclic garbage, as on the reference build.
+
+The tree now lives 10,000 kB after it has built, not 8,000. The workers' old
+collection at 132 MB still marks 30,519 real objects of the first tree, and
+their young collection at 134 MB finds 12,796 where the one before found
+30,519. The build churn falls from 1.17 to 1.07 kB a kB of tree, which puts the
+legacy gen 0 collections during a build at 15,488 real objects against the
+workers' 15,260 to 15,600.
+
+## Consequences
+
+async_tree_io_tg's incremental columns on the presets page:
+
+| Series | Before | After |
+|---|---|---|
+| gen 0 examined | 37% | 9% |
+| gen 1 work | 25% | 10% |
+| gen 1 budget | 12% | 3% |
+| gen 1 examined | 4% | 4% |
+
+Its legacy gen 0 examined falls from 3% to 2%, and gen 1 examined from 4% to
+2%. Its legacy gen 1 yield stays at 16%. The workers' young collection at
+134 MB finds 12,796 real objects, and the run's finds none. The other presets
+keep their records.
+
+The fit hangs on the tree's lifetime: below 10,000 kB, gen 0 examined comes
+within about 20%, and at 10,500 or 11,000 kB within 12%.
+
+The tree grows from 52,487 objects to 55,429, and its slider's largest from
+59,300 kB to 62,200. The guide's chapters on the old generation and the work
+budget take the new runs' numbers: 12 sweeps where there were 9, and old
+collections that mark about 1,900 objects each. Without the freed credit, the
+trees with parent pointers now go at 172, 324 and 500 MB, and the sweeps fall
+from 10 to 6.
+
+The playground and the request name the shape "task_groups", and a workload
+source names it `TaskGroups()`.
+
+## Considered Options
+
+- Keep the Hierarchy and fit its lifetime and churn. Each object would still
+  stand for a task and reach its six children, so marking would still pull the
+  young objects 16 times too fast.
+- Chains of tasks in groups of 16, without the ready queue, the timers and the
+  links back. It reached 20% on gen 0 examined.

284.bodyHTML:
Closes #280

xml_etree_parse's incremental young collections found each value's own tree one collection early: at the 25th, 37th and 49th, where the workers' find it at the 25th and 27th, then the 39th and 51st. A probe on the reference build shows why.

What a worker's value does

Step kB
build_xml_tree 359
tostring and write of that tree 1,923
60 parses 21,620
tostring of the last two parsed trees, as bench_parse returns 1,920

A value runs 25,826 kB, where the preset took 25,560. Each tree starts 1,920 kB after the last parse of the value before, where the preset built it as that parse ended. Serialising keeps 66 real objects alive, against the about 1,000 the preset's chains held. The first tree starts at about 5,709 kB, not 5,284.

Two structure parameters (ADR 0027)

  • delay: the kB after the loops start that a repeating structure first falls due.
  • skips_while_busy: the structure skips a rebuild that falls due while another structure builds or waits.

Before, nothing could follow a value's parses within the value, and a parse due during the serialising would have queued in front of the next tree. Both fields default to the old behaviour, and the other presets' digests stay the same, connected_components' among them. Making every structure skip changed async_tree_io_tg's runs, so it stays a field.

The request, the workload source, the editor and the legend carry both fields. Links written before open at the defaults.

The preset

  • Values of 72 slots of 359 kB, 25,848 kB.
  • The parses start 2,410 kB into each value and skip while it serialises, so each value parses 60.
  • The last two parsed trees' serialising follows the 60th parse.
  • The serialising keeps 4 simulated objects alive, and a set-up puts the first tree at 5,708 kB.

Fit

Series Before After
incremental gen 0 examined 8% 1%
incremental gen 0 yield 4% 2%
incremental gen 0 budget 1% 0%
incremental gen 1 budget 1% 0%
legacy gen 0 examined 4% 4%

The young collections that find each tree examine 944, 4,208 and 5,152 real objects, against the workers' 1,130, 4,029 and 5,158, at the same collections. The budget stays within 1% at each collection, and the gen 0 running yield within 4%.

Legacy gen 0 examined stays at 4%: the workers' last two parsed trees live until bench_parse returns, and the run's go two slots after they build. The workers' 39th collection examines 10,343 real objects there, the run's 64. That needs another mechanism, left for later.

@@ -0,0 +1,78 @@
+# A repeating structure can wait into the loops and skip while another builds
+
+xml_etree_parse's young collections examined within 8% of its workers' under
+the incremental collector. The workers' young collections find each value's
+own tree at their 25th and 27th collections, split 1,130 and 4,029 real
+objects, then at their 39th and 51st. The run's found it whole at the 25th,
+37th and 49th, a young collection early each time.
+
+A probe on the reference build logs where each of a worker's values builds its
+tree, serialises it and parses, against the collections around them:
+
+- A value builds its tree, 359 kB, serialises and writes it, 1,923 kB, parses
+  60 times, 21,620 kB, then serialises the last two parsed trees as
+  `bench_parse` returns, 1,920 kB. The workers' values run 25,826 kB, where
+  the preset took 25,560.
+- So each value's tree comes 1,920 kB after the last parse of the value before.
+  The preset built it as the last parse ended.
+- Serialising leaves 66 real objects alive besides the tree. The preset's
+  serialising chains held about 1,000.
+- The first value's tree starts at about 5,709 kB, after what pyperf allocates
+  to start the benchmark. The preset started it as start-up ended, at 5,284.
+
+The workload could not build that order. Every repeating structure first fell
+due as the loops started, so nothing could follow a value's parses within the
+value. A rebuild that fell due while another structure built waited for it, so
+a parse due during the serialising would have come between it and the next
+tree.
+
+A repeating structure now takes two more parameters. Its `delay` is the kB
+after the loops start that it first falls due; each rebuild after that comes
+its interval later. With `skips_while_busy`, it skips a rebuild that falls due
+while another structure builds or waits, where it would otherwise wait and
+build once the other ends. A structure that builds once takes neither. Both
+default to the old behaviour, and the other four presets keep their records.
+
+xml_etree_parse's value takes 72 slots of 359 kB, 25,848 kB. The parsed trees
+first fall due 2,410 kB into the loops and skip while the value serialises,
+so each value parses 60. The serialising of the last two parsed trees falls
+due as the 60th parse's tree ends. The serialising builds 4 simulated objects
+and churn for the rest of its kB. A set-up of chains that go as they build
+fills the 428 kB from start-up's end to the first tree, at 5,708 kB.
+
+## Consequences
+
+xml_etree_parse's columns on the presets page:
+
+| Series | Before | After |
+|---|---|---|

+and 5,152 real objects against the workers' 1,130, 4,029 and 5,158, at the
+same collections. The gen 0 running yield stays within 4% of the workers' at
+each young collection, and the budget within 1% at each collection.

+Under the legacy collector, the gen 0 collections during each value's
+serialising still differ: the workers' last two parsed trees stay alive until
+`bench_parse` returns, and the run's go two slots after they build. The
+workers' 39th collection examines 10,343 real objects there, the run's 64.

+when a structure first falls due and that it skips, and a workload source
+writes them as `delay=` and `skips_while_busy=True`. Links written before
+leave them out and open at the defaults.

+  value's tree would then start 1,920 kB after start-up, where the workers'

+- Make every repeating structure skip while another builds. async_tree_io_tg's
+  runs change.
+- Fit the value's length and the tree's churn alone. The tree still follows the
+  last parse at once, so the young collection that finds it still comes early.

286.bodyHTML:
Closes #279

The workers' gen 1 collection at 264 MB comes 1.1 MB before their second run ends and examines 37,693 real objects. The run's examined 64: the preset dropped all the finishing tasks kept 2 MB before each run ends.

What the probe shows

A probe on the reference build follows each collection window's young objects until they die, under the legacy collector.

  • The tree dies in build order. Its leaves go over about 5 MB and end near 1.5 MB before the run ends. The inner tasks and the finishing go near the end.
  • A sixth of what the finishing tasks allocate outlives the tree: 4,268 of 25,605 real objects in a window still stand at 264 MB.
  • What the run allocates as its tree goes stays to the run's end: 39,390 real objects at the 392 MB collection.
  • The workers' young collections fall back after each run ends, not 2 MB before it, so the old comment goes.

The preset

The finishing tasks now build two structures:

Structure Share Goes
kept 1/6 300 kB before the run ends
finished the rest 2 MB before the run ends, as before

A third structure takes the 600 kB after them and stays until 300 kB before the end. The 300 kB comes from the legacy workers' third run, which ends 225 kB before the preset's. The 600 kB puts the 132nd collection at 35,936. The tree keeps index 6, and the home page's slider still sizes it.

Fit

Mean gaps from the legacy workers' median:

Series Before After
gen 0 examined 3.6% 3.1%
gen 1 examined 6.1% 1.5%
gen 2 examined 7.5% 7.4%
Collection Before After Workers
132nd, gen 1 64 35,936 37,693
193rd, gen 1 217,216 217,216 199,934
133rd, gen 2 28,176 28,208 30,468

The incremental collector's gaps stay the same, though its digest moves. Five of the guide's numbers move, the most 725 to 742. The other presets keep their digests, connected_components' among them.

The incremental workers' young collections at 134, 262 and 390 MB find 12,796, 12,554 and 3,228 real objects, and the run's find none. A tree that goes leaf group by leaf group closed part of that gap but shifted the old collections' marking and worsened the incremental fit, so it stays out. That gap belongs with #263.

sergey-miryanov/gcmon#242.title: Record the trigger's remaining allocation budget with each collection
sergey-miryanov/gcmon#242.author: sergey-miryanov
sergey-miryanov/gcmon#242.bodyHTML:
Problem

A record tells you what a collection did but not how much the program
allocated since the collection before it. pep848-sim
(sergey-miryanov/pep848-sim) plots a worker's collections against its model of
them, and its model counts time in kB allocated. Without that figure, the
plots fall back to the collection's number in the worker.

Counting automatic collections gives a rough clock, threshold0 kB for each,
but gc.collect() resets the budget without one. A worker of
create_gc_cycles makes about 1,000 gc.collect() calls, and on that clock
they all land on a few points.

Context

  • On the PEP 848 reference branch, _PyObject_GC_Link takes each new
    object's size off young.available_memory in the interpreter's GC state,
    and schedules a collection when it drops below 0, clamping it to 0. Every
    collection resets it to threshold0 times the nursery's size unit.
  • So threshold0 kB minus available_memory at a collection's start gives
    the kB the program allocated since the collection before. For an automatic
    collection the clamp loses what the program allocated between the schedule
    and the run, a few eval-breaker checks' worth.
  • CPython's allocator reports no gross bytes allocated, and this is a
    different figure: the trigger's own budget.
  • The branch's gc_generation_stats does not carry available_memory yet,
    so a record cannot report it without a change on CPython's side.

Requirements

  • Each record carries available_memory as it stood when the collection
    started.
  • The CSV extract writes it as a column.

Constraints

  • A trace of a build without the field still loads, and the column comes out
    empty.

Out of scope

  • Any clock gcmon works out itself from the column.
  • Gross bytes allocated, from the allocator or from RSS.

Acceptance criteria

  • A trace of pyperformance on a reference branch that carries the field
    extracts to a CSV whose available_memory column holds a value for every
    record.
  • In that CSV, a create_gc_cycles worker's gc.collect() records show
    values above 0.

sergey-miryanov/gcmon#228.title: Extract a trace's records into a CSV file
sergey-miryanov/gcmon#228.author: sergey-miryanov
sergey-miryanov/gcmon#228.bodyHTML:
Problem

A trace holds every record gcmon read from a pyperformance run, but nothing
in gcmon writes those records out as a table another tool can load. Reading
them takes Perfetto's trace processor and SQL against gcmon's track layout.

pep848-sim needs them as a table (sergey-miryanov/pep848-sim#117). Its
presets model pyperformance benchmarks, and a test holds each preset's
yield, collected over candidates, to its benchmark's, per collector,
generation and kind of collection. The targets come from gcmon traces of
pyperformance on the PEP 848 reference branch, loaded from files that a
fresh trace replaces, so no figure from a trace gets typed into that repo.

Context

Read by SQL from a gcmon trace of pyperformance on the reference branch, 160
workers once the six calibration workers are left out:

Benchmark gen 0 gen 1 gc.collect(), gen 2
create_gc_cycles 0 candidates 0 candidates 22.1%, 20,488 runs
json_loads 0 candidates 0 candidates 26.1%, 10 runs
async_tree_io_tg 0.01% 0.00% 35.2%, 15 runs
connected_components 0.03% 0.00% 97.4%, 25 runs
  • gc.collect() frees most of each benchmark's cyclic garbage. Only
    create_gc_cycles calls it itself; the rest come from pyperf or from the
    interpreter shutting down. pep848-sim takes each worker whole, start-up and
    shutdown included: it models the worker's object graph and how the
    collector processes it, so the table needs no split between a benchmark's
    timed part and the rest.
  • collections, candidates and collected are lifetime totals per
    interpreter and generation. Gaps in collections show lost records, and a
    lost record's counts fold into the next one read.
  • pyperformance takes no external hook the way pyperf's --hook does, so
    gcmon's pyperf hook does not run in its workers and a pyperformance trace
    carries no marks. gcmon-results' prepare already joins each worker to its
    benchmark in _group_pyperformance_workers: it reads the bm_* script, the
    arguments after it, --worker-task and --calibrate-loops from the
    worker's command line, and matches them against pyperformance's results
    JSON. pyperf starts separate workers for each benchmark a script runs, and
    --worker-task says which: bm_xml_etree's workers split 21 to a task
    across tasks 0 to 3, one task per XML benchmark.
  • On the same trace, prepare matched 70 workers to 54 of the results' 119
    benchmarks and listed the rest as missing, async_tree_io_tg among them.
  • Perfetto's Python API launched a v57 trace_processor_shell, which read the
    trace's zstd batches as an empty trace with no error. A v58.2 binary read
    it in full.
  • gcmon-results prepare selects gc.% slice names and extracted no slices
    from the same trace.
  • A trace records neither the build nor the thresholds, and spec 0020, which
    would add both, needs a change on CPython's side. The build does not: gcmon
    and its target run the same CPython version, so gcmon names the build from
    its own interpreter.

Requirements

  • One row per record in the trace, carrying these fields under the names a
    record gives them:

    Field What pep848-sim reads from it
    benchmark which benchmark the record ran in
    the worker's pid and pid epoch which worker a row belongs to
    iid which of the worker's interpreters a row continues
    whether the worker calibrates calibration workers are left out
    ts the order of a worker's records
    generation, auto_collect the kind of collection
    collections, candidates, collected lifetime totals, as read
    heap_size, heap_size_stop how large the heap was around the run
    old_work, survivor_count the incremental collector's budget and survivors, empty on a stock build
    increment_size how far the object graph's links reach in an old collection's increment

  • A record's benchmark is the name pyperformance's results JSON gives the
    benchmark its worker ran.

  • Only the benchmarks named can be kept, so the files stay small enough to
    commit.

  • Beside the table, the run it came from: the build's commit, the collector
    (-X gc=legacy or not), the thresholds, gcmon's and pyperformance's
    versions, the date and the trace's hash. What neither the trace nor
    pyperf's JSON holds can be given on the command line.

Constraints

  • It reads the traces gcmon 0.9.1 writes, zstd batches included.
  • Python's standard csv module reads the table, and a header row names the
    fields: pep848-sim's loader takes no third-party package.
  • The counters stay lifetime totals as read. The reader takes the differences,
    which keeps a lost record's counts in the totals.

Out of scope

  • Running pyperformance again under gcmon: pep848-sim#117 does that.
  • Anything the table feeds, such as yields or plots.
  • A GC run's reason, which records do not carry yet: #229. Once both land,
    the table carries it like any other field.

Acceptance criteria

  • On a gcmon trace of pyperformance, with calibration workers left out, each
    benchmark's rows end with the lifetime totals that SQL reads from the last
    pause spans of that benchmark's workers.
  • On such a trace, xml_etree_parse's rows come from its own workers, apart
    from the other three XML benchmarks', and every async_tree_io_tg worker
    has rows.
  • Keeping one benchmark leaves only its rows.
  • docs/cli.md and docs/formats.md describe the command and the table's
    fields, and CHANGELOG has a line for it.

sergey-miryanov/gcmon#229.title: Carry a GC run's reason on its record
sergey-miryanov/gcmon#229.author: sergey-miryanov
sergey-miryanov/gcmon#229.bodyHTML:
Problem

A record says whether the collector started its GC run on its own
(auto_collect 1) or something else did (auto_collect 0), but not what
that something was. A gc.collect() call and a run the interpreter makes
while it shuts down both read auto_collect 0, and nothing in a trace or a
capture tells them apart.

pep848-sim (sergey-miryanov/pep848-sim#117) splits pyperformance workers' GC
runs by generation and by whether the collector started the run. Among the
auto_collect 0 runs, it needs a benchmark's gc.collect() calls told apart
from the interpreter's own.

Context

  • The reference branch already knows the reason. _PyGC_Collect takes a
    _PyGC_Reason: _Py_GC_REASON_HEAP, _Py_GC_REASON_SHUTDOWN or
    _Py_GC_REASON_MANUAL. The per-run stats keep auto_collect, which says
    only whether the run was asked for as GENERATION_AUTO, and drop the reason.
  • _PyGC_CollectNoFail passes _Py_GC_REASON_SHUTDOWN. finalize_modules in
    Python/pylifecycle.c calls it twice and interpreter_clear in
    Python/pystate.c once more.
  • In a gcmon trace of pyperformance on the reference branch, each worker's
    last auto_collect 0 run, where gcmon read one, holds 99.9% of
    async_tree_io_tg's collected among auto_collect 0 runs, 62.6% of
    xml_etree's four benchmarks', 33.4% of connected_components' and 15.8% of
    json_loads'.

Requirements

  • On a build whose per-run stats carry the reason, every record carries it
    as a field, with a trace's pause span and a capture's record showing it
    under one name.
  • A build whose stats lack it reads as before: the record leaves the field
    out.
  • docs/formats.md names the field and its three values.

Constraints

  • The branch's stats have to carry the reason first, and
    _remote_debugging's GCMonitor has to return it; gcmon cannot derive it
    from what a record holds today.
  • auto_collect stays as it is: pep848-sim reads it whether or not a build
    carries the reason.

Out of scope

  • Writing the field into the CSV table of #228; once both land, the table
    carries it like any other field.
  • The runs a target makes after gcmon's last poll of it. gcmon can be between
    polls when the target exits, so a trace holds the shutdown runs a poll
    happened to reach, and no count of them is reliable.

Acceptance criteria

  • On a build that stores the reason, gcmon run -s on a script whose
    collector runs on its own and that calls gc.collect() yields records
    naming heap for the first and manual for the call, in both a trace and a
    capture.
  • On a stock build, records carry no reason field, as before.
  • CHANGELOG has a line for it.

rhysd/actionlint#711.title: Support the new `$/` self-repository `uses:` syntax
rhysd/actionlint#711.author: tristanbes
rhysd/actionlint#711.bodyHTML:
Hi, and thanks for actionlint — we run it as a required check on our shared workflows repository, and it has caught real mistakes for us.

GitHub announced a new uses: syntax today (2026-07-30) that actionlint doesn't recognise yet:

Reference same-repository actions with self-repository syntax

A uses: value that starts with $/ resolves to your workflow's own repository at the exact commit that is running, with no checkout required.

Per the announcement it works "everywhere the workspace-relative ./ syntax works, including workflow steps, composite action steps, nested composition, and reusable workflow calls". It requires runner 2.336.0 or newer and is currently github.com only.

Current behaviour

With actionlint 1.7.12:

# .github/workflows/example.yml
name: Example
on: workflow_dispatch
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: $/.github/actions/my-action
example.yml:8:15: specifying action "$/.github/actions/my-action" in invalid format because ref is missing. available formats are "{owner}/{repo}@{ref}" or "{owner}/{repo}/{path}@{ref}" [action]

Expected behaviour

$/<path> accepted without a @ref, since the absence of a ref is precisely the point — the action resolves to the commit already running.

Why it matters

The syntax exists to remove a real desynchronisation risk. Referencing an action of the same repository as owner/repo/path@v1 hardcodes a version inside the workflow, so a caller pinning workflow.yml@v1.5.0 still loads the @v1 action, and any push before the tag moves leaves a window where a new workflow runs against an older action.

Workaround in the meantime

For anyone landing here, -ignore scoped to this single message keeps the rest of the linting intact:

actionlint -ignore 'specifying action "\$/.+" in invalid format because ref is missing'

Happy to help test a fix if that's useful. Thanks again for the tool.

For anyone landing here, -ignore scoped to this single message keeps the rest of the linting intact:

actionlint -ignore 'specifying action "$/.+" in invalid format because ref is missing'

Similarly, the paths.<path-glob>.ignore config setting:

paths:
  .github/workflows/**/*.{yaml,yml}:
    ignore:
      - reusable workflow call "\$/.+" at "uses" is not following the format
      - specifying action "\$/.+" in invalid format because ref is missing

Update: Added ignore config for $/ self-reference reusable workflows.

last.author: konard
last.html:
Confirmed with the current stable 1.7.12 Docker distribution at rhysd/actionlint@sha256:b1934ee5f1c509618f2508e6eb47ee0d3520686341fec936f3b79331f9315667 during link-foundation/meta-sovereign#55. Runner 2.338.0 successfully resolves and executes uses: $/.github/actions/npm-cache, while actionlint rejects the same reference as missing a ref.

Minimal reproduction:

name: Self-reference
on: workflow_dispatch
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: $/.github/actions/npm-cache

Run the pinned image against this workflow: the valid reference produces [action] specifying action ... in invalid format because ref is missing.

Our temporary workaround uses paths to ignore only that exact action reference/diagnostic in its two calling workflow files. A separate contract verifies that the referenced action exists. A real bundled-checker rehearsal confirms a different invalid reference and a genuine ShellCheck SC2086 still fail; no global action/shell rule is disabled. The exception has an explicit removal condition when support ships.

Suggested implementation: recognize $/<nonempty-relative-path> as a distinct same-repository reference before remote owner/repo@ref validation, preserve validation of malformed/empty paths, and add action/composite/reusable-workflow cases. The downstream reproducible positive/negative experiment is experiments/issue-54/rehearse-actionlint.py in the linked PR. No duplicate issue opened because this report already tracks the cause.
